1.pericope_label: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, separated unto the gospel

schools.summary: Chrysostom says Moses, having written five books, has nowhere put his own name to them, neither have they who after him put together the history of events after him, no nor yet has Matthew, nor John, nor Mark, nor Luke; but the blessed Paul everywhere in his Epistles sets his own name. Now why was this? Because they were writing to people who were present, and it had been superfluous to show themselves when they were present; but this man sent his writings from afar and in the form of a letter, for which cause also the addition of the name was necessary. But if in the Epistle to the Hebrews he does not do the same, this too is after his own wise judgment: for since they felt prejudiced against him, lest on hearing the name at the outstart they should stop up all admission to his discourse, he subtly won their attention by concealing the name. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says governors and generals superscribe their letters with the designations of their respective dignities, priding themselves thereon and puffed up in fancied greatness by each fresh tide of honour; the holy apostle is content to call himself one born out of due time and the chief of sinners, and to pronounce himself unworthy the apostleship, while yet, for the benefit of such as should receive his epistles, he prefixes to them the appellations which by grace he had obtained, that so, by seeing the honours belonging to the writer, they might the more readily and zealously welcome them. And he begins by Paul, Theodoret says, not as having been so named of old by his parents, but as preferred to it after his call, as was Simon to that of Peter, and the sons of Zebedee to those of Sons of Thunder, Jacob to that of Israel, and Abram to that of Abraham.

Gill says the name of the author of this epistle is Paul, who formerly was called Saul; some think his name was changed upon his own conversion, others upon the conversion of the Roman deputy Sergius Paulus, others that he was so called from the littleness of his stature, but rather it should seem that he had two names, which was usual with the Jews, one by which they went among the Gentiles and another by which they were called in their own land. A servant of Jesus Christ, Gill says, means not a servant of sin, nor of Satan, nor of man, nor of Moses and his law, nor of the traditions of the elders, but of Jesus Christ; and not by creation only, but by redemption and by powerful efficacious grace in conversion, which is no ways contrary to true liberty, nor a disgraceful but a most honourable character, and which chiefly regards him as a minister of the Gospel. Calvin quotes Turrettin that the inscription of the Pauline Epistles is according to the manner of the ancients, both Greeks and Romans, who were wont to prefix their name and to add their good wishes to those they wrote to. With regard to the word Paul, Calvin says the subject is of no such moment as ought to detain us, and nothing can be said which has not been mentioned by other expounders; but those who think that the Apostle attained this name as a trophy for having brought Sergius the proconsul to the faith of Christ are confuted by the testimony of Luke, who shows that he was so called before that time.

Henry says the person who writes the epistle is described as Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, which is his title of honour and one he glories in, not as the Jewish teachers, Rabbi, Rabbi, but a servant, a more immediate attendant, a steward in the house. Called to be an apostle: some think he alludes to his old name Saul, which signifies one called for or enquired after, since Christ sought him to make an apostle of him. He here builds his authority upon his call, Henry notes: he did not run without sending, as the false apostles did, and the Greek reads called an apostle, as if this were the name he would be called by, though he acknowledged himself not meet to be called so. Separated to the gospel of God: the Pharisees had their name from separation, because they separated themselves to the study of the law, and might be called separated unto the law.

Clarke says that St Paul was the author of this epistle, and that it possesses every evidence of authenticity that any work of the kind can possess, or that even the most fastidious scepticism can require, has been most amply proved by Dr Paley in his Horae Paulinae, which compares the epistles bearing his name with the Acts of the Apostles and with one another. Saul, afterwards called Paul, was born in Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, of Jewish parents who possessed the right of Roman citizens, and when young was sent to Jerusalem for his education. Wesley says the introduction is answered by the conclusion in the fifteenth chapter; called to be an apostle means made an apostle by that calling, since while God calls he makes what he calls. As the Judaizing teachers disputed his claim to the apostolical office, Wesley says, it is with great propriety that he asserts it in the very entrance of an epistle wherein their principles are entirely overthrown; and various other proper and important thoughts are suggested in this short introduction, particularly the prophecies concerning the gospel, the descent of Jesus from David, the great doctrines of his Godhead and resurrection, the sending of the gospel to the Gentiles, the privileges of Christians, and the obedience and holiness to which they were obliged in virtue of their profession. Separated means separated by God, not only from the bulk of other men, from other Jews, from other disciples, but even from the rest.

Barnes opens with a preface saying the Epistle to the Romans has usually been regarded as the most difficult portion of the New Testament, and that it is from this cause, probably, as well as from the supposition that its somewhat abstruse discussions could not be made interesting to the young, that so few efforts have been made to introduce it into Sunday Schools and Bible Classes; he adds that in the Sacred Scriptures there is a happy adaptedness to the circumstances of the world, in that so large a portion of the volume can be made interesting to children and youth, being occupied with historical narrative, with parables, with biographies of the holy men of other times and with the life of our blessed Lord. Ellicott says servant is more strictly, here as elsewhere in the New Testament, slave, and yet not wrongly translated servant, because the compulsory and degrading side of service is not put forward, the idea of slavery in the present day having altogether different associations. Of separated he compares especially the command at Antioch to separate Barnabas and Saul, where human instruments, the leaders of the Church there, are employed to carry out the divine will; the reference here is to the historical fact of the selection of St Paul to be an Apostle, whereas in Galatians, where it pleased God who separated him from his mother's womb, it is rather to the more distant act of divine predestination. Unto the gospel of God means singled out and set apart to convey the message of salvation from God to man, the ambiguous genitive seeming to mean the gospel which proceeds from God, of which God is the author. Robertson says To the Romans is the title in the oldest Greek manuscripts, that we do not know whether Paul gave any title at all, and that later manuscripts add other words up to the received text; the Epistle is put first in the manuscripts because it is the most important of Paul's Epistles. Paul is the Roman name, and servant is bond-slave of Jesus Christ, appearing for the first time in the Epistles in the opening sentence, though the phrase is already in Galatians and recurs in Philippians. Called to be an apostle means, in Denney's phrase, an apostle by vocation.

debates: Where the name Paul came from: Theodoret holds it was given after his call, like Simon to Peter and Abram to Abraham; Gill reports the same proposal along with the conversion of Sergius Paulus and the littleness of his stature, and prefers that he simply bore two names as Jews commonly did; Calvin rules out the proconsul by Luke's record, which shows he was so called before that time

Why Paul names himself where the earlier writers did not: Chrysostom answers from the circumstances, that the others wrote to people present while Paul wrote from afar in the form of a letter, and explains the silence of Hebrews as a device to disarm prejudice; Theodoret answers from character, contrasting the self-styling of governors and generals with an apostle who called himself the chief of sinners, and allows the names only for the readers' benefit

How servant should be rendered: Ellicott says the word is more strictly slave, but defends the received rendering because the compulsory and degrading side is not in view and the modern idea of slavery carries different associations, where Robertson keeps bond-slave and Gill and Henry treat the title as one of honour

What the separation refers to: Ellicott distinguishes the historical selection at Antioch from the more distant act of divine predestination in Galatians, while Henry reads it against the Pharisees, who took their very name from separating themselves to the law, and Wesley makes it successive, from other men, other Jews and other disciples
outliers: Chrysostom's explanation of the anonymity of Hebrews, that Paul subtly won their attention by concealing the name
Clarke's appeal to Paley's Horae Paulinae as proof against the most fastidious scepticism
Denney's phrase, quoted by Robertson, that Paul is an apostle by vocation
Gill's catalogue of what Paul is not a servant of, including the traditions of the elders
Henry's contrast between the Jewish teachers' Rabbi, Rabbi and the title of servant
Theodoret's picture of governors puffed up in fancied greatness by each fresh tide of honour
Wesley's sentence that while God calls, he makes what he calls

2.pericope_label: The gospel promised before in the holy scriptures, concerning his Son

schools.summary: Gill says the Gospel is here further commended from its antiquity: it was no novel doctrine, an upstart notion, but what God had conceived in his own breast from eternity; this mystery was hid in him from the beginning of the world and was ordained before the world was, and in time God was pleased to make it known to the sons of men, promising it, speaking of it and declaring it. Of the third verse he says the words are in connection with the gospel of God and express the subject matter of it, the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord; for Christ, as the Son of God, the Saviour of sinners, the only Mediator between God and men, who is Lord both of the dead and living, is the sum and substance of the Gospel. He is here described by his relation to God, his Son, of the same nature with him, equal to him and distinct from him; and by his usual names, Jesus Christ, the one signifying a Saviour and the other anointed, and both showing that he was anointed of God to be the Saviour. Calvin says that, as the suspicion of being new subtracts much from the authority of a doctrine, Paul confirms the faith of the gospel by antiquity, as though he said, Christ came not on the earth unexpectedly, nor did he introduce a doctrine of a new kind and not heard of before, inasmuch as he, and his gospel too, had been promised and expected from the beginning of the world. But as antiquity is often fabulous, Calvin says, he brings witnesses, and those approved, even the Prophets of God, that he might remove every suspicion; and he in the third place adds that their testimonies were duly recorded, that is, in the Holy Scriptures. Of the Son he says this is a remarkable passage, by which we are taught that the whole gospel is included in Christ, so that if any removes one step from Christ, he withdraws himself from the gospel; for since he is the living and express image of the Father, it is no wonder that he alone is set before us as one to whom our whole faith is to be directed and in whom it is to centre. It is then a definition of the gospel, Calvin says, by which Paul expresses what is summarily comprehended in it.

Clarke says that both in the law and in the prophets God showed his purpose to introduce into the world a more perfect and glorious state of things, which state was to take place by and under the influence of the Messiah, who should bring life and immortality to light by his Gospel. Of the Son he says the Gospel relates everything concerning the conception, birth, preaching, miracles, passion, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ, who was of the seed-royal, being, as far as his humanity was considered, the son of David, and then the only rightful heir to the Israelitish throne. Wesley says the promise was made of old time, frequently and solemnly, and that the promise and the accomplishment confirm each other, citing Deuteronomy, Isaiah and Jeremiah. Of the seed of David according to the flesh means with regard to his human nature, Wesley says: both the natures of our Saviour are here mentioned, but the human is mentioned first, because the divine was not manifested in its full evidence till after his resurrection.

Barnes says the epistle has been with great uniformity attributed to the apostle Paul and received as part of the sacred canon, never having been called in question in the church as a genuine and inspired book except by three of the ancient sects deemed heretical, the Ebionites, the Encratites and the Cerinthians, who did not deny that Paul wrote it but rejected it because they could not make its doctrines harmonise with their views of other parts of the Scriptures, so that their rejection does not militate against its genuineness. Of the third verse he says it is connected with the first, with the word gospel: the gospel of God concerning his Son, since the design of the gospel was to make a communication relative to his Son Jesus Christ, and this is the whole of it, there being no good news to man respecting salvation except that which comes by Jesus Christ. The word translated was made, Barnes says, means usually to be or to become, but it is used in the sense of being born, as where God sent forth his Son made of a woman, that is born of a woman, and where it is said that before Abraham was, I am; and in this sense it seems to be used here. Ellicott says the clause is more correctly rendered, which he promised before by his prophets in holy writ, and that there is a nicety of meaning expressed by the absence of the article before this last phrase, a slight stress being thus thrown upon the epithet holy: it is not merely in certain books which go by the name of holy scriptures, but in certain writings the character of which is holy, and they are holy as containing the promises referred to in the text and others like them. It will thus be seen, he adds, how even this faint shade of meaning works into the general argument. Robertson says he promised afore is a first aorist middle, that the preposition means through or by means of, by intermediate agency, and that in the holy scriptures has no article yet is definite, being perhaps the earliest use of the phrase, as Sanday and Headlam suggest; Paul definitely finds God's gospel in the Holy Scriptures. Concerning his Son is just as Jesus found himself in the Old Testament, and the deity of Christ is here stated, while according to the flesh sets his real humanity alongside of his real deity.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that he promised afore by his prophets in the holy Scriptures, for the Old Testament is full of predictions concerning the Lord. Nor does he call them holy for no reason, Theodoret says, but firstly to show that he acknowledged their inspiration, and secondly as excluding all other writings, for the inspired book alone contains all things we can need. And he adds the nature of the promise, concerning his Son, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh: by all the prophets, says he, God has prophesied of the things relating to his Son, who, in his nature begotten of him before all eternity, yet made himself of the seed of David.

debates: Why the scriptures are called holy: Ellicott finds the point in the missing article, which throws stress on the epithet, so that the writings are holy in character and not merely so called; Robertson notes the same absence and follows Sanday and Headlam in calling it perhaps the earliest use of the phrase; Theodoret makes it an argument about the canon, that the word acknowledges inspiration and excludes all other writings

What the word rendered was made means: Barnes says it usually means to be or to become but is here used in the sense of being born, comparing made of a woman and before Abraham was, where Robertson simply takes the clause as stating the real humanity alongside the real deity

Why the human nature is named first: Wesley says it is because the divine was not manifested in its full evidence till after the resurrection, where Theodoret puts both in one clause, the Son begotten before all eternity yet making himself of David's seed

How much of the gospel is Christ: Calvin says the whole gospel is included in him, so that whoever removes one step from Christ withdraws from the gospel, and calls the verse a definition of the gospel; Barnes states it negatively, that there is no good news to man except that which comes by Jesus Christ; Clarke instead widens the content to the whole course of the incarnate life
outliers: Calvin's three-step argument from antiquity, approved witnesses, and duly recorded testimony
Clarke's summary of the gospel as relating everything from the conception to the ascension
Ellicott's remark that even this faint shade of meaning works into the general argument
Gill's description of the gospel as what God had conceived in his own breast from eternity
Robertson's conclusion that Paul definitely finds God's gospel in the Holy Scriptures
Theodoret's canon argument, that the inspired book alone contains all things we can need
Wesley's compression of the promise into three words, of old time, frequently, solemnly

4.pericope_label: Declared Son of God by the resurrection, and grace and apostleship

schools.summary: Gill says that Christ is declared to be the Son of God, not made, as he is said to be in the verse before, when his incarnation is spoken of; nor did he begin to be the Son of God when he was made of the seed of David, but he, the Son of God, who existed as such from everlasting, was manifested in the flesh, or human nature, and this his divine sonship and proper deity are declared and made evident. Of grace and apostleship Gill says the words mean that we have received them either by the Holy Spirit, from whom all grace and gifts come, qualifying for the discharge of any office, or by the Lord Jesus Christ, who is full of grace and truth and has received gifts for men and gives them to fit them for whatever service he calls them to. By grace and apostleship, Gill says, may be meant either one and the same thing, the favour and honour of being the apostles of Christ, or different things, and the one in order to the other; grace may design special saving grace in calling, justification, pardon, adoption and sanctification. Calvin says that some of the ancients, such as Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril and others, have given to the verb rendered declared the meaning of proved, demonstrated or exhibited; but it is said that the word has not this meaning in the New Testament, and that it means limited, determined, decreed, constituted, being found besides here only in Luke, Acts and Hebrews. The word, if adopted here, would amount to the same thing, Calvin says, that is, that Christ was visibly determined or constituted the Son of God. Of the fifth verse he says that, having completed his definition of the gospel, which he introduced for the recommendation of his office, Paul now returns to speak of his own call, and it was a great point that this should be proved to the Romans. By mentioning grace and apostleship apart, Calvin says, he adopts a form of speech, hypallage, a figure in grammar by which a noun or an adjective is put in a form or in a case different from that in which it ought grammatically to be; which must be understood as meaning gratuitous apostleship, or the favour of the apostleship, by which he means that it was wholly through divine favour, not through his own worth.

Clarke says the word we render declared comes from a verb meaning to bound, define, determine or limit, and hence our word horizon, the line that determines the farthest visible part of the earth in reference to the heavens; in this place the word signifies such a manifest and complete exhibition of the subject as to render it indubitable. The resurrection of Christ from the dead, he says, was such a manifest proof of our Lord's innocence, the truth of his doctrine, and the fulfilment of all that the prophets had spoken. Of grace and apostleship he says they are the peculiar influence and the essential qualifications which such an office requires: without the grace, favour and peculiar help of God he could not have been an apostle, having had an extraordinary conversion and an extraordinary call to preach the Gospel; and probably grace and apostleship mean the same as the grace of the apostleship, that is, the apostolical office, for so the word grace means in several other places of Paul. Wesley says the phrase is, powerfully declared to be the Son of God, according to the Spirit of Holiness, that is, according to his divine nature, by the resurrection from the dead; for this is both the fountain and the object of our faith, and the preaching of the apostles was the consequence of Christ's resurrection. By whom we have received, Wesley says, means I and the other apostles; grace and apostleship mean the favour to be an apostle and the qualifications for it; for obedience to the faith in all nations means that all nations may embrace the faith of Christ; and for his name means for his sake, out of regard to him.

Barnes says the word translated declared to be means properly to bound, to fix limits to, as to a field, to determine its proper limits or boundaries, to define, as where it is said that God hath determined the bounds of their habitation; hence it means to determine, constitute, ordain, decree. He notes the versions: the ancient Syriac has, and he was known to be the Son of God by might and by the Holy Spirit, who rose from the house of the dead; the Latin Vulgate, who was predestinated the Son of God; the Arabic, the Son of God destined by power peculiar to the Holy Spirit. Of the fifth verse he says the apostle here returns to the subject of the salutation and states his authority to address them, an authority derived from the Lord Jesus and not from man, a fact on which Paul not infrequently insisted, as where he says he neither received it of man neither was taught it but by revelation of Jesus Christ; and the plural we is probably put for the singular, as was usual for those clothed with office. Ellicott says with power means in a transcendent and superhuman manner, and that according to the spirit of holiness stands in antithesis to according to the flesh, and therefore comes where we should expect the words, in his divine nature; and yet there is a difference, the precise shade of which is not easy to define. What are we to understand by the spirit of holiness? Are we to regard it as simply convertible with Holy Spirit? Not quite. Or are we to look upon it as corresponding to the flesh, as spirit and flesh correspond in man? Again, not quite, or not merely, Ellicott says, for the spirit of Christ is human, Christ having taken upon him our nature. Of the fifth verse he says that through Christ the Son, Paul had received his own special endowment and commission to bring over the Gentiles into that state of loyal and dutiful submission which has its root in faith, all which would tend to the glory of his name. We have received: the Apostle means himself alone, but the plural is used, as frequently in Greek, with delicate tact, so as to avoid an appearance of egotism or assumption. Grace is here divine favour manifested in various ways, but especially in his conversion; and Ellicott notes that St Augustine observes grace to be common to the Apostle with all believers, while the apostleship is his own. Robertson says the participle rendered who was declared is a first aorist passive: he was the Son of God in his preincarnate state and still so after his Incarnation, being of the seed of David, but it was the resurrection of the dead, the general resurrection implied by that of Christ, that definitely marked Jesus off as God's Son, because of his claims about himself as God's Son and his prophecy that he would rise on the third day; and this event gave God's seal with power. Unto obedience of faith, he adds, is a subjective genitive, the obedience which springs from faith, the act of assent or surrender.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus recites the fourth verse whole, that he was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord. Of the fifth he says that by him we have received grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations, for his name; for he himself sent us forth as teachers, committing to us the salvation of all nations, and giving grace suitable to that preaching, that they who hear it may hearken unto us and believe the word.

debates: What the word rendered declared means: Calvin reports that Origen, Chrysostom and Cyril gave it the sense of proved or demonstrated, while others hold it means limited or determined, and judges that either would come to the same thing; Barnes finds the versions equally divided, the Syriac reading known, the Vulgate predestinated and the Arabic destined; Clarke takes it of an exhibition so complete as to be indubitable

What the spirit of holiness is: Ellicott raises and refuses both the obvious identifications, that the phrase is simply convertible with Holy Spirit and that it corresponds to the flesh as spirit does in man, saying not quite to each, since the spirit of Christ is human; Wesley makes the identification Ellicott declines, glossing it as his divine nature

Whether grace and apostleship are one thing or two: Gill leaves the alternative open, Clarke thinks them one and takes the phrase for the apostolical office, Calvin names the construction a hypallage and reads it as gratuitous apostleship, and Ellicott keeps them distinct on Augustine's ground that grace is common to all believers while the apostleship is Paul's own

When the sonship was declared: Gill and Robertson agree that Christ did not begin to be Son at the incarnation but was manifested in the flesh, Robertson dating the declaration to the resurrection because of Christ's own claims and his prophecy of the third day, where Wesley makes the resurrection both the fountain and the object of faith
outliers: Augustine's distinction, quoted by Ellicott, that grace is common to the Apostle with all believers while the apostleship is his own
Barnes's collation of the Syriac, Vulgate and Arabic readings of the word declared
Calvin's naming of the construction as a hypallage, a noun put in a case other than the one it ought to have
Clarke's derivation of horizon from the same root as the word rendered declared
Ellicott's note that the plural is used with delicate tact, to avoid an appearance of egotism
Robertson's account of obedience of faith as a subjective genitive, the obedience which springs from faith
Theodoret's summary that Christ committed to the apostles the salvation of all nations and gave grace suitable to that preaching

6.pericope_label: Among whom are ye also, called of Jesus Christ: the address and salutation

schools.summary: Gill says the Romans, though they were the chief, were among the nations of the world to whom the apostles were sent; and since Paul was called to be an apostle, and had grace and apostleship, and particularly the apostleship of the uncircumcision, he was more especially an apostle to them, and as such was to be regarded by them. This, Gill says, seems to point out what they were originally: they were among all nations which lay in darkness, and were without Christ and hope and God in the world. The inscription, he adds, is not to the Roman emperor, nor to the Roman senate, nor to all the inhabitants in Rome, but to all the saints there, whether rich or poor, bond or free, male or female, Jew or Gentile, without any distinction, being all one in Christ Jesus. Calvin says that by this happy arrangement Paul sets forth what there is in us worthy of commendation: first the Lord through his own kindness made us the objects of his favour and love, then he has called us, and thirdly he has called us to holiness; but this high honour only then exists when we are not wanting to our call. Paul, Calvin says, does by no means ascribe the praise of our salvation to ourselves, but derives it altogether from the fountain of God's free and paternal love towards us; for he makes this the first thing, that God loves us, and what is the cause of his love except his own goodness alone? On this depends our calling, by which in his own time he seals his adoption to those whom he had before freely chosen. None rightly connect themselves with the number of the faithful, Calvin says, except they feel assured that the Lord is gracious, however unworthy and wretched sinners they may be, and except they be stimulated by his goodness and aspire to holiness. Nothing is more desirable than to have God propitious to us, and then to have prosperity and success in all things flowing from him; for however things may seem to smile on us, if God be angry, even blessing itself is turned to a curse. Calvin quotes Turrettin, that the ancient Greeks and Romans wished to those to whom they wrote health, joy and happiness, but Paul prays for far higher blessings, the grace of God, the fountain of all good things, and peace, in which the Hebrews included all blessings. There are those, he says, who prefer to regard the word peace as signifying quietness of conscience, and that this meaning belongs to it sometimes he does not deny; but since it is certain that the Apostle wished to give a summary of God's blessings, the former meaning is much the most suitable. Nor must we omit to notice, Calvin says, that he prays at the same time to the Lord Jesus Christ for these blessings; worthily is this honour rendered to him, who is not only the administrator and dispenser of his Father's bounty to us, but also works all things in connection with him.

Barnes says that among whom means among the Gentiles who had become obedient to the Christian faith, and that this proves the church at Rome was made up, partly at least if not mainly, of Gentiles or pagans, as is fully proved in the sixteenth chapter by the names of the persons whom Paul salutes. The word called, he says, denotes not merely an external invitation to a privilege, but also the internal or effectual call which secures conformity to the will of him who calls, and is thus synonymous with the name Christians or believers. Called to be saints means so called, or influenced by God who had called them, as to become saints; the word saints means those who are holy, those devoted or consecrated to God, and the radical idea of the word is that which is separated from a common to a sacred use, answering to the Hebrew word, applied to the temple, to the sacrifices, to the utensils about the temple, to the garments of the priests and to the priests themselves, and to the Jews as a people separated from other nations. Grace, Barnes says, properly means favour, and he lists from Schleusner the many senses it bears in the New Testament; in these salutations it seems to include all those blessings applicable to Christians in common, and is to be understood as connected with a word implying invocation, I pray that grace may be conferred on you. Peace is the state of freedom from war, and as war conveys the idea of discord and numberless calamities, peace conveys the idea of concord, safety and prosperity; the word is also used in contrast with that state of agitation and conflict which a sinner has with his conscience and with God, the sinner being like the troubled sea which cannot rest. A prayer for peace, therefore, is not a mere formal salutation but has special reference to those spiritual blessings which result from reconciliation with God. From connecting the Lord Jesus with the Father in this place, Barnes says, we may see that the apostle regarded him as the source of grace and peace as really as he did the Father, that he introduced them in the same connexion, that if the mention of the Father implies a prayer or an act of worship the mention of the Lord Jesus implies the same, and that all this shows his mind was familiarised to the idea that Christ was Divine; no man would introduce his name in such connections if he did not believe that he was equal with God, and it is from this incidental and unstudied manner of expression that we have one of the most striking proofs of the manner in which the sacred writers regarded him. These seven verses, Barnes adds, are one sentence, and a striking instance of the manner of Paul: at the mention of some single words his mind seems to catch fire, and to burn and blaze with signal intensity; he leaves the immediate subject before him and advances some vast thought that awes us, and then returns to his subject. Ellicott says it is perhaps best not to put a comma at also: among these Gentile churches, to which Paul is specially commissioned, the Romans too are called to the same obedience of faith, and therefore he has the more right to address them; and called of Jesus Christ means not called by Jesus Christ but called and so belonging to Jesus Christ, your Master's own elect ones, as the Septuagint calls the guests of Adonijah the called of Adonijah. Ellicott observes that one manuscript of some importance, the Codex Boernerianus, omits the words in Rome, and that the same manuscript with some others alters beloved of God to in the love of God, thus substituting for the special address to the Romans a general address to all who are in the love of God; traces of a similar reading appear to be found in Origen and the Ambrosian Hilary; the same manuscript also omits at Rome in the fifteenth verse, while at the end of the epistle it interposes a blank space. These peculiarities, he says, give some support to the theory that the Epistle to the Romans was circulated, most probably with the sanction of the Apostle himself, in the form of a general treatise with the personal matter eliminated. Beloved of God means reconciled to God through the death of his Son, and called to be saints means consecrated or set apart by his own special summons, brought within the sphere and range of the holy life. These epithets, Ellicott says, high-sounding as they are, if applied by a modern writer to a modern church would seem to be indiscriminating or conventional, but as coming from St Paul they have not yet lost their freshness and reality; they correspond to no actual condition of things, but to that ideal condition in which all Christians, by the mere fact of their being Christians, are supposed to be, and the Apostle will not let them forget this, but holds it up before them as a mirror to convict them if they are unfaithful. Grace and peace nearly correspond to two ordinary forms of Jewish salutation, the first of which has also something of a counterpart among the Greeks and Romans, but the Apostle has given them a heightened and deepened Christian signification: grace is the peculiar state of favour with God and Christ into which the sincere Christian is admitted, and peace is the state of mind resulting from the sense of that favour. Robertson says that called to be Jesus Christ's is a predicate genitive after the verbal adjective, though it is possible to consider it the ablative case, called of or from Jesus Christ. Of the words in Rome he says one late uncial of the tenth century and a cursive omit them here, and one or two other late manuscripts omit in Rome in the fifteenth verse; this possibly proves the epistle was circulated as a circular to a limited extent, but the evidence is late and slight and by no means shows that this was the case in the first century, and it is not comparable with the absence of in Ephesus from the two oldest and best manuscripts at Ephesians 1:1. Beloved of God is an ablative after the verbal adjective. Of the salutation Robertson quotes Sanday and Headlam, that St Paul, if not formally enunciating a doctrine of the Divinity of Christ, held a view which cannot really be distinguished from it, and says Paul's theology is clearly seen in the terms used in these seven verses.

Clarke says ye Romans are all invited to believe in Christ Jesus for the salvation of your souls, and to you, with the rest, his apostolical mission extends; this appears to be the most obvious sense of the word called in this place, for to be called by the Gospel is to be invited to believe in Christ Jesus and become his disciples, though the word sometimes means constituted or made, as in the first verse. Called to be saints means invited to become holy persons by believing the Gospel and receiving the gifts of the Holy Ghost; or the word may here have the meaning of made or constituted saints, for they had already received the Gospel grace and were formed into a Christian Church. Grace, Clarke says, means may you be partakers of the Divine favour, the source whence every blessing is derived; and he thinks it necessary once for all to give the several acceptations of this word in the sacred writings, distinguishing twelve: general favour or benevolence, especially that favour which is powerful and active; the blessing which such favour dispenses; the whole of the Christian religion, as where grace and truth are opposed to the law given by Moses; all the blessings and benefits Christ has purchased; the apostolic and ministerial office, as in the fifth verse of this chapter; a gift, salary or money collected for the poor; thanks or thanksgiving; remuneration, wages or reward; whatever is the means of procuring the favour of another; joy, pleasure and gratification; the performance of an act pleasing to others; and suavity, kindness or gentle demeanour, as where the people wondered at the gracious words. He notes that the Graces were a deity among the ancients, the three being called mild persuasion, dignity, and liberality and joyfulness, and that they were always painted naked, to show that all benefits should be gratuitous, this being essential to the nature of a gift. Peace, Clarke says, is the same as the Hebrew shalom, generally signifying all kinds of blessing but especially harmony and unity and the bond of such unity; the most probable derivation of the Greek word is from a verb meaning I bind and the word for one, because peace unites and binds those who were by discord before disunited. He distinguishes nine senses of it: peace public or private, implying reconciliation and friendship; regularity or good order; the labour or study of preserving peace and concord; the author or procurer of peace, as where Christ is our peace; the Gospel and its blessings; all kinds of mental and corporeal happiness; good wishes and affectionate prayers, as when the disciples were to salute a house; praise, as in peace in heaven and glory in the highest; and benignity or favour, as in being justified by faith we have peace with God. Wesley says that among whom means the nations brought to the obedience of faith, and that in saying ye also St Paul gives them no preeminence above others. Most of those at Rome, Wesley says, were heathens by birth, though with Jews mixed among them; they were scattered up and down in that large city and not yet reduced into the form of a church, only some had begun to meet in the house of Aquila and Priscilla. Beloved of God means that from his free love, not from any merit of yours, you were called by his word and his Spirit to believe in him, and now through faith are holy as he is holy. Grace is the peculiar favour of God, and peace all manner of blessings, temporal, spiritual and eternal; this is both a Christian salutation and an apostolic benediction. Wesley notes that the apostles usually say God the Father or God our Father, and do not often use the word Lord of him as it implies the proper name of God; in the Old Testament the holy men generally said the Lord our God, for they were then as it were servants, whereas now they are sons, and sons so well know their father that they need not frequently mention his proper name. It is one and the same peace, and one and the same grace, which is from God and from Jesus Christ; our trust and prayer fix on God as he is the Father of Christ, and on Christ as he presents us to the Father.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that of these nations, whose husbandry is thus entrusted to Paul, the Romans are part; for think not, he says, that I am appropriating what belongs to another, or seizing on fields allotted to some one else, for the Lord hath constituted me the minister of all the Gentiles.

debates: Whether the words in Rome belong to the text: Ellicott takes the omission in the Codex Boernerianus, together with its reading in the love of God, its second omission at the fifteenth verse and traces in Origen and the Ambrosian Hilary, as some support for the epistle having circulated as a general treatise with the personal matter removed; Robertson grants the same manuscript facts but calls the evidence late and slight, by no means showing this was so in the first century, and not comparable with the absence of in Ephesus from the two best manuscripts

What called imports: Barnes takes it of the internal or effectual call which secures conformity to the will of him who calls, and treats it as synonymous with believers; Clarke takes the most obvious sense to be invitation, to be called by the Gospel being to be invited to believe, and allows the sense constituted only as an alternative

Whose the called are: Ellicott insists called of Jesus Christ means not called by him but called and so belonging to him, your Master's own elect ones; Robertson reads the genitive as predicate but allows the ablative, called of or from Jesus Christ

What peace means in the salutation: Calvin knows the reading that makes it quietness of conscience and refuses it here, since Paul meant a summary of all God's blessings; Ellicott makes it precisely the state of mind resulting from the sense of God's favour
outliers: Barnes's remark that at the mention of some single words the mind of Paul seems to catch fire, and to burn and blaze with signal intensity, before returning to his subject
Clarke's twelve acceptations of the word grace and nine of the word peace, given once for all for the sacred writings
Clarke's note that the three Graces were always painted naked, to show that all benefits should be gratuitous, this being essential to the nature of a gift
Ellicott's judgement that the epithets correspond to no actual condition of things but to an ideal one, held up as a mirror to convict the readers if they are unfaithful
Robertson's citation of Sanday and Headlam, that Paul held a view of Christ which cannot really be distinguished from a doctrine of his Divinity
Wesley's report that the Roman believers were not yet reduced into the form of a church, only some having begun to meet in the house of Aquila and Priscilla

8.pericope_label: Thanksgiving for a faith spoken of in all the world, and the oath of his constant prayer

schools.summary: Gill says that after the inscription and salutation follows a thanksgiving, which begins the epistle; it is usual with the apostle in all his epistles to make requests for the churches with thanksgivings for mercies, his view being to glorify God, to testify his affection to the saints, and to show that all they had must be referred to the grace of God. The object of thanksgiving is God, not merely as a creator and preserver but as a Father, the Father of Christ and our Father in Christ; and the apostle styles him my God, which distinguishes him from all others, points out his particular interest in him, expresses his knowledge of him and faith in him, and demonstrates that what he did now he did in faith. The person through whom thanks are given is Jesus Christ, for there is no coming to God but through Christ, nor is any sacrifice either of prayer or praise acceptable without him. Of the ninth verse Gill says the words are an appeal to God and carry in them the nature and form of an oath; the reason of the apostle's using it was that he was personally unknown to the Romans, and they to him, and so might doubt of his affectionate regard, and this was a case known only to God and himself. The object of his oath is not himself, nor anything that belonged to him, nor any creature in heaven or on earth, but God, who in a solemn oath is only to be appealed to and sworn by; and he describes him as the God whom he served, to distinguish him from all false gods, and to show that he who takes an oath should be one that fears and serves the Lord. Calvin says the beginning is altogether adapted to the occasion, as Paul seasonably prepares them for receiving instruction by reasons connected with himself as well as with them: what he states respecting them is the celebrity of their faith, for he intimates that they, being honoured with the public approbation of the churches, could not reject an Apostle of the Lord without disappointing the good opinion entertained of them by all. With regard to himself, he disposes them to a teachable spirit by testifying his love towards them, and there is nothing more effectual in gaining credit to an adviser than the impression that he is cordially anxious to consult our wellbeing. Calvin remarks that in commending their faith Paul implies that it had been received from God, for thanksgiving is an acknowledgment of a benefit, and he who gives thanks to God for faith confesses that it comes from him; and since the Apostle ever begins his congratulations with thanksgiving, we are reminded that all our blessings are God's free gifts. He calls him my God, which is the faithful's special privilege, and on them alone God bestows this honour; there is implied a mutual relationship, as in the promise that he will be to them a God and they shall be to him a people, and so Hezekiah called God the God of Isaiah when he desired the testimony of a true and faithful prophet, and he is called in an especial manner the God of Daniel. The eulogy of faithful men, Calvin says, was to Paul equal to that of the whole world with regard to the faith of the Romans, for the unbelieving, who deemed it detestable, could not have given an impartial or correct testimony respecting it; we then understand that it was by the mouths of the faithful that the faith of the Romans was proclaimed through the whole world, and that they alone were able to judge rightly of it; that this small and despised handful of men were unknown as to their character to the ungodly, even at Rome, was a circumstance he regarded as nothing, for Paul made no account of their judgment. On the ninth verse Calvin says Paul proves his love by its effects, for had he not greatly loved them he would not have so anxiously commended them to the Lord; and as he knew it necessary for establishing confidence in his preaching that the Romans should be fully persuaded of his sincerity, he added an oath, a needful remedy whenever a declaration which ought to be received as true vacillates through uncertainty. Since an oath is nothing else but an appeal to God as to the truth of what we declare, Calvin says, most foolish is it to deny that the Apostle used here an oath; he did not notwithstanding transgress the prohibition of Christ, and it hence appears that it was not Christ's design, as the superstitious Anabaptists dream, to abolish oaths altogether, but on the contrary to call attention to the due observance of the law, and the law, allowing an oath, only condemns perjury and needless swearing. If we would use an oath aright, let us imitate the seriousness and reverent manner exhibited by the Apostles, knowing that God is so called as a witness that he is also appealed to as an avenger in case we deceive. The passage in Matthew has been often wholly misunderstood, Calvin says: that oaths in common conversation are alone prohibited is quite evident, for in solemn oaths there was no swearing by heaven, or by God's throne, or by the earth, or by Jerusalem, or by the head; such forms were only used in conversation, and these kinds of swearing are alone condemned by our Saviour. Paul here speaks of his own piety in order to gain credit, for those in whom the fear of God prevails will dread to swear falsely; and he sets his own spirit in opposition to the outward mask of religion, testifying that he served God from the heart. It may be that he alluded to the ancient ceremonies, in which alone the Jews thought the worship of God consisted, intimating that though he retained not the observance of these he was yet a sincere worshipper. Calvin adds that Paul gives proof of this by his ministry, for it was the fullest evidence that he was devoted to God's glory when he denied himself and hesitated not to undergo reproach, poverty, hatred and even the peril of death in advancing the kingdom of God; and it ought to add no little encouragement to the ministers of the gospel to hear that in preaching it they render an acceptable and valuable service to God. Of the constant prayer he says Paul speaks not of every kind of calling on God, but of those prayers to which the saints, being at liberty and laying aside all cares, apply their whole attention, as our Lord himself sought retirement for this purpose; he might have often expressed suddenly this or that wish when the Romans did not come into his mind, but whenever he had previously intended and, as it were, prepared himself to offer up prayers to God, among others he remembered them.

Matthew Henry says it is good to begin every thing with blessing God, to make that the alpha and omega of every song; and my God Paul speaks with delight and triumph, for in all our thanksgivings it is good to eye God as our God, which makes every mercy sweet when we can say of God that he is ours in covenant. All our duties and performances are pleasing to God only through Jesus Christ, praises as well as prayers. We must express our love to our friends, Henry says, not only by praying for them but by praising God for them, and God must have the glory of all the comfort we have in our friends, for every creature is that to us, and no more, which God makes it to be. Many of these Romans Paul had no personal acquaintance with, and yet he could heartily rejoice in their gifts and graces, and his true catholic love extends to them all, not only to those who were his helpers in Christ. That their faith is spoken of Paul mentions not to make them proud but to quicken them to answer the general character people gave of them; the greater reputation a man hath for religion, the more careful he should be to preserve it, because a little folly spoils him that is in reputation. Throughout the whole world means the Roman empire, into which the Roman Christians, upon Claudius's edict to banish all the Jews from Rome, were scattered abroad, but had now returned and, it seems, left a very good report behind them wherever they had been, in all the churches; there was this good effect of their sufferings, that if they had not been persecuted they had not been famous. It is a desirable thing, Henry says, to be famous for faith; and the faith of the Roman Christians came to be thus talked of not only because it was excelling in itself but because it was eminent and observable in its circumstances, Rome being a city upon a hill where every one took notice of what was done. The church of Rome was then a flourishing church, he adds, but since that time how is the gold become dim, how is the most fine gold changed; she was then espoused a chaste virgin to Christ and excelled in beauty, but she has since degenerated, dealt treacherously, and embraced the bosom of a stranger, so that, as that good old book the Practice of Piety makes appear in no less than twenty-six instances, even the epistle to the Romans is now an epistle against the Romans. Of the ninth verse Henry says that though a famous flourishing church they had need to be prayed for, for they had not yet attained; one of the greatest kindnesses we can do our friends, and sometimes the only kindness in the power of our hands, is by prayer to recommend them to the loving-kindness of God. From Paul's example we may learn constancy in prayer, always without ceasing, for he did himself observe the rules he gave to others; not that Paul did nothing else but pray, but he kept up stated times for the solemn performance of that duty, very frequent and observed without fail. We may learn charity in prayer also, for though he had no particular acquaintance with them he made express mention of them; it is not unfit sometimes to be express in our prayers for particular churches and places, not to inform God but to affect ourselves, and we are likely to have the most comfort in those friends that we pray most for. Concerning this, Henry says, he makes a solemn appeal to the searcher of hearts, for God is my witness; it was in a weighty matter, and in a thing known only to God and his own heart, that he used this asseveration, and it is very comfortable to be able to call God to witness to our sincerity and constancy in the discharge of a duty. God is particularly a witness to our secret prayers, the matter of them and the manner of the performance. Those that serve God with their spirits may with a humble confidence appeal to him; hypocrites who rest in bodily exercise cannot.

Barnes says that first means in the first place, not in point of importance but before speaking of other things, or before proceeding to the main design of the epistle; and that the expression of thanks to God for his mercy to them was fitted to conciliate their feelings and prepare them for the truths he was about to communicate. It is proper to give thanks to God for his mercies to others as well as ourselves, Barnes says, since we are members of one great family. Of through Jesus Christ he says the duty of presenting our thanks to God through Christ is often enjoined in the New Testament, Christ being the Mediator or the medium by which we are to present our prayers and also our thanksgivings; we are not to approach God directly but through a mediator at all times, and it is no less proper to present thanks in his name than prayer. For you all, Barnes says, is one evidence that the church was then remarkably pure, and how few churches have there been of whom a similar commendation could be expressed. Faith is put here for the whole of religion and means the same as piety, being one of the principal things of religion and one of its first requirements, and hence it signifies religion itself; the readiness with which the Romans had embraced the gospel and the firmness with which they adhered to it was so remarkable that it was known and celebrated everywhere. They were in the capital of the Roman empire, in a city remarkable for its wickedness and whose influence extended everywhere; the religious or irreligious influence of a great city will be felt far and wide, and this is one reason why the apostles preached the gospel so much in such places. The term world, Barnes says, is often limited in the Scriptures, and here it denotes those parts of the Roman empire where the Christian church was established. Of the ninth verse he says the reason of this strong appeal to God is to show the Romans the deep interest he felt in their welfare, manifested in his prayers and in his earnest desires to see them; whom I serve denotes that he was devoted to God, obeyed him and had given himself to do his will in making known his gospel; with my spirit means in my heart, not an external service merely but internal, real and sincere. Without ceasing means constantly, always, without intermission; it was not only once but repeatedly, and had been the burden of his prayers. I make mention means I call you to remembrance and present your case before God, which evinces a remarkable interest in a church he had never seen and shows that Paul was a man of prayer, praying not for his friends and kindred only but for those whom he had never seen; if with the same intensity of prayer all Christians and Christian ministers would remember the churches, Barnes says, what a different aspect would the Christian church soon assume. Ellicott asks how the Apostle can be said to thank God through Jesus Christ, and answers that Christ is as it were the medium through whom God has been brought into close relation to man, so that all intercourse between God and man is represented as passing through him; he is not only the divine Logos by whom God is revealed to man, but also the Head of humanity by whom the tribute of thanks and praise is offered to God. Throughout the whole world Ellicott calls a hyperbole, which is the more natural as the Apostle is speaking of Rome, the centre and metropolis of the world as he knew it. Of the ninth verse he says the proof that the Apostle takes this lively interest in the Roman Church is conveyed through a solemn adjuration; the word for serve is strictly used for voluntary service paid to God, especially in the way of sacrifice and outward worship, and here it is somewhat metaphorical, whom I serve not so much with outward acts as with the ritual of the spirit. Spirit, Ellicott says, is with St Paul the highest part or faculty in the nature of man, the seat of his higher consciousness, the organ by which he communicates with God; and he quotes Bacon, that certainly man is of kin to the beasts by his body, and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit he is a base and ignoble creature. Of itself the spirit of man is neutral: when brought into contact with the Spirit of God it is capable of a truly religious life, but apart from this influence it is apt to fall under the dominion of the flesh, that is, of those evil appetites and desires to which man is exposed by his physical organisation. In the gospel of his Son names the sphere to which the Apostle feels himself called and in which this heart-worship finds its field of operation, the defence and preaching of the gospel. Robertson says the adverb rendered first is in the accusative case, but no answering adverb meaning in the next place follows, as it does in Hebrews and James; the rush of thoughts crowds out the balanced phraseology, as elsewhere in Paul. Through means as the mediator or medium of thanksgiving; the conjunction may be either declarative or causal, that or because, and either makes sense. Your faith Robertson glosses with Sanday and Headlam as your Christianity, and is proclaimed is the present passive of a verb meaning to announce up and down, which he sets beside the kindred verbs meaning to bring back news, to announce from one as the source, and to announce far and wide beforehand. Throughout all the world is natural hyperbole, but the faith was widely known because the church was in the central city of the empire. I serve, he says, is an old verb from a word meaning hire, and a word meaning hireling, so to serve for hire, then to serve in general, gods or men, whether in sacred services or in spiritual service as here. Unceasingly is a late adverb found in the New Testament only here and in the Thessalonian letters; and of always Robertson remarks that one might think Paul prayed for no others, but he uses both adverbs of the Thessalonians too, so that he seems to have had prayer lists, and he never omitted the Romans.

Clarke says that from this verse to the end of the seventeenth belongs to the preface, in which the apostle endeavours to conciliate the good opinion of the Christians at Rome and to prepare their minds for his reproofs and exhortations. Your faith is spoken of means is celebrated throughout the whole world, that is, in every place where the Christian religion is professed, through all parts of the Roman dominions, for in this sense we should understand the words the whole world. Of the ninth verse Clarke says that whom I serve with my spirit means whom I worship with the profoundest religious reverence, for so the original certainly means: I not only employ all the powers of my body in this service, but all those of my soul, being thoroughly convinced of the absolute truth of the religion I preach. Probably St Paul opposes in this place, Clarke says, the spiritual worship of the Gospel to the external, or what some call the carnal, worship of the Jews: mine is not a religion of ceremonies, but one in which the life and power of the eternal Spirit are acknowledged and experienced. Wesley says that in the very entrance of this one epistle are the traces of all spiritual affections, but of thankfulness above all, with the expression of which almost all St Paul's epistles begin; and he here particularly thanks God that what otherwise himself should have done was done at Rome already. My God, Wesley says, is a very word that expresses faith, hope, love, and consequently all true religion; and through Jesus Christ means that the gifts of God all pass through Christ to us, and all our petitions and thanksgivings pass through Christ to God. In this kind of congratulations St Paul describes either the whole of Christianity or some part of it, and accordingly here he mentions the faith of the Romans, suitably to his design. Through the whole world means this joyful news spreading everywhere, that there were Christians also in the imperial city; and the goodness and wisdom of God established faith in the chief cities, in Jerusalem and Rome particularly, that from thence it might be diffused to all nations. Of the ninth verse Wesley says that God whom I serve means as an apostle, that in my spirit means not only with my body but with my inmost soul, and that in the gospel means by preaching it.

John Chrysostom calls this an exordium worthy of this blessed spirit, and able to teach all men to offer unto God the firstlings of their good deeds and words, and to render thanks not only for their own but also for others' well-doings, which also maketh the soul pure from envy and grudging, and draweth God in a greater measure towards the loving spirit of them that so render thanks. It is fitting, he says, that we render thanks not only when rich but also when poor, not when in health only but also when sick, not when we thrive only but also when we have to bear the reverse; for when our affairs are borne onward with a fair wind, to be thankful is not matter of wonder, but when no small tempests be upon us, and the vessel veers about and is in jeopardy, then is the great time for displaying patience and goodness of heart. For this cause Job also gained a crown, Chrysostom says, and stopped the shameless mouth of the devil, and showed clearly that not even when he saw good days was it through his wealth that he was thankful, but through his much love toward God. And see too what things he is thankful for: not for things earthly and perishing, as power and authority and glory, for these things are of no account, but for real blessings, faith and boldness of speech; and with how much feeling he gives thanks, for he saith not to God but to my God, which also the Prophets do, so making that which is common to all their own. Theodoret of Cyrrhus recites both verses whole, that Paul first thanks his God through Jesus Christ for them all, that their faith is spoken of throughout the whole world, and that God is his witness, whom he serves with his spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing he makes mention of them always in his prayers.

debates: What throughout the whole world covers: Ellicott and Robertson both call it hyperbole, natural in speaking of the metropolis, and Barnes limits the term to those parts of the empire where the church was planted; Calvin restricts it not geographically but by the witnesses, holding that only the faithful proclaimed this faith, since the unbelieving who deemed it detestable could give no correct testimony, and counting it nothing that the handful were unknown to the ungodly even at Rome

Whether an oath is used here and whether it is lawful: Gill, Henry and Calvin all read the appeal as an oath, and Calvin turns it against the Anabaptists, arguing that Christ's prohibition touched only the conversational forms of swearing by heaven, the throne, the earth, Jerusalem or the head, and not the solemn oath the law allows

What first governs: Barnes and Calvin's Stuart take it of order rather than importance, Stuart looking for its answering clause at the thirteenth verse, while Robertson observes that the balancing adverb never arrives at all, the rush of thoughts crowding out the balanced phraseology

What serving with the spirit is set against: Clarke makes it a polemic, the spiritual worship of the Gospel against the external or carnal worship of the Jews; Ellicott keeps the sacrificial sense of the word and makes the contrast internal, service rendered with the ritual of the spirit rather than with outward acts
outliers: Bacon's sentence, quoted by Ellicott, that man is of kin to the beasts by his body, and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit he is a base and ignoble creature
Chrysostom's figure of the vessel veering about in the tempest as the great time for thankfulness, and his note that Paul says not to God but to my God
Henry's judgement that if the Roman Christians had not been persecuted they had not been famous, their scattering under Claudius's edict having carried their report through the empire
Henry's excursus on the later church of Rome, that the epistle to the Romans is now an epistle against the Romans, on the authority of the Practice of Piety in twenty-six instances
Robertson's inference that Paul seems to have had prayer lists, and never omitted the Romans
Calvin's distinction between sudden wishes and the prayers for which the saints deliberately prepare themselves, as our Lord sought retirement for the purpose

10.pericope_label: The request for a prosperous journey, the spiritual gift, the mutual comfort, and the hindrance

schools.summary: Gill says a principal thing which Paul incessantly and importunately requested at the throne of grace was that he might have an opportunity of coming to them, that God in his providence would open a way for him, and that he might have a safe and comfortable journey in a very little time, all which he submits to the will of God, as a good man ought to do. Of his longing to see them Gill says it was not the city of Rome, which was one of Austin's three wishes to have seen in its glory, nor the emperor of it, nor the senate in it, nor its populous inhabitants, fine buildings, riches and grandeur, but the poor saints there, which were the excellent men of the earth of the whole Roman empire, and in whom was his delight; nor was his desire to gratify his curiosity, nor to spend his time in idle chat with them, nor with a view to enrich himself by them. Of the mutual comfort Gill says that what makes for establishment makes for comfort, and what makes for comfort makes for establishment; when souls are established ministers are comforted as well as they, and whilst ministers are imparting their spiritual gifts for the use of others they themselves are sometimes comforted of God in their work, and particularly when they find there is an agreement between their doctrine and the experience of the saints. He notes that Paul calls them brethren because many of them were Jews, his brethren and kinsmen according to the flesh, and all of them were his brethren in a spiritual relation, and this he does to express his affection and to engage their attention and credit. Calvin says that since it is not probable that we from the heart study the benefit of one whom we are not ready to assist by our labours, Paul shows by another proof his love to them, as before God, by requesting that he might be able to advance their interest; and by saying the will of God he shows not only that he looked to the Lord's favour for success in his journey, but that he deemed his journey prosperous if it was approved by the Lord, according to which model all our wishes ought to be formed. He might, Calvin says, while absent have confirmed their faith by his doctrine, but as advice is better taken from one present he had a desire to be with them, and he wished to undertake the toil of a journey not for his own but for their advantage. The phrase some spiritual gift seems to be of general import: some, such as Chalmers and Haldane, have supposed a miraculous power is intended, which the Apostles alone conveyed, such as the power of speaking with tongues, but most commentators agree in the general view; the expression includes any gift or benefit, whether miraculous or ordinary, which the Apostle might have been made the means of conveying, whether of doctrine, or of exhortation, or of prophecy, which he knew had come to him through God's favour. Calvin says Paul has strikingly pointed out the use of gifts, for different gifts are distributed to each individual that all may in kindness mutually assist one another, and transfer to others what each one possesses; and he modifies what he had said of imparting, lest he should seem to regard them as such as were yet to be instructed in the first elements of religion, so that he wished to lend his aid to those who had for the most part made a proficiency, for a confirmation is what we all want until Christ be fully formed in us. Being not satisfied with this modest statement he qualifies it, Calvin says, and shows that he did not so occupy the place of a teacher but that he wished to learn also from them, as though he said, I desire so to confirm you according to the measure of grace conferred on me, that your example may also add courage to my faith, and that we may thus mutually benefit one another. See to what degree of modesty his pious heart submitted itself, Calvin says, so that he disdained not to seek confirmation from unexperienced beginners; nor did he speak dissemblingly, for there is no one so void of gifts in the Church of Christ who is not able to contribute something to our benefit, but we are hindered by our envy and by our pride from gathering such fruit from one another. Such is our high-mindedness, such is the inebriety produced by vain reputation, that despising and disregarding others, every one thinks that he possesses what is abundantly sufficient for himself. Calvin prefers to read with Bucer encouragement rather than comfort, since it agrees better with the former part, and he sets out the renderings of others: Grotius connects the verb with the longing of the preceding verse and says Paul softens what he had said by showing that he would not only bring some joy to them but they also to him; Piscator renders it that I may receive consolation, Castelio that we may be together refreshed, Beza in order to receive common exhortation, Schleusner either that I may receive joy and pleasure from you or that by mutual comfort we may console and strengthen one another. The compound verb is only found here, he notes, though the simple verb frequently occurs, its common meaning being to beseech, to exhort, to encourage, and by these means to comfort; and he quotes Professor Stuart, that he has rendered the word as he has only because he cannot find any English word which will convey the full sense of the original, and Professor Hodge, that which of the senses is to be preferred it is not easy to decide, most probably the Apostle intending to use the word in a wide sense as expressing the idea that he might be excited, encouraged and comforted by his intercourse with his Christian brethren. Of the hindrance Calvin says that what Paul had testified, that he continually requested of the Lord that he might visit them, might have appeared a vain thing had he neglected to seize the occasion when offered; he therefore says that the effort had not been wanting but the opportunity, for he had been prevented from executing a purpose often formed. We hence learn, Calvin says, that the Lord frequently upsets the purposes of his saints in order to humble them, and by such humiliation to teach them to regard his Providence, that they may rely on it; though the saints, who design nothing without the Lord's will, cannot strictly be said to be driven away from their purposes, for it is the presumption of impiety to pass by God and without him to determine on things to come, as though they were in our own power, which is what James sharply reprehends. That he was hindered must be taken in no other sense but that the Lord employed him in more urgent concerns, which he could not have neglected without loss to the Church; and thus the hindrances of the godly and of the unbelieving differ, for the latter perceive only that they are hindered when they are restrained by the strong hand of the Lord so as not to be able to move, but the former are satisfied with a hindrance that arises from some approved reason, nor do they allow themselves to attempt anything beyond their duty or contrary to edification. Of the fruit Calvin says Paul no doubt speaks of that fruit for the gathering of which the Lord sent his Apostles, and though he gathered it not for himself but for the Lord he yet calls it his own, for the godly have nothing more as their own than the work of promoting the glory of the Lord; and he records what had happened to him with respect to other nations, that the Romans might entertain hope that his coming to them would not be unprofitable.

Barnes says that making request shows it was Paul's earnest desire to see them, and that he presented the subject before God; if by any means shows the earnestness of the desire and implies that he had designed it and had been hindered; now at length shows he had purposed it a long time, and the expressions in the Greek imply an earnest wish that this long-cherished purpose might be accomplished before long. A prosperous journey means a safe, pleasant journey; it is right, Barnes says, to regard all success in travelling as depending on God, and to pray for success and safety from danger, yet all such prayers are not answered according to the letter of the petition. The prayer of Paul that he might see the Romans was granted, but in a remarkable way: he was persecuted by the Jews and arraigned before king Agrippa, he appealed to the Roman emperor, and was taken there in chains as a prisoner; yet the journey might in this way have a more deep effect on the Romans than if he had gone in any other way, so mysteriously does God often hear the prayers of his people. Of the spiritual gifts Barnes says some have understood the expression as referring to miraculous gifts which the apostles could confer on others, but this interpretation is forced and unnatural, for there is no instance where the expression denotes the power of working miracles; besides, the apostle in the next verse explains his meaning, from which it appears that he desired to be among them to exercise the office of the ministry, to establish them in the gospel and to confirm their hopes. To make known to them more fully the blessings of the gospel, and thus to impart spiritual gifts, was the design he had in view. Ye may be established means that they might be confirmed in the truths of the gospel, which is one design of the ministry; it is not to have dominion over their faith but to be helpers of their joy, and Paul's wish was to preach not simply where he must but where he might. Of the mutual comfort Barnes says it was not merely to confirm them that Paul wished to come, for he sought the communion of saints and expected to be himself edified and strengthened by seeing their strength of faith; one effect of religion is to produce the desire of the communion of saints, nothing is better fitted to produce growth in grace than such communion, and every Christian should have one or more Christian friends to whom he may unbosom himself, since no small part of the difficulties which young Christians experience would vanish if they should communicate their feelings and views to others. Nothing, he adds, is better fitted to excite the feelings and confirm the hopes of Christian ministers than the firm faith of young converts; the apostle did not disdain to be taught by the humblest Christian, and Barnes quotes Calvin, that there is none so poor in the church of Christ that he cannot make some addition of importance to our stores. Of the thirteenth verse Barnes says one instance of Paul's having purposed to go to Rome is recorded in the Acts, where after the things at Ephesus were ended he purposed in the spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying that after he had been there he must also see Rome; and this purpose, expressed in this manner in the epistle and in the Acts of the Apostles, has been shown by Dr Paley in the Horae Paulinae to be one of those undesigned coincidences which strongly show that both books are genuine, since a forger would not have thought of such a contrivance as to feign such a purpose and to mention it in that manner; such coincidences are among the best proofs that can be demanded that the writers did not intend to impose on the world. The word let means to hinder or to obstruct, and in what way this was done we do not know, though it is probable he refers to the various openings for preaching where he had been and to the obstructions of his enemies. To have fruit means to obtain success in bringing men to the knowledge of Christ; it was not curiosity to see the splendid capital of the world that prompted the desire, nor the love of roaming from clime to clime, but the specific purpose of doing good to the souls of men. Ellicott notes the accumulation of particles denoting the earnestness of his desire, all this time I have been longing to come to you, and now at last I hope that it may be put in my power. The spiritual gift he takes to be such gifts as would naturally flow to one Christian, or to many collectively, from the personal presence and warm sympathy of another, in St Paul's case heightened in proportion to the wealth and elevation of his own spiritual consciousness and life; his head and his heart alike are full to overflowing, and he longs to disburthen himself and impart some of these riches. Inasmuch as he regards all his own religious advancement and experience as the result of the Spirit working within him, he calls the fruits of that advancement spiritual gifts, and all the apostolic gifts, miraculous as well as non-miraculous, would be included in the expression; indeed, Ellicott says, we may believe that the Apostle would hardly draw the distinction that we do between the two kinds, both alike being in his eyes the direct gift of the Spirit.
