As a rule the great outpouring of spiritual gifts was at the first foundation of a church; St Paul was not the founder of the church at Rome, but he hoped to contribute to its advance and consolidation. Of the twelfth verse Ellicott says it is a beautiful touch of true courtesy: he is anxious to see them that he may impart some spiritual gift, but no, he hastily draws back and corrects himself, not wishing it to be implied that it is for him only to impart and for them only to receive, nor assuming any such air of superiority; in the impulse of the moment and the expansiveness of his own heart he had seemed to put it so, but his real meaning was that they should receive mutual comfort and edification. The Greek word, he says, has rather more of the sense of our encouraged, though the idea of comfort is also contained in it, and it is a similar word to that translated comforter in John. Together with you means that he may be comforted at the same time that they are comforted, by his intercourse with them, through that mutual faith which acts and reacts upon each; the Apostle looks to obtain benefit from his intercourse with the Roman Christians and expects that their faith will help to increase his own. There is a truth underlying the Apostle's courtesy which is not mere compliment, Ellicott says: the most advanced Christian will receive something from the humblest, there are very few men whose spirits are not finely touched somewhere, and St Paul was conscious that even an Apostle might not be equally strong at every point. Of the thirteenth verse he says that in the previous verses the Apostle has been speaking of his desire, and here of his purpose, which is one step nearer to the realisation; he had intended to add the Roman Church to the harvest he was engaged in gathering in. Let is an archaism for hindered, the Greek meaning literally and was prevented hitherto; and it is hardly worth while, Ellicott says, to speculate, as some commentators have done, on the causes that may have hindered the Apostle from going to Rome, for in a life like his there may have been many. Robertson says the four particles together express Paul's feelings of emotion that now at length somehow it may really come true, and that the clause is a condition of the first class in the form of an indirect question; Paul's way lay in God's will. Impart is the second aorist active subjunctive of a verb meaning to share with one; to the end ye may be established is a final clause of a kind common in Paul. Of the twelfth verse Robertson quotes Denney, that it is an explanatory correction, and insists the particle should not be ignored: instead of saying that he had a spiritual gift for them, Paul wishes to add that they also have one for him, my being comforted in you together with you, a mutual blessing to each party. Oftentimes I purposed is the second aorist middle of an old verb meaning to place or to propose to oneself, found in the New Testament only here and twice elsewhere; and was hindered is an adversative use of the conjunction; and that I might have some fruit uses an ingressive aorist, so that it means might get some fruit.

Clarke says that by this we see how earnestly the apostle longed to see Rome, and that it had long been a subject of continual prayer to God that he might have a prosperous journey to, or rather meeting with, them, for so we should understand the word; that he had a prosperous meeting with them we cannot doubt, and that he had a disastrous journey to them the twenty-seventh chapter of the Acts fully proves. Some spiritual gift, Clarke says, probably means some of the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, which, being given to them, might tend greatly to establish their faith in the Gospel of Christ; and it is very likely that such gifts were only conferred by means of apostles, and as the apostle had not yet been at Rome, consequently the Roman Christians had not yet received any of these miraculous gifts, and thus they differed widely from all the other Churches which had been raised by the apostle's ministry. Of the twelfth verse Clarke says that Paul here, with great address, intimates that he longs for this opportunity as well on his own account as on theirs, and to show them that he arrogates nothing to himself, for he intimates that it will require the conjoint action of their faith as well as his own to be the means of receiving those blessings from God to which he refers. The word let, Clarke says, is from the Anglo-Saxon to hinder, and signifies impediment or hindrance of any kind, but it is likely that the original word, meaning I was forbidden, refers to a Divine prohibition: he would have visited them long before, but God did not see right to permit him. Wesley says that always means in all his solemn addresses to God, and that the accumulation of particles declares the strength of his desire. That I may impart to you means face to face, by laying on of hands, prayer, preaching the gospel, private conversation; with such gifts the Corinthians, who had enjoyed the presence of St Paul, abounded, and so did the Galatians likewise, and indeed all those churches which had had the presence of any of the apostles had peculiar advantages in this kind from the laying on of their hands. But as yet the Romans were greatly inferior to them in this respect, Wesley says, for which reason the apostle in the twelfth chapter also says little, if anything, of their spiritual gifts; he therefore desires to impart some, that they might be established, for by these was the testimony of Christ confirmed among them. That St Peter had no more been at Rome than St Paul at the time when this epistle was written, Wesley says, appears from the general tenor thereof and from this place in particular, for otherwise what St Paul wishes to impart to the Romans would have been imparted already by St Peter. Of the twelfth verse Wesley says that Paul not only associates the Romans with, but even prefers them before, himself, and asks how different this style of the apostle is from that of the modern court of Rome. Brethren he calls a frequent, holy, simple, sweet and yet grand appellation, noting that the apostles but rarely address persons by their names, that St Paul generally uses this appellation, sometimes with my beloved, that St James says brethren and my beloved brethren, that St Peter and Jude always say beloved, and St John frequently beloved, once brethren, and oftener than once my little children. Though I have been hindered hitherto means either by business, or persecution, or the Spirit; and that I might have some fruit means of his ministerial labours, even as he had already had from the many churches he had planted and watered among the other Gentiles.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus recites the tenth verse whole, that Paul makes request, if by any means now at length he might have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come unto them. Of the eleventh he says that what Paul says is full of humility, for his words are not that I may give but that I may impart, that is, of what I myself have received I may communicate unto you; and inasmuch as the great Peter had already conveyed to them the doctrines of the gospel, he necessarily adds, to the end ye may be established, for I desire, says he, not to bring you some other doctrine, but to confirm that already preached among you, and to water trees already planted. Full of modesty again, Theodoret says, is what he adds in the twelfth verse, that he may be comforted together with them by the mutual faith both of them and him; for not only does he wish to give, but to receive also from them, since the zeal of the disciple comforts and invigorates the master. Of the thirteenth he recites that Paul would not have them ignorant, brethren, that often times he purposed to come unto them, but was prevented hitherto.

debates: What the spiritual gift is: Clarke restricts it to the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, conferred only through apostles, so that the Romans had none and differed widely from every other church of Paul's raising; Barnes calls that forced and unnatural and denies the expression ever denotes miraculous power; Calvin reports Chalmers and Haldane with Clarke but sides with the general sense, any gift miraculous or ordinary; Ellicott includes both and doubts the Apostle would have drawn the distinction at all

Whether Peter had reached Rome before this letter: Wesley infers from this very clause that he had not, since what Paul wishes to impart would otherwise have been imparted already; Theodoret reasons from the same clause that the great Peter had already conveyed the doctrines of the gospel, and that Paul therefore speaks only of establishing and of watering trees already planted

Why the journey was hindered: Ellicott declines to speculate, holding that in a life like Paul's there may have been many causes; Clarke reads the Greek as a divine prohibition, Wesley offers business or persecution or the Spirit, and Calvin says the Lord employed him in more urgent concerns and frequently upsets the purposes of his saints to humble them

How to render the compound verb of the twelfth verse: Calvin prefers Bucer's encouragement, and collects Piscator, Castelio, Beza and Schleusner against one another; Stuart admits he cannot find any English word that will convey the full sense; Hodge calls the choice not easy and settles for a wide sense; Ellicott hears rather more of encouraged than of comfort

Barnes's observation that the prayer for a prosperous journey was granted in a remarkable way, Paul reaching Rome in chains after appealing to the emperor

14.pericope_label: Debtor to Greeks and Barbarians, ready to preach at Rome, and not ashamed of the gospel

schools.summary: Gill says the meaning is that Paul was obliged, by the call he had from God, the injunction laid upon him, and the gifts with which he was qualified, to preach the Gospel to all sorts of men, who are here distinguished into Greeks and Barbarians. Sometimes by Greeks are meant the Gentiles in general in opposition to the Jews, but here they design only a part of the Gentiles, the inhabitants of Greece, in opposition to all the world besides, for the Greeks used to call all others that were not of themselves Barbarians; or else by Greeks are meant the more cultivated nations of the world, and by Barbarians the ruder and more uncivil parts of it. Of the sixteenth verse Gill says the reason why Paul was so ready and willing to preach the Gospel, even where he ran the greatest risk of his character and life, was because it was the Gospel of Christ he preached, and he was not ashamed of it. This supposes that some were ashamed of it, as all such are who hide and conceal it, who have abilities to preach it and do not; or who preach, but not the Gospel; or who preach the Gospel only in part; who own that in private which they will not preach in public, and use ambiguous words of doubtful signification to cover themselves; who blend the Gospel with their own inventions, seek to please men, and live upon popular applause, regard their own interest and not Christ's, and cannot bear the reproach of his Gospel. It expresses that the apostle was not ashamed to preach it, which he did fully and faithfully, plainly and consistently, openly and publicly, and boldly, in the face of all opposition. Calvin says that those whom Paul means by the Greeks and the Barbarians he afterwards explains by the wise and the unwise, which Erasmus has not rendered amiss by learned and unlearned, though Calvin prefers to retain the very words of Paul. He then takes an argument from his own office, and intimates that it ought not to be ascribed to his arrogance that he thought himself in a manner capable of teaching the Romans, however much they excelled in learning and wisdom and in the knowledge of things, inasmuch as it had pleased the Lord to make him a debtor even to the wise. Calvin notes Chalmers's paraphrase, that he is bound by the duties of his office to preach both to Greeks and Barbarians, both to the wise and the unwise, and observes that the two last terms are not exactly parallel to the two first, as many unlearned were among the Greeks, or the civilized, as well as among the Barbarians. Two things are here to be considered, Calvin says: that the gospel is by a heavenly mandate destined and offered to the wise, in order that the Lord may subject to himself all the wisdom of this world, and make all variety of talents, and every kind of science, and the loftiness of all arts, to give way to the simplicity of his doctrine; and what is more, that they are to be reduced to the same rank with the unlearned, and to be made so meek as to be able to bear those to be their fellow-disciples under their master, Christ, whom they would not have deigned before to take as their scholars. And then, that the unlearned are by no means to be driven away from this school, nor are they to flee away from it through groundless fear, for if Paul was indebted to them, being a faithful debtor, he had doubtless discharged what he owed. All teachers have also a rule here which they are to follow, Calvin says, and that is, modestly and kindly to accommodate themselves to the capacities of the ignorant and unlearned; hence it will be that they will be able, with more evenness of mind, to bear with many absurdities and almost innumerable things that may disgust them, by which they might otherwise be overcome. They are, however, to remember that they are not so indebted to the foolish as that they are to cherish their folly by immoderate indulgence. Of the fifteenth verse Calvin says that the phrase means literally, as to me is readiness, or, according to Stuart, is a readiness so far as it respects me, but that I am ready or I am prepared conveys the meaning sufficiently; by saying that he was prepared, Paul intimates that the event depended on another, even on God. He concludes what he had before said of his desire, that as he knew it to be his duty to spread the gospel among them, in order to gather fruit for the Lord, he was anxious to fulfil God's calling as far as he was allowed to do so by the Lord. The sixteenth verse Calvin calls an anticipation of an objection, for Paul declares beforehand that he cared not for the taunts of the ungodly, and thus provides a way by which he proceeds to pronounce an eulogy on the value of the gospel, that it might not appear contemptible to the Romans. He intimates that it was contemptible in the eyes of the world by saying that he was not ashamed of it, and thus prepares them for bearing the reproach of the cross of Christ, lest they should esteem the gospel of less value by finding it exposed to the scoffs of the ungodly. If the power of God ought to be extolled by us, Calvin says, that power shines forth in the gospel; if the goodness of God deserves to be sought and loved by us, the gospel is a display of his goodness. But observe how much Paul ascribes to the ministry of the word, when he testifies that God thereby puts forth his power to save, for he speaks not here of any secret revelation but of vocal preaching; it hence follows that those as it were wilfully despise the power of God, and drive away from them his delivering hand, who withdraw themselves from the hearing of the word. At the same time, as he works not effectually in all, but only where the Spirit, the inward Teacher, illuminates the heart, the gospel is indeed offered to all for their salvation, but the power of it appears not everywhere; and that it is the savour of death to the ungodly does not proceed from what it is, but from their own wickedness. By setting forth but one salvation Paul cuts off every other trust, Calvin says, and when men withdraw themselves from this one salvation they find in the gospel a sure proof of their own ruin; since the gospel invites all to partake of salvation without any difference, it is rightly called the doctrine of salvation, for Christ is there offered, whose peculiar office is to save that which was lost, and those who refuse to be saved by him shall find him a Judge. Everywhere in Scripture, Calvin observes, the word salvation is simply set in opposition to the word destruction; and since the gospel delivers from ruin and the curse of endless death, its salvation is eternal life. He notes Pareus's remark that the abstract, after the Hebrew manner, is put for the concrete, so that the power of God means the instrument of God's power, and cites Stuart, that it is powerful through the energy which God imparts, Chalmers, that it is that to which God by his own power gives effect for the recovery of the life all men had forfeited by sin, and Olshausen, that the gospel continues to operate through all ages of the world, and that not in the first place outwardly but inwardly, in the depths of the soul, and for eternal purposes. Under the word Greek, Calvin says, Paul includes all the Gentiles, the two clauses comprehending all mankind; and it is probable that he chose especially this nation to designate other nations because it was admitted, next to the Jews, into a participation of the gospel covenant, and because the Greeks, on account of their vicinity and the celebrity of their language, were more known to the Jews. He does not thrust the Jews from their own eminence and dignity, since they were the first partakers of God's promise and calling, but reserves for them their prerogative, and immediately joins the Gentiles, though in the second place, as being partakers with them.

Matthew Henry says Paul here enters upon a large discourse of justification, laying down his thesis in the latter part of this chapter and, in order to the proof of it, describing the deplorable condition of the Gentile world; his transition is very handsome, and like an orator, for he was ready to preach the gospel at Rome, though a place where the gospel was run down by those that called themselves the wits. There is a great deal in the gospel, Henry says, which such a man as Paul might be tempted to be ashamed of, especially that he whose gospel it is was a man hanged upon a tree, that the doctrine of it was plain and had little in it to set it off among scholars, and that the professors of it were mean and despised and everywhere spoken against; yet Paul was not ashamed to own it, and Henry reckons him a Christian indeed who is neither ashamed of the gospel nor a shame to it. The excellency of the gospel, he says, lies in this, that it reveals to us the salvation of believers as the end, for it is the power of God unto salvation; Paul is not ashamed of it, how mean and contemptible soever it may appear to a carnal eye, for the power of God works by it the salvation of all that believe, it shows us the way of salvation and is the great charter by which salvation is conveyed and made over to us. But it is through the power of God, Henry says, for without that power the gospel is but a dead letter, and the revelation of the gospel is the revelation of the arm of the Lord, as power went along with the word of Christ to heal diseases; and it is to those, and those only, that believe, for believing interests us in the gospel salvation, and to others it is hidden, since the medicine prepared will not cure the patient if it be not taken. To the Jew first means that the lost sheep of the house of Israel had the first offer made them, both by Christ and his apostles, but upon their refusal the apostles turned to the Gentiles; Jews and Gentiles now stand upon the same level, both equally miserable without a Saviour and both equally welcome to the Saviour. Such doctrine as this was surprising to the Jews, Henry says, who had hitherto been the peculiar people and had looked with scorn upon the Gentile world, but the long-expected Messiah proves a light to enlighten the Gentiles as well as the glory of his people Israel.

Barnes says that I am debtor does not mean that they had conferred any favour on Paul which bound him to make this return, but that he was under obligation to preach the gospel to all to whom it was possible, an obligation arising from the favour God had shown him in appointing him to this work; he was specially chosen as a vessel to bear the gospel to the Gentiles, and did not feel that he had discharged the obligation until he had made the gospel known as far as possible among all the nations of the earth. Greeks properly denotes those who dwelt in Greece, but as the Greeks were the most polished people of antiquity the term came to be synonymous with the polished, the refined, the wise, as opposed to barbarians; in this place it doubtless means the same as the wise, and includes the Romans also, since it cannot be supposed that Paul would designate the Romans as barbarians, and besides the Romans claimed an origin from Greece, Dionysius of Halicarnassus showing that the Italian and Roman people were of Greek descent. Barbarians means all who were not included under the general name of Greeks; Ammonius says that all who were not Greeks were barbarians, and the word properly denotes one who speaks a foreign language, the Greeks applying it to all who did not use their tongue, so that it did not of necessity denote any rusticity of manners or want of refinement. To the wise means those who esteemed themselves to be wise, and unwise those regarded as the ignorant and unpolished part of mankind, the expression being equivalent to ours, to the learned and the unlearned; it was an evidence of the proper spirit to be willing to preach the gospel to either, since the gospel claims to have power to instruct all mankind. Of the fifteenth verse Barnes says that as much as in me is means as far as opportunity may be offered and according to his ability, and that he was prepared to preach among them and to show the power of the gospel even in the splendid metropolis of the world, not deterred by any fear; this closes the introduction to the epistle. Of the sixteenth Barnes says the Jews had cast Paul off and regarded him as an apostate, and by the wise among the Gentiles he had been persecuted and despised and driven from place to place, yet he was not ashamed of the gospel, having so firm a conviction of its value and truth, and having experienced so much of its consolations; men should be ashamed of crime and folly, but not of that which they feel to be right and know will contribute to their welfare. The power of God means that it is the way in which God exerts his power in the salvation of men, the efficacious or mighty plan by which power goes forth to save; it is God's plan and not the device of man, it is adapted to the end and has an inherent adaptedness to it, and it is mighty, having shown its power as applicable to every degree of sin and to every combination of wickedness. Unto salvation means complete deliverance from sin and death and all the foes and dangers that beset man, and cannot imply anything less than eternal life; if a man should believe and then fall away, Barnes says, he could in no correct sense be said to be saved, and hence when the apostle declares that it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, it implies that all who become believers shall be kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, and that none shall ever fall away and be lost, so that the apostle thus commences his discussion with one of the important doctrines of the Christian religion, the final preservation of the saints. To every one that believeth expresses the condition or terms on which salvation is conferred; it is not indiscriminately to all men whatever their character, but only to those who confide or trust in it. All men know what faith is, Barnes says, for it is exercised when we confide in a parent, a friend, a benefactor; a sinner credits the threatenings of God and fears, this is faith; he credits his promises and hopes, this is faith; he feels that he is lost and relies on Jesus Christ for mercy, this is faith. To the Jew first means first in order of time, not that the gospel was any more adapted to Jews than to others, but to them had been committed the oracles of God, the Messiah had come through them, and they had had the law, the temple and the service of God; this was the order in which the gospel was actually preached to the world. And also to the Greek means to all who were not Jews, that is, to all the world, for it was not confined in its intention or efficacy to any class or nation of men. Ellicott says the Apostle does not intend to place the Romans any more in the one class than in the other, but merely means all mankind, no matter what their nationality or culture, the classification being exhaustive; it must be remembered that the Greeks called all who did not speak their own language Barbarians, and the Apostle, writing from Greece, adopts their point of view. Of the wise and foolish he says the gospel was at first most readily received by the poor and unlearned, but it did not therefore follow that culture and education were by any means excluded, St Paul himself being a conspicuous instance to the contrary; and so, in the next century, the Church which began with such leaders as Ignatius and Polycarp could number among its members before the century was out Irenaeus, and Tertullian, and Clement of Alexandria, and Hippolytus, and Origen, the last the most learned man of his time. Of the fifteenth verse Ellicott says that so far as depends upon his own will, and not upon the external ruling of events by God, the Apostle is ready to preach the gospel at Rome as to the other Gentiles; and he sets out three ways of taking the sentence, though the meaning remains in any case the same, adding that perhaps of these three the last, which looks the most unnatural in English, is the most natural in the Greek. Of the sixteenth he says the Apostle will not be ashamed of his mission even in the metropolis of the world, and cannot be ashamed of a scheme so beneficent and so grand; he has perhaps in his mind the reception he had met with in other highly civilised cities, and he had himself once found a stumbling-block in the humiliation of the Cross, but now, so far from being ashamed of it, it is just that of which he is most proud, the preaching of the Cross being the cardinal point of the whole gospel. The words of Christ, Ellicott says, are wanting in the oldest manuscripts and should be omitted. Power of God means a powerful agency put forth by God himself, the lever, as it were, by which he would move the world; and unto salvation names its object, to open the blessings of the Messianic kingdom to mankind. To the Jew first gives another exhaustive division of mankind, Greek being intended to cover all who are not Jews; before, the Apostle was making the secular classification of men, and here the religious, and from his exceptional privileges the Jew was literally placed in a class alone. St Paul certainly assigns a prerogative position to the Jews, Ellicott says: they have an advantage, to them belong the special privileges of the first dispensation, they are the original stock of the olive tree in comparison with which the Gentiles are only wild branches grafted in, and it was only right that the salvation promised to their forefathers should be offered first to them. But the word first raises a difficult question of textual criticism, being absent from the Vatican manuscript, from a citation by Tertullian, and from the Graeco-Latin Codex Boernerianus at Dresden, though present in all other manuscripts and versions; the evidence for the omission is thus small in quantity though good in quality, and internal considerations do not tell strongly either way, but it seems a degree more probable that the word was accidentally dropped in some early copy. Robertson says the whole human race is meant from the Greek point of view, the Jews coming under barbarians, and asks whether Paul considered the Romans as Greeks, answering that they had absorbed the Greek language and culture. Of the fifteenth verse he says the phrase is literally, thus the according to me affair is ready, an awkward idiom like another in the twelfth chapter. Of the sixteenth he says that this Paul knew by much experience, for he had seen the dynamite of God at work; that Jesus had taught the priority of the Jew; that the Jew is first in privilege and in penalty; and that it is not certain the word first is genuine here, though it stands in the second chapter.

Clarke says it has been remarked that all the nations of the earth, themselves excepted, were termed barbarians by the Greeks, and that the apostle considers himself, by his apostolical office and call, under obligation to preach the Gospel to all people as far as the providence of God might open his way, for this is implied in the Divine commission to go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature, to the wise and the unwise, to the learned and cultivated as well as to the unlearned and uncultivated. Of the fifteenth verse he says the word means I have a ready mind, and that he was only prevented by the providence of God from visiting them long ago; his time is best, and in the meantime Paul writes, by his direction, to comfort and instruct them. The sixteenth verse Clarke says is best illustrated by Isaiah, quoted by the apostle in the tenth chapter, that whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed, that is, they shall neither be confounded nor disappointed of their hope; the Jews, by not believing on Jesus Christ, by not receiving him as the promised Messiah but trusting in others, have been disappointed, ashamed and confounded from that time to the present day, their expectation cut off, and while rejecting Christ and expecting another Messiah they have continued under the displeasure of God and are ashamed of their confidence. On the other hand, Clarke says, those who have believed on Christ have in and through him all the blessings of which the prophets spoke, every promise of God being yea and amen through him; Paul as a Jew believed on Christ Jesus, and in believing he had life through his name, so that, filled with that happiness which an indwelling Christ produces, he could cheerfully say that he was not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ, because he felt it to be the power of God to the salvation of his believing soul. This interpretation acquires additional strength, Clarke says, from the consideration that St Paul is here most evidently addressing himself to the Jews. The almighty power of God accompanies this preaching to the souls of them that believe, and the consequence is that they are saved; and what but the power of God can save a fallen, sinful soul? To the Jew first, Clarke says, means that not only have the Jews the first offer of this Gospel, but they have the greatest need of it, being so deeply fallen, and having sinned against such glorious privileges, they are much more culpable than the Gentiles, who never had the light of a Divine revelation; and also to the Greek means that though the salvation of God has hitherto been apparently confined to the Jewish people it shall be so no longer, God having put no difference between them, and Jesus Christ having tasted death for every man. Wesley says Paul includes the Romans under the Greeks, so that this division comprises all nations, and that both to the wise and the unwise is said because there were unwise even among the Greeks and wise even among the barbarians; I am a debtor to all means, I am bound by my divine mission to preach the gospel to them. Of the sixteenth verse Wesley says that to the world the gospel is folly and weakness, and therefore in the judgment of the world Paul ought to be ashamed of it, especially at Rome, the head and theatre of the world; but Paul is not ashamed, knowing it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, the great and gloriously powerful means of saving all who accept salvation in God's own way. As St Paul comprises the sum of the gospel in this epistle, Wesley says, so he does the sum of the epistle in this and the following verse; and there is a noble frankness, as well as a comprehensive sense, in the words both to the Jew and to the Gentile, by which he on the one hand shows the Jews their absolute need of the gospel, and on the other tells the politest and greatest nation in the world both that their salvation depended on receiving it, and that the first offers of it were in every place to be made to the despised Jews.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says Paul has been appointed the teacher of all nations, wherefore he owes the debt of an evangelist not to the Greeks only but to the Barbarians also; for this was it that the grace of the Spirit conferred on them the gift of other tongues, and it behoves them to discharge their debt both to those who boast in their wisdom and to those who are unlearned likewise. By wise, Theodoret says, Paul means those who prided themselves on their eloquence, and by unwise those who for their ignorance were so denominated by such as were called philosophers or wise men. And as not all would receive the preaching of the gospel, fitly has he added, as much as in me lies, for it is mine to preach, but the believing depends on the hearers; and as he frequently calls this preaching by the name of the gospel, and the gospel contains an account of our Lord's passion, cross and death, all which to the unbeliever seemed full of dishonour, he seasonably adds that he is not ashamed of it, looking not to the apparent disgrace but to the blessing arising therefrom, namely, that from it believers obtain salvation. Cyril of Jerusalem urges that we not be ashamed of the Cross of our Saviour but rather glory in it, for the word of the Cross is unto Jews a stumbling-block and unto Gentiles foolishness, but to us salvation, and to them that are perishing it is foolishness, but unto us which are being saved it is the power of God. For it was not a mere man who died for us, Cyril says, but the Son of God, God made man; if the lamb under Moses drove the destroyer far away, did not much rather the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world, deliver us from our sins, and if the blood of a silly sheep gave salvation, shall not the Blood of the Only-begotten much rather save? If any disbelieve the power of the Crucified, Cyril says, let him ask the devils; if any believe not words, let him believe what he sees; for many have been crucified throughout the world, but by none of these are the devils scared, yet when they see even the Sign of the Cross of Christ, who was crucified for us, they shudder.

debates: Where the Romans stand in the division of Greeks and Barbarians: Barnes places them among the Greeks, since Paul could not be supposed to call them barbarians, and cites Dionysius of Halicarnassus for their Greek descent; Wesley says the same flatly; Robertson only observes that they had absorbed Greek language and culture; Ellicott refuses to put them in either class, taking the pair to mean all mankind whatever their nationality

What unto salvation implies: Barnes infers the final preservation of the saints, holding that one who believed and then fell away could in no correct sense be called saved; Wesley states the same clause with the condition kept in view, as the means of saving all who accept salvation in God's own way; Calvin holds the gospel offered to all without difference, though its power appears not everywhere, since it works effectually only where the Spirit illuminates the heart

Why the gospel came to the Jew first: Barnes makes it purely a matter of order in time, and denies the gospel was any more adapted to them; Clarke makes it a matter of desert the other way, that they have the greatest need of it, being more culpable than Gentiles who never had a divine revelation; Ellicott assigns them a genuine prerogative position, and Robertson has them first in privilege and in penalty

Whether the word first belongs to the text at all: Ellicott sets out its absence from the Vatican manuscript, from a citation by Tertullian and from the Codex Boernerianus, calls the evidence small in quantity though good in quality, and judges accidental omission the more probable; Robertson says only that its genuineness is uncertain here, though it stands in the second chapter
outliers: Barnes's citation of Ammonius, that all who were not Greeks were barbarians, and his note that the word carried no imputation of rustic manners
Calvin's warning to teachers that they are not so indebted to the foolish as to cherish their folly by immoderate indulgence
Cyril's appeal to the devils, that many have been crucified throughout the world but by none of these are the devils scared
Ellicott's roll of learned Christians produced within a century of Ignatius and Polycarp, ending with Origen as the most learned man of his time
Ellicott's three constructions of as much as in me is, with the judgement that the one most unnatural in English is the most natural in the Greek
Henry's maxim that he is a Christian indeed who is neither ashamed of the gospel nor a shame to it, and his figure of the medicine that will not cure the patient if it be not taken
Theodoret's division of labour, that it is Paul's to preach but the believing depends on the hearers

17.pericope_label: The righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith, and the just shall live by faith

schools.summary: Gill says that by the righteousness of God is not meant the essential righteousness of God, the rectitude of his nature, his righteousness in fulfilling his promises, and his punitive justice, which though revealed in the Gospel is yet not peculiar to it; nor the righteousness by which Christ himself is righteous, either as God or as Mediator; but that righteousness which he wrought out by obeying the precepts and bearing the penalty of the law in the room of his people, and by which they are justified in the sight of God. This is called the righteousness of God, Gill says, in opposition to the righteousness of men, and because it justifies men in the sight of God, and because of the concern which Jehovah, Father, Son and Spirit have in it: Jehovah the Father sent his Son to work it out, and being wrought out he approves and accepts of it, and imputes it to his elect; Jehovah the Son is the author of it by his obedience and death; and Jehovah the Spirit discovers it to sinners, works faith in them to lay hold upon it, and pronounces the sentence of justification by it. Calvin says this is an explanation and a confirmation of the preceding clause, that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation; for if we seek salvation, that is, life with God, righteousness must first be sought, by which being reconciled to him we may obtain that life which consists only in his favour, since in order to be loved by God we must first become righteous, God regarding unrighteousness with hatred. Paul therefore intimates that we cannot obtain salvation otherwise than from the gospel, since nowhere else does God reveal to us his righteousness, which alone delivers us from perdition; and so he reasons from the cause to the effect. Notice further, Calvin says, how extraordinary and valuable a treasure God bestows on us through the gospel, even the communication of his own righteousness. He takes the righteousness of God to mean that which is approved before his tribunal, as, on the contrary, that is usually called the righteousness of men which is by men counted and supposed to be righteousness, though it be only vapour; and he doubts not that Paul alludes to the many prophecies in which the Spirit makes known the righteousness of God in the future kingdom of Christ. Some explain it as the righteousness which is freely given us by God, Calvin says, and he confesses the words will bear this sense, for God justifies us by the gospel and thus saves us, though the former view seems to him more suitable. Of greater moment is what some think, that this righteousness does not only consist in the free remission of sins but also in part includes the grace of regeneration; but Calvin considers that we are restored to life because God freely reconciles us to himself. Instead of the expression he used before, to every one who believeth, Paul says now from faith, for righteousness is offered by the gospel and is received by faith; and he adds, to faith, for as our faith makes progress, and as it advances in knowledge, so the righteousness of God increases in us at the same time, and the possession of it is in a manner confirmed. When at first we taste the gospel, Calvin says, we indeed see God's smiling countenance turned towards us, but at a distance; the more the knowledge of true religion grows in us, by coming as it were nearer, we behold God's favour more clearly and more familiarly. What some think, that there is here an implied comparison between the Old and New Testament, is more refined than well-founded, for Paul does not here compare the Fathers who lived under the law with us, but points out the daily progress made by every one of the faithful. By the authority of the Prophet Habakkuk, Calvin says, Paul proves the righteousness of faith, for the prophet, predicting the overthrow of the proud, adds this, that the life of the righteous consists in faith; now we live not before God except through righteousness, and it then follows that our righteousness is obtained by faith. The verb being future designates the real perpetuity of that life of which he speaks, as though he had said that it would not be momentary but continue for ever; for even the ungodly swell with the false notion of having life, but when they say peace and safety a sudden destruction comes upon them, so that theirs is a shadow which endures only for a moment. Faith alone secures the perpetuity of life, Calvin says, and this because it leads us to God and makes our life depend on him; Paul would not have aptly quoted this testimony had not the meaning of the Prophet been that we then only stand when by faith we recumb on God, and he has ascribed life to the faith of the godly only in so far as they, having renounced the arrogance of the world, resign themselves to the protection of God alone. Calvin notes that Paul here quotes the Old Testament neither exactly from the Hebrew, which reads the just by his faith shall live, nor from the Septuagint, which turns his into my; the passage is quoted twice besides in the same words, without either pronoun, his object being to state the general truth contained in the passage and not to give a strictly verbal quotation. Paul does not professedly handle the subject of gratuitous justification here, Calvin says, and hence makes no mention of it, but it is sufficiently evident from the nature of faith that this testimony is rightly applied; and we necessarily gather from his reasoning that there is a mutual connection between faith and the gospel, for as the just is said to live by faith, he concludes that this life is received by the gospel. We have now, Calvin says, the principal point or the main hinge of the first part of this Epistle, that we are justified by faith through the mercy of God alone.

Barnes says the word for implies that Paul is now about to give a reason why he was not ashamed of the gospel, that the reason is stated in this verse, that it embodies the substance of all that is contained in the epistle, and that there is not perhaps a more important passage in the Bible than this verse, or one more difficult to be understood. The righteousness of God, he says, is capable of only three interpretations. Some have said it means that the attribute of God denominated righteousness or justice is here displayed; but the leading design of the gospel is not to evince the justice of God but the love of God, and the attribute principally evinced is rather mercy, or mercy in a manner consistent with justice. A second interpretation makes it the same as goodness, but this does not comport with the design of the argument, is a departure from the established meaning of the word, and would be remarkable, since the usual words expressive of goodness or mercy were not used. The phrase, Barnes concludes, is equivalent to God's plan of justifying men, his scheme of declaring them just in the sight of the law, of acquitting them from punishment and admitting them to favour; in this sense it stands opposed to man's plan of justification by his own works. No small part of the perplexity attending the subject will be avoided, he says, if it is remembered that the discussion pertains to the question how mortal man can be just with God: Paul shows that it cannot be by works and that it can be by faith. To justify means properly to be just, to be innocent, to be righteous; it then means to declare or treat as righteous, as when a man charged with an offence is acquitted; it then means to treat as if innocent, that is, to pardon and to treat as if the offence had not occurred. It does not mean that the man did not commit the offence, or that the law might not have held him answerable for it, but that the offence is forgiven. Barnes notes that the expression before us does not imply any particular manner in which this is done, does not touch the question whether it is by imputed righteousness or not, and does not say that it is on legal principles; it simply affirms that the gospel contains God's plan of justifying men by faith. It is called God's righteousness because it is God's plan, in distinction from all the plans set up by men, and because it is the way by which he receives and treats men as righteous; and the same plan was foretold where righteousness is nearly synonymous with salvation, as in Isaiah and Daniel. Of this plan, Barnes says, it may be observed that it is not to declare that men are innocent and pure, for that would not be true and the truth is just the reverse; it is not to take part with the sinner and mitigate his offences, for it admits them to their full extent and makes him feel them; it is not that we become partakers of the essential righteousness of God, for that is impossible; and it is not that his righteousness becomes ours, for this is not true, and there is no intelligible sense in which that can be understood. It is God's plan for pardoning sin and for treating us as if we had not committed it, adopting us as his children and admitting us to heaven on the ground of what the Lord Jesus has done in our stead. Revealed means made known and communicated; the fact seems to have been understood by Abraham and the patriarchs, but the full mode in which it was to be accomplished was not revealed until it was done in the gospel. From faith Barnes takes to be connected with the expression the righteousness of God, so that God's plan of justifying men by faith is revealed in the gospel. The common interpretation, that the righteousness of God is revealed from one degree of faith to another, he rejects with five objections: it is not true, for the gospel did not suppose that men had a certain degree of faith by nature which needed only to be strengthened; it does not make good sense, since to say that God's essential justice is revealed from one degree of faith to another is to use words without any meaning; the connexion of the passage does not admit of it, the design being to set forth the doctrine of justification; the epistle is intended clearly to establish the fact that men are justified by faith; and the passage which he immediately quotes shows that he did not speak of different degrees of faith. To faith means to those who believe, the abstract being put for the concrete. Of the quotation Barnes says the Septuagint translate the passage in Habakkuk, if any man shall draw back my soul shall have no pleasure in him, but the just by my faith shall live, the very words being used which the apostle employs except for the pronoun; the Syriac renders it similarly, and the meaning of the Hebrew is the same. It does not refer originally to the doctrine of justification by faith, Barnes says, but means that the righteous man shall live by his confidence in God; the prophet is speaking of the woes attending the Babylonish captivity, when the Chaldeans were to come upon the land and destroy it, and this was not to be perpetual, for they who had confidence in God should live, that is, should be restored to their country and be blessed. The apostle did not quote it as referring primarily to justification, but it expressed a general principle, that those who had confidence in God should be happy and preserved and blessed; it was not by relying on his own merit that the Israelite would be delivered, but by confidence in God, and on the same principle would men be saved under the gospel. Shall live in Habakkuk means to be made happy or blessed, to find comfort and support and deliverance; and so in the gospel the blessings of salvation are represented as life, eternal life, sin being represented as death. Ellicott says the gospel attains its end, the salvation of the believer, by revealing the righteousness of God, that is, the plan or process designed by him for men to become just or righteous in his sight, the essential part on man's side, the beginning and end of that plan, being faith, for which there was authority in the Old Testament. By the righteousness of God is not meant, as might perhaps be supposed, an attribute of the divine nature, as if the essential righteousness of God were first made known through the gospel, since Paul goes on to show that so much at least of the nature of God might be known without any supernatural revelation; of God means in the present instance which proceeds from God, and the righteousness which thus proceeds from God is that condition of righteousness in man into which he enters by his participation in the Messianic kingdom. The whole object of the coming of the Messiah, Ellicott says, was to make men righteous before God, and this was done more especially by the death of Christ upon the cross, which had the effect of making God propitious towards men; the benefit of this act is secured to all who make good their claim to be considered members of the Messianic kingdom by a loyal adhesion to the Messiah, and such persons are treated as if they were righteous, though the righteousness thus attributed to them is not any actual merit of their own but an ideal condition in which they are placed by God, which is the well-known doctrine of justification by faith. Revealed means that God's purpose of thus justifying men is in process of being revealed or declared in the gospel: theoretically in the express statements of the way in which man may be justified, and practically in the heartfelt acceptance of those statements and the change of life which they involve; to the Romans the moment of revelation was that in which they first heard the gospel, and St Paul wishes them to know the full significance, the philosophy as it might be called, of that which they had heard. From faith to faith means that it is by faith that man first lays hold on the gospel, and its latest product is a heightened and intensified faith; apart from faith the gospel remains null and void for the individual and is not realised, but when it has once been realised and taken home to the man's self, its tendency is to confirm and strengthen that very faculty by which it was apprehended, doing that for which the disciples prayed when they said, Lord, increase our faith. The words from Habakkuk, Ellicott says, are part of the consolatory answer which the prophet receives in the stress of the Chaldean invasion, that though the irresistible hosts sweep over the land, the righteous man who puts his trust in God shall live; and perhaps St Paul intended the words by faith to be taken rather with the just than as they stand in the English version, the man whose righteousness is based on faith shall live. The Apostle uses the word faith in his own peculiar and pregnant sense, Ellicott says, but this is naturally led up to by the way in which it was used by Habakkuk: the intense personal trust and reliance which the Jew felt in the God of his fathers is directed by the Christian to Christ, and is further developed into an active energy of devotion. Faith as understood by St Paul, he adds, is not merely head-belief, a purely intellectual process such as that of which St James spoke when he said the devils also believe and tremble, neither is it merely trust, a passive dependence upon an Unseen Power, but it is a further stage of feeling developed out of these, a current of emotion setting strongly in the direction of its object, an ardent and vital apprehension of that object, and a firm and loyal attachment to it. Robertson says a righteousness of God is a subjective genitive, a God kind of righteousness, one that each must have and can obtain in no other way save from faith unto faith, faith the starting point and faith the goal. Is revealed means that it is a revelation from God, this God kind of righteousness, that man unaided could never have conceived or still less attained; in these words we have Paul's statement in his own way of the theme of the Epistle, and every word is important, salvation, gospel, is revealed, righteousness of God, faith and believing. By righteousness, Robertson says, we shall see that Paul means both justification and sanctification, and it is important to get a clear idea of his use of the word here, for it controls the thought throughout the Epistle; Jesus set up a higher standard of righteousness in the Sermon on the Mount than the Scribes and Pharisees taught and practised, and here Paul claims that in the gospel there is revealed a God kind of righteousness with two ideas in it, the righteousness that God has and that he bestows. It is an old word for quality from the word for a righteous man, and that from the word for right or justice, called a goddess in the Acts, and that allied with a verb meaning to show or to point out; and Robertson sets beside it the allied words meaning to declare or make righteous, that which is deemed righteous, and the act of declaring righteous. We use justice in distinction from righteousness, he says, and sanctification for the result that comes after justification, the setting one right with God; Paul is consistent and usually clear in his use of these great words.

Clarke says that therein means in the Gospel of Christ, and that the righteousness of God means God's method of saving sinners; revealed from faith to faith means shown to be by faith and not by the works of any law, for Abraham, the father and founder of the Jewish people, was justified by faith before even the law was given, and by believing in reference to the spiritual object held forth in the various ordinances of the law, and now revealed under the Gospel, he and all his believing descendants have been justified. Thus the faith of the old covenant led on to the faith of the new covenant, Clarke says, which shows that salvation has been by faith from the call of Abraham to the present time; and from the beginning all that were just or righteous in the earth became such by faith, and by this principle alone they were enabled to persevere. That the word we translate righteousness in this verse signifies God's method of saving mankind by faith in Christ is fully evident, Clarke says, from the use of the term in the ninth and tenth chapters, where the Gentiles who followed not after righteousness attained to it, and Israel, following after the law of righteousness, did not attain to it because they sought it not by faith but as it were by the works of the law, being ignorant of God's righteousness and going about to establish their own. This collation of passages, he says, most evidently shows that the word righteousness here means simply God's method of saving sinners, in opposition to the ways and means invented by the fancies or prejudices of men. There are few words in the sacred writings taken in a greater variety of acceptations than the Hebrew and Greek words we generally translate righteousness, Clarke says; our English word was originally rightwiseness, from the Anglo-Saxon words for justice or right and to know, and thus the righteous man was a person who was allowed to understand the claims of justice and right, and who, knowing them, acted according to their dictates, so that the righteous man is he that knows most and acts best. The Hebrew word in its ideal meaning contains the notion of a beam or scales in equipoise, what we call even balance, and it is well known that in all the personifications of Justice, ancient and modern, she is represented as a beautiful female with a bandage on her eyes and a beam and scales in her hand, so perfectly poised that neither end preponderates; the Greek word has been derived from a verb meaning to divide, because it is the property of this virtue to divide to each his due. Clarke then distinguishes ten acceptations of the noun, the act of distributing to each man his due, a holy life proceeding from piety towards God, benignity and liberality and particularly almsgiving, God's method of saving sinners, the reward or issue of liberality, the whole collection of graces which constitute the complete Christian character, the result of faith in God and submission to his will exemplified in a holy and useful life, an exact observance of religious ordinances and precepts, the favour or pardoning mercy of God, and the concrete righteous person put for the abstract; and seven of the verb we translate to justify, to declare or pronounce one just, to esteem a thing properly, to approve and praise and commend, to clear from all sin, to be found or declared righteous in a forensic sense, to set free or escape from, and to receive one into favour or pardon sin. In all these texts, Clarke says, the word justify is taken in the sense of remission of sins through faith in Christ Jesus, and does not mean making the person just or righteous, but treating him as if he were so, having already forgiven him his sins. The just shall live by faith has been understood two ways, Clarke says: that the just or righteous man cannot live a holy and useful life without exercising continual faith in our Lord Jesus, which is strictly true, for he only who has brought him into that state of salvation can preserve him in it, and he stands by faith; or, as some able critics contend, that the words of the original should be pointed so as to read, the just by faith shall live, that is, he alone who is justified by faith shall be saved, which is also true, since it is impossible to get salvation in any other way. This last meaning is probably the true one, Clarke says, as the original text in Habakkuk speaks of those who believed the declarations of God when the Chaldeans besieged Jerusalem, and, having acted conformably to them, escaped with their lives. Wesley says the expression the righteousness of God sometimes means God's eternal, essential righteousness, which includes both justice and mercy, and is eminently shown in condemning sin and yet justifying the sinner; sometimes it means that righteousness by which a man, through the gift of God, is made and is righteous, both by receiving Christ through faith and by a conformity to the essential righteousness of God. St Paul, when treating of justification, means hereby the righteousness of faith, Wesley says, therefore called the righteousness of God because God found out and prepared, reveals and gives, approves and crowns it; and in this verse the expression means the whole benefit of God through Christ for the salvation of a sinner. Mention is made here and in the eighteenth verse of a twofold revelation, of wrath and of righteousness, the former little known to nature and revealed by the law, the latter wholly unknown to nature and revealed by the gospel; that goes before and prepares the way, and this follows, and each is revealed at the present time, in opposition to the times of ignorance. From faith to faith, Wesley says, means by a gradual series of still clearer and clearer promises. St Paul had just laid down three propositions, that righteousness is by faith, that salvation is by righteousness, and that both are to the Jews and to the Gentiles, and all these are confirmed by that single sentence, the just shall live by faith, which was primarily spoken of those who preserved their lives when the Chaldeans besieged Jerusalem, by believing the declarations of God and acting according to them; here it means, Wesley says, that he shall obtain the favour of God and continue therein by believing.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus recites the verse, that therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith, and adds that it is not revealed to all, but to those who have the eyes of faith.

debates: What the righteousness of God is: Barnes enumerates three possible senses and rejects the attribute of justice and the attribute of goodness, settling on God's plan of justifying men, and Clarke and Ellicott agree that it is not an attribute at all; Calvin takes it as that which is approved before God's tribunal; Robertson calls it a God kind of righteousness carrying two ideas at once, the righteousness God has and the righteousness he bestows; Wesley allows three senses of the phrase and finds here the whole benefit of God through Christ for the salvation of a sinner

Whether Christ's righteousness becomes the believer's: Gill says the Father approves the righteousness the Son wrought and imputes it to his elect; Ellicott says the believer is treated as righteous by an ideal condition in which God places him, no actual merit of his own; Barnes denies the transfer outright, that it is not that his righteousness becomes ours, this is not true, and there is no intelligible sense in which it can be understood

How far the word reaches: Robertson holds that by righteousness Paul means both justification and sanctification, and that this controls the thought of the whole epistle; Calvin knows the suggestion that the righteousness includes in part the grace of regeneration and declines it, holding that we are restored to life because God freely reconciles us to himself

What from faith to faith means: Clarke reads it historically, the faith of the old covenant leading on to the faith of the new; Calvin calls that comparison more refined than well-founded and reads it of the daily progress of each believer, as does Ellicott; Wesley makes it a gradual series of clearer promises; Barnes rejects every degree-to-degree reading with five objections and attaches the words to the righteousness itself

How Habakkuk should be pointed and applied: Clarke prefers the just by faith shall live to the just shall live by faith, and Ellicott inclines the same way; Barnes and Wesley agree the prophet spoke primarily of those preserved alive in the Chaldean siege, Barnes adding that the words express only a general principle of confidence in God
outliers: Barnes's judgement that there is not perhaps a more important passage in the Bible than this verse, or one more difficult to be understood
Calvin's figure of God's smiling countenance seen at first from a distance and afterwards more clearly and familiarly
Calvin's note that Paul quotes Habakkuk exactly from neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint, dropping the pronoun that each carries
Clarke's derivation of righteousness from the Anglo-Saxon rightwiseness, right and to know, so that the righteous man is he that knows most and acts best
Clarke's account of the Hebrew root as a beam or scales in equipoise, and of Justice figured blindfold with a balance neither end of which preponderates
Ellicott's definition of faith as neither head-belief, such as the devils have who believe and tremble, nor passive trust, but a current of emotion setting strongly towards its object
Wesley's pairing of the twofold revelation, of wrath by the law and of righteousness by the gospel, the one preparing the way for the other

18.pericope_label: The wrath of God revealed from heaven against those who hold the truth in unrighteousness

schools.summary: Gill says that the apostle, having hinted at the doctrine of justification by faith in the righteousness of Christ, now represents from here to the end of the chapter the sad estate and condition of the Gentiles with the law of nature, and of the Jews with the law of Moses, by which it most clearly appears that neither of them could be justified by their obedience to the respective laws under which they were, but that they both stood in need of the righteousness of God. By the wrath of God, Gill says, is meant the displeasure and indignation of God at sin and sinners, his punitive justice and awful vengeance, the judgments which he executes in this world, and that everlasting displeasure of his, and wrath to come in another world, which all through sin are deserving of. Of the nineteenth verse Gill says there are some things which could not be known of God by the light of nature: a trinity of persons in the Godhead; the knowledge of God in Christ as Mediator; the God-man and Mediator Jesus Christ; his incarnation, sufferings, death and resurrection; the will of God to save sinners by a crucified Jesus; the several peculiar doctrines of the Gospel, particularly the resurrection of the dead, and the manner of worshipping of God with acceptance. But there are some things which may be known of God without a revelation, Gill says: Adam had a perfect knowledge of him, and his sons, though fallen, even the very Heathens have some notion of him, as that there is a God; and by the light of nature it might be known that there is but one God, who is glorious, full of majesty, and possessed of all perfections, all powerful, wise, good and righteous. Calvin says that Paul reasons now by stating things of a contrary nature, and proves that there is no righteousness except what is conferred, or comes through the gospel, for he shows that without this all men are condemned. He brings as the first proof of condemnation the fact that though the structure of the world, and the most beautiful arrangement of the elements, ought to have induced man to glorify God, yet no one discharged his proper duty; it hence appears that all were guilty of sacrilege, and of wicked and abominable ingratitude. To some it seems that this is a main subject, and that Paul forms his discourse for the purpose of enforcing repentance, Calvin says, but he thinks the discussion of the subject begins here and that the principal point was stated in a former proposition, Paul's object being to teach us where salvation is to be found; and as the flesh will not willingly humble itself so far as to assign the praise of salvation to the grace of God alone, Paul shows that the whole world is deserving of eternal death, from which it follows that life is to be recovered in some other way, since we are all lost in ourselves. Some make a difference between the two words, Calvin says, and think that by the former is meant the profanation of God's worship, and by the latter injustice towards men; but as the Apostle immediately refers this unrighteousness to the neglect of true religion, we shall explain both as referring to the same thing. By these two words one thing is designated, and that is ingratitude towards God, for we thereby offend in two ways: it is said to be impiety, as it is a dishonouring of God, and unrighteousness, because man, by transferring to himself what belongs to God, unjustly deprives God of his glory. The word wrath, according to the usage of Scripture, speaking after the manner of men, means the vengeance of God, Calvin says, for God in punishing has, according to our notion, the appearance of one in wrath; it imports therefore no such emotion in God, but only has a reference to the perception and feeling of the sinner who is punished. Though the expression from heaven is taken by some in the sense of an adjective, as though he had said the wrath of the celestial God, Calvin thinks it more emphatical when taken as having this import, that wheresoever a man may look around him he will find no salvation, for the wrath of God is poured out on the whole world, to the full extent of heaven. The truth means the true knowledge of God, and to hold it is to suppress or to obscure it, hence they are charged as guilty of robbery; and Calvin's editor collects the renderings of others, Turrettin unjustly detaining the truth, Chalmers who stifle the truth in unrighteousness, Stuart who hinder the truth by unrighteousness, Hodge who wickedly oppose the truth, and Macknight who confine the truth by unrighteousness, with the comment of Pareus that they rushed headlong into impiety against God and into injustice against one another, not through ignorance but knowingly, not through weakness but wilfully and maliciously, which the Apostle expresses by a striking metaphor taken from tyrants, who against right and justice, by open violence, oppress the innocent, bind them in chains, and detain them in prison. Calvin also records that Stuart connected this verse, as the former one, with the sixteenth, and that Macknight was of the same opinion, so that the revelation of wrath from heaven is that which is made by the gospel, a view which certainly gives a meaning to the words from heaven which is hardly done by any other; that the gospel reveals wrath as well as righteousness to be obtained by faith is undeniable, salvation to the believer and condemnation to the unbeliever being its sum and substance, and Haldane's objection is of no force, that the Apostle subsequently shows the sins of mankind as committed against the light of nature and not against the gospel, for he seems to have brought forward the evidence from the light of nature in order to confirm the evidence from the light of revelation; this is the view taken by Turrettin, and Pareus says there is nothing to prevent us from referring the revelation of wrath, as well as the revelation of righteousness, to the gospel. Of the nineteenth verse Calvin says that what may be known of God designates what it behoves us to know of him, all that appertains to the setting forth of the glory of the Lord, or whatever ought to move and excite us to glorify God; and by this expression he intimates that God in his greatness can by no means be fully comprehended by us, and that there are certain limits within which men ought to confine themselves, inasmuch as God accommodates to our small capacities what he testifies of himself. Insane then are all they, Calvin says, who seek to know of themselves what God is, for the Spirit, the teacher of perfect wisdom, does not in vain invite our attention to what may be known. Paul said in them rather than to them for the sake of greater emphasis, for though the Apostle adopts everywhere Hebrew phrases, he seems here to have intended to indicate a manifestation by which they might be so closely pressed that they could not evade it, since every one of us undoubtedly finds it to be engraven on his own heart; though Calvin's editor notes that Stuart took the phrase to mean in the midst of them, or before their eyes, that is, in the visible world, while many refer it with Calvin to the moral sense, as written in their hearts. By God's showing it, Calvin says, Paul means that man was created to be a spectator of this formed world, and that eyes were given him that he might, by looking on so beautiful a picture, be led up to the Author himself.

Matthew Henry says the apostle begins to show that all mankind need the salvation of the gospel, because none could obtain the favour of God, or escape his wrath, by their own works; for no man can plead that he has fulfilled all his obligations to God and to his neighbour, nor can any truly say that he has fully acted up to the light afforded him. The sinfulness of man is described, Henry says, as ungodliness against the laws of the first table and unrighteousness against those of the second, and the cause of that sinfulness is holding the truth in unrighteousness: all, more or less, do what they know to be wrong and omit what they know to be right, so that the plea of ignorance cannot be allowed from any. Our Creator's invisible power and Godhead are so clearly shown in the works he has made, Henry says, that even idolaters and wicked Gentiles are left without excuse; they foolishly followed idolatry, and rational creatures changed the worship of the glorious Creator for that of brutes, reptiles and senseless images. They wandered from God till all traces of true religion must have been lost, had not the revelation of the gospel prevented it; for whatever may be pretended as to the sufficiency of man's reason to discover Divine truth and moral obligation, or to govern the practice aright, facts cannot be denied, and these plainly show that men have dishonoured God by the most absurd idolatries and superstitions, and have degraded themselves by the vilest affections and most abominable deeds.

Barnes says this verse commences the argument of the epistle, designed to establish the proposition that God's plan of justification is revealed in the gospel; to show this it was necessary to show that all other plans had failed, and the design of the argument is to show that men were sinners, for which it was necessary to show that they were under law. This was clear in regard to the Jews, who had the Scriptures, and the apostle in this chapter shows that it was equally clear in regard to the Gentiles; there can be but two ways of justification conceived of, one by obedience to law and the other by grace. The word rendered wrath, Barnes says, properly denotes that earnest appetite or desire by which we seek anything, and is particularly applied to the desire which a man has to take vengeance who is injured and enraged, so that it is synonymous with revenge; but it is also often applied to God, and when we think of the word as applicable to him it must be divested of everything like human passion, and especially of the passion of revenge. As God cannot be injured by the sins of men he has no motive for vengeance, properly so called, and it is one of the most obvious rules of interpretation that we are not to apply to God passions and feelings which among us have their origin in evil; in making a revelation it was indispensable to use words which men used, but it does not follow that when applied to God they mean precisely what they do when applied to man. When the Saviour is said to have looked on his disciples with anger, Barnes says, the same Greek word being used, it is not to be supposed that he had the feelings of an implacable man seeking vengeance, for the nature of the feeling is to be judged of by the character of the person; so here the word denotes the Divine displeasure or indignation against sin, the opposition of the Divine character against sin and the determination of the Divine Mind to express that opposition in a proper way. It is not an unamiable or arbitrary principle of conduct, he says: we all admire the character of a father who is opposed to disorder and vice and disobedience in his family and who expresses his opposition in a proper way, and the character of a ruler who is opposed to all crime in the community; and why shall we not be equally pleased with God, who is opposed to all crime in all parts of the universe. Is revealed means revealed to the Jews by their law, and to the Gentiles in their reason and conscience; and from heaven Barnes takes to mean simply that the Divine displeasure against sin is made known by a Divine appointment, by an arrangement of events, communications and arguments which evince that they have had their origin in heaven. It does not mean that the wrath will be sent from heaven, he says, nor that the heavens declare his wrath, nor that the heavenly bodies are proofs of his wrath against sin, nor that Christ, the executioner of wrath, will be manifest from heaven, nor that it is from God who is in heaven, but that it is by an arrangement which shows that it had its origin in heaven. Ungodliness properly means impiety towards God, and unrighteousness iniquity towards men, all offences against our neighbour, our parents, our country; the two words express that which comprehends the violation of all the commands of God. Barnes observes that the apostle here shows that the wrath of God is as really revealed against the neglect of God as it is against positive iniquity, and that this is an offence of so much consequence as to be placed first. Who hold the truth means who keep back or restrain the truth, for the word sometimes means to maintain, to keep, to observe, but it also means to hold back, to detain, to hinder, as where the people stayed Jesus, or where Paul would have retained Onesimus with him; in this place it means that they held back or restrained the truth by their wickedness. Their vice and tendency to iniquity was the reason why they had so little knowledge of a holy God, Barnes says; as they were determined to practise iniquity, they chose to exclude the knowledge of a pure God and to worship impure idols, by which they might give a sanction to their lusts; and the same thing is substantially true now, men holding back or resisting the truth of the gospel by their sins, by employing influence and wealth against it, by resisting its doctrines since they know they could not hold them without abandoning their sins, by resolving to live in sin, by pride and vanity and the love of the world, by unlawful business that begins in evil and ends in evil, such as traffic in ardent spirits and the slave trade, and by indulgence in vice of any kind. There is nothing that prevents the universal spread and influence of truth but sin, Barnes says, and men of wickedness are answerable for all the ignorance and woe which are spread over the community. Of the nineteenth verse he says the apostle proceeds to show how it was that the heathen hindered the truth by their iniquity, by showing that the truth might be known by the works of creation and that nothing but their iniquity prevented it. That which may be known of God means that which is knowable concerning God, the expression implying that there may be many things concerning God which cannot be known, but that there are also many things which may be ascertained, such as his existence and many of his attributes; the object of the apostle was not to say that everything pertaining to God could be known by them, or that they could have as clear a view of him as if they had possessed a revelation, but that they knew enough to prove that they had no excuse for their sins. Is manifest means is known, is understood; in them means among them, and the great mass of the heathen world was indeed ignorant of the true God, but their leaders, or their philosophers, had this knowledge, though this was not true of the mass or body of the people. God hath showed it unto them, Barnes says: he had endowed them with reason and conscience, had made them capable of seeing and investigating his works, and had spread before them the proofs of his wisdom and goodness and power. Ellicott says that as a preliminary stage to the revelation of justification and of faith there is another which is its opposite, a revelation and disclosure of divine wrath, the proof of which is seen in the present condition both of the Gentile and Jewish world.
