The revelation of righteousness is, while the Apostle writes, being made in the Person of Christ and in the salvation offered by him; the revelation of wrath is to be inferred from the actual condition, the degradation doubly degraded, in which sin leaves its votaries. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven, Ellicott says, inasmuch as the state of things in which it is exhibited is the divinely-inflicted penalty for previous guilt, and it is directed against that guilt, shown in outrage against all religion and all morality; the two words stand respectively for offences against religion and offences against morality. Who hold the truth in unrighteousness means rather who suppress and thwart the truth, the light of conscience that is in them, by unrighteousness: conscience tells them what is right, but the will, actuated by wicked motives, prevents them from obeying its dictates; the truth is their knowledge of right, from whatever source derived, which finds expression in conscience, and hold is the word translated hinder in the Thessalonian letter, having the force of to hold down or suppress. Of the nineteenth verse Ellicott says the Apostle goes on to show how the Gentiles came to have such a knowledge of right, and how they repressed and contravened it: they had it because all the knowledge that mankind generally possessed of God they also possessed, and so much as could be known without special revelation they knew. That which may be known means rather that which is generally and universally known, the truths of so-called natural religion; and is manifest in them means manifest or imprinted upon their consciences, because God had so imprinted it upon them, the marginal rendering to them being hardly tenable. Robertson notes Paul's use of the conjunction in Romans, now argumentative, now explanatory, now both as here, and says there is a parallel and antecedent revelation of God's wrath corresponding to the revelation of God's righteousness, this an unwritten revelation but plainly made known. The word for wrath is from a verb meaning to teem, to swell, and it is the temper of God towards sin, not rage, but, as Shedd says, the wrath of reason and law; the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel was necessary because of the failure of men to attain it without it, for God's wrath justly rested upon all, both Gentiles and Jews. Ungodliness is irreligion, want of reverence toward God; unrighteousness is lack of right conduct toward men, injustice, and this follows naturally from irreverence, since the basis of ethical conduct rests on the nature of God and our attitude toward him, otherwise the law of the jungle. Truth, Robertson says, is out in the open, but wicked men, so to speak, put it in a box and sit on the lid and hold it down in unrighteousness, their evil deeds concealing the open truth of God from men. Of the nineteenth verse he says the conjunction gives the reason for the revelation of God's wrath; that which may be known of God is a verbal adjective meaning either the known, as elsewhere in the New Testament, or the knowable, as usual in ancient Greek, that is, the knowledge of God; manifest in them means in their hearts and consciences; and God manifested it is not mere tautology.

Clarke says the apostle has now finished his preface and comes to the grand subject of the epistle, namely to show the absolute need of the Gospel of Christ because of the universal corruption of mankind, which was so great as to incense the justice of God and call aloud for the punishment of the world. He shows first that all the heathen nations were utterly corrupt and deserved this threatened punishment, which is the subject of the rest of this chapter; then that the Jews, notwithstanding the greatness of their privileges, were no better than the Gentiles, and therefore the wrath of God was revealed against them also; and then he returns upon both and proves that, as the Jews and Gentiles were equally corrupt, they could not be saved by the deeds of any law, that they stood equally in need of that salvation which God had provided, and that both were equally entitled to it, for God was the God of the Gentiles as well as of the Jews. By the wrath of God, Clarke says, we are not to understand any uneasy passion in the Divine Being, but the displeasure of his righteousness, which is expressed by the punishments inflicted on the ungodly, those who retain not God in their knowledge, and the unrighteous, those whose lives are profligate; as in the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed for the salvation of the ungodly, so is the wrath of God revealed against the workers of iniquity, and those who refuse to be saved in the way revealed by his mercy must be consumed in the way revealed by his justice. Ungodliness, from a negative prefix and a verb meaning I worship, is probably intended here to express atheism, polytheism and idolatry of every kind; unrighteousness, from a negative prefix and the word for justice, means everything contrary to strict morality, all viciousness and profligacy of conduct. In what sense, Clarke asks, could it be said that the heathen held the truth in unrighteousness, when they really had not that truth? Some think this refers to the conduct of their best philosophers, such as Socrates, Plato and Seneca, who knew much more of the Divine nature than they thought safe or prudent to discover, and who acted in many things contrary to the light which they enjoyed; others think it is spoken of the Gentiles in general, who either did know, or might have known, much of God from the works of creation. But Rosenmuller and some others contend, Clarke says, that the word here does not signify to hold but to hinder, and that the place should be translated, who through maliciousness hinder the truth, that is, prevent it from taking hold of their hearts and from governing their conduct; this is certainly a very usual acceptation of the verb, which Hesychius interprets to retain, to hinder, these men hindering by their vicious conduct the truth of God from being propagated in the earth. Of the nineteenth verse Clarke quotes Dr Taylor's paraphrase, that although the Gentiles had no written revelation, yet what may be known of God is everywhere manifest among them, God having made a clear discovery of himself to them; for his being and perfections, invisible to our bodily eyes, have been ever since the creation of the world evidently to be seen, if attentively considered, in the visible beauty, order and operations observable in the constitution and parts of the universe, especially his eternal power and universal dominion and providence, so that they cannot plead ignorance in excuse of their idolatry and wickedness. Wesley says there is no other way of obtaining life and salvation, and that having laid down his proposition the apostle now enters upon the proof of it; his first argument is that the law condemns all men as being under sin, and none therefore is justified by the works of the law, whence he infers that justification is by faith. The wrath of God is revealed not only by frequent and signal interpositions of divine providence, Wesley says, but likewise in the sacred oracles, and by us, his messengers. From heaven speaks the majesty of him whose wrath is revealed, his all-seeing eye, and the extent of his wrath: whatever is under heaven is under the effects of his wrath, believers in Christ excepted. Of men, Wesley says, means that Paul is speaking here of the Gentiles, and chiefly the wisest of them; who detain the truth, for it struggles against their wickedness; and in unrighteousness, the word here including ungodliness also. Of the nineteenth verse he says that what is to be known of God means those great principles which are indispensably necessary to be known, and that it is manifest in them because God has showed it to them by the light which enlightens every man that cometh into the world.

John Chrysostom bids us observe the discretion of Paul, how after encouraging by the gentler things he turns his discourse to the more fearful; for after saying that the Gospel is the cause of salvation and of life, that it is the power of God, that it gendereth salvation and righteousness, he mentions what might well make them fear that were heedless of it. Since in general most men are not drawn so much by the promise of what is good as by the fear of what is painful, Chrysostom says, he draws them on both sides; for this cause too did God not only promise a kingdom but also threaten hell, and the Prophets spake thus with the Jews, ever intermingling the evil with the good. Paul thus varies his discourse, yet not any how, but he sets first the good things and after the evil, to show that the former came of the guiding purpose of God but the latter of the wickedness of the backsliding; and in this way the prophet puts the good first, saying that if ye be willing and will obey me ye shall eat the good of the land, but if ye be not willing and will not obey me the sword shall devour you. But observe him, Chrysostom says: Christ came to bring forgiveness, righteousness, life, yet not in any way, but by the Cross, which is greatest too and wonderful, that he not only gave such things but that he also suffered such things; if then ye insolently scorn the gifts, then will the penalties await you. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that nature taught them both that God was the Maker of all things, and that they ought to avoid unrighteousness and seek righteousness, but they used not the instructions which it gave as they ought to have done, wherefore he threatened them with future punishment; and of the nineteenth verse he asks, who then gave them this knowledge, answering that God hath showed it unto them.

debates: Whether the word wrath imports anything in God: Barnes strips it of human passion, especially revenge, since God cannot be injured, and leaves Divine displeasure and a determination to express opposition to sin; Clarke calls it not an uneasy passion but the displeasure of his righteousness; Calvin denies it imports any emotion in God at all, referring it wholly to the perception and feeling of the sinner who is punished; Robertson keeps it as a temper of God towards sin, the wrath of reason and law

What from heaven adds: Barnes rejects five current readings and leaves only that the displeasure is made known by an arrangement showing it originated in heaven; Ellicott makes the state of things in which it is exhibited the divinely-inflicted penalty for previous guilt; Calvin refuses the adjectival sense and reads it of the wrath poured out on the whole world to the full extent of heaven; Wesley takes it of the majesty and the extent of the wrath, excepting believers in Christ

Whether the gospel itself reveals the wrath: Calvin records Stuart and Macknight connecting this verse to the sixteenth, and Pareus and Turrettin allowing that wrath as well as righteousness is revealed by the gospel, against Haldane's objection that the sins here are committed against the light of nature and not against the gospel; Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson locate the revelation outside the gospel, in the law, the conscience and the condition of the heathen world

Whether ungodliness and unrighteousness name two faults or one: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson keep them distinct as offences against God and against men, and Henry maps them onto the two tables; Calvin knows the distinction and rejects it, holding that both words designate one thing, ingratitude towards God

Where the knowledge of God is manifest: Ellicott says imprinted on their consciences and calls the marginal to them hardly tenable; Barnes glosses in them as among them and locates the knowledge with the philosophers rather than the mass; Calvin reads it as engraven on every heart, while noting Stuart's view that it means before their eyes, in the visible world
outliers: Barnes's analogy of the father opposed to disorder in his family and the ruler opposed to crime in the community, whose opposition we admire
Barnes's list of the modern ways of holding down the truth, ending with traffic in ardent spirits and the slave trade
Calvin's image of man created to be a spectator of the formed world, given eyes that by looking on so beautiful a picture he might be led up to the Author
Chrysostom's observation that most men are drawn less by the promise of good than by the fear of pain, so that God both promised a kingdom and threatened hell
Clarke's suggestion, reported from others, that the clause fits Socrates, Plato and Seneca, who knew more of the Divine nature than they thought safe or prudent to discover
Pareus's metaphor, quoted by Calvin's editor, of tyrants who by open violence oppress the innocent, bind them in chains and detain them in prison
Robertson's figure of wicked men putting the truth in a box and sitting on the lid

20.pericope_label: The invisible things clearly seen by the things that are made, and the darkened heart

schools.summary: Gill says that by the invisible things of him are meant not the angels, the invisible inhabitants of heaven, nor the unseen glories of another world, nor the decrees of God, nor the persons in the Godhead, but the perfections of God, or his properties, as the Arabic version reads it, and which are explained by his eternal power and Godhead. Of the twenty-first verse he says that though they had such a knowledge of the being and perfections of God, yet they glorified him not as God. Calvin cites a passage from Aristotle which remarkably coincides with a part of this verse, that God, unseen by any mortal nature, is to be seen by the works themselves; God is in himself invisible, but as his majesty shines forth in his works and in his creatures everywhere, men ought in these to acknowledge him, for they clearly set forth their Maker, and for this reason the Apostle says elsewhere that this world is a mirror, or the representation of invisible things. Paul does not mention all the particulars which may be thought to belong to God, Calvin says, but states that we can arrive at the knowledge of his eternal power and divinity; and Calvin's editor notes that the word used here is not the word used at Colossians, that Elsner and others make a difference between the two, the former meaning the divinity or majesty of God and the latter his nature or being, and that there seems to be the idea of goodness conveyed in the word used here, since in the following verse there are two things laid to the charge of the Gentiles which bear a reference to the two things said here, that they did not glorify him as God and were not thankful; God made himself known by his power as God, and by the beneficent exercise of that power he had laid a claim to the gratitude of his creatures, and Venema shows that goodness was regarded by many of the heathens as the primary attribute of Deity, the Greeks distinguishing the Supreme Being by the expression the good. He who is the framer of all things must necessarily be without beginning and from himself, Calvin says, and when we arrive at this point the divinity becomes known to us, which cannot exist except accompanied with all the attributes of a God, since they are all included under that idea; it hence clearly appears what the consequence is of having this evidence, that men cannot allege anything before God's tribunal for the purpose of showing that they are not justly condemned. Yet let this difference be remembered, Calvin says, that the manifestation of God, by which he makes his glory known in his creation, is, with regard to the light itself, sufficiently clear, but that on account of our blindness it is not found to be sufficient; we are not however so blind that we can plead our ignorance as an excuse for our perverseness. We conceive that there is a Deity, and then we conclude that whoever he may be he ought to be worshipped, but our reason here fails, because it cannot ascertain who or what sort of being God is; hence the Apostle in Hebrews ascribes to faith the light by which man can gain real knowledge from the work of creation, and not without reason, for we are prevented by our blindness so that we reach not to the end in view, yet we see so far that we cannot pretend any excuse. Both these things are strikingly set forth by Paul in the Acts, when he says that the Lord in past times left the nations in their ignorance, and yet that he left them not without witness, since he gave them rain and fertility from heaven; but this knowledge of God, which avails only to take away excuse, differs greatly from that which brings salvation. Of the twenty-first verse Calvin says Paul plainly testifies that God has presented to the minds of all the means of knowing him, having so manifested himself by his works that they must necessarily see what of themselves they seek not to know, that there is some God, for the world does not by chance exist, nor could it have proceeded from itself; but we must ever bear in mind the degree of knowledge in which they continued. No idea can be formed of God, Calvin says, without including his eternity, power, wisdom, goodness, truth, righteousness and mercy: his eternity appears evident because he is the maker of all things; his power, because he holds all things in his hand and continues their existence; his wisdom, because he has arranged things in such an exquisite order; his goodness, for there is no other cause than himself why he created all things, and no other reason why he should be induced to preserve them; his justice, because in his government he punishes the guilty and defends the innocent; his mercy, because he bears with so much forbearance the perversity of men; and his truth, because he is unchangeable. He then who has a right notion of God ought to give him the praise due to his eternity, wisdom, goodness and justice, Calvin says; and since men have not recognised these attributes in God, but have dreamt of him as though he were an empty phantom, they are justly said to have impiously robbed him of his own glory. Nor is it without reason that Paul adds that they were not thankful, for there is no one who is not indebted to God for numberless benefits, and even on this account alone, because he has been pleased to reveal himself to us, he has abundantly made us indebted to him. Of the words rendered they became vain in their imaginations Calvin's editor collects the renderings, that they became vain in their reasonings, or foolish by their own reasonings, and quotes Pareus at length: whatever the right reason within, or the frame of the world without, might have suggested respecting God, they indulged in pleasing speculations, specious reasonings, and subtle and frivolous conclusions; some denied the existence of a God, as Epicurus and Democritus; others doubted, as Protagoras and Diagoras; others affirmed the existence of many gods, and these, as the Platonics, maintained that they are not corporeal, while the Greeks and Romans held them to be so, who worshipped dead men, impious, cruel, impure and wicked; there were also the Egyptians, who worshipped as gods brute animals, oxen, geese, birds, crocodiles, yea, what grew in their gardens, garlics and onions; a very few, such as Plato and Aristotle, acknowledged one Supreme Being, but even these deprived him of his providence. Heart, after the manner of the Hebrews, Calvin says, is to be taken here for the whole soul, especially the mind; having forsaken the truth of God they turned to the vanity of their own reason, all the acuteness of which is fading and passes away like vapour, and thus their foolish mind, being involved in darkness, could understand nothing aright but was carried away headlong in various ways into errors and delusions. Their unrighteousness was this, Calvin says, that they quickly choked by their own depravity the seed of right knowledge, before it grew up to ripeness.

Barnes says the expression his invisible things refers to those things which cannot be perceived by the senses, and does not imply that there are any things pertaining to the Divine character which may be seen by the eye, but that there are things which may be known of him though not discoverable by the eye. What Paul means by the invisible things of God he specifies at the close of the verse, his eternal power and Godhead, and the affirmation extends only to that, the argument implying that this was enough to leave them without any excuse for their sins. The word creation may mean either the act of creating or, more commonly, the thing created, and the word from may mean since or may denote by means of; the latter is doubtless the true meaning, Barnes says, both because this is the common meaning of the word creation and because it accords with the design of the argument, which is not to state an historical fact but to show that they had the means of knowing their duty within their reach. Things that are made means not the original act of creation but the continual operations of God in his Providence, by what he is continually producing and accomplishing in the displays of his power and goodness. His eternal power implies two things, that the universe contains an exhibition of his power and that this power has existed from eternity; it does not mean that this power has been exerted from eternity, for the very idea of creation supposes that it had not, but that there is proof in the works of creation of power which must have existed from eternity. The proof of this was clear even to the heathen with their imperfect views of creation and of astronomy, Barnes says, the majesty and grandeur of the heavens striking their eye; but to us, under the full blaze of modern science, with our knowledge of the magnitude and distances and revolutions of the heavenly bodies, the proof of this power is much more grand and impressive, and the proof to human view is continually rising with every new discovery, for which he refers the reader to Chalmers's Astronomical Discourses and Dick's Christian Philosopher. God's power was called forth at the creation, Barnes says, and by that one great act he gave eternal demonstration that he was almighty; the proof is not weakened because we do not see the process of creation constantly going on, but is rather augmented by the fact that he sustains all things. Godhead means his Deity, Divinity, Divine nature or essence, a word not elsewhere used in the New Testament, and it proves that the supremacy of God was exhibited in the works of creation; it would not be proper to press the word as implying that all we know of God by revelation was known to the heathen, but that so much was known as to show his supremacy and the folly of idolatry. So that they are without excuse, Barnes says: it is implied that in order that men should be responsible they should have the means of knowledge, and that God does not judge them when their ignorance is involuntary; but where men have these means within their reach and will not avail themselves of them, all excuse is taken away. If this was true of the pagan world then, he asks, how much more is it true of the world now, and especially of that great multitude in Christian lands who have the Bible and never read it, who are within the reach of the sanctuary and never enter it, and who look upon the heavens and yet see no proof of the eternal power and Godhead of him who made them all; nay, there are those apprised of the discoveries of modern astronomy who yet do not seem to reflect that all these glories are proof of the existence of an eternal God, and for such there is no excuse or shadow of excuse to be offered in the day of doom. Of the twenty-first verse Barnes says the apostle is showing that it was right to condemn men for their sins, and that the true source of their idolatries was a corrupt and evil heart. That many of the philosophers of Greece and Rome had a knowledge of one God there can be no doubt, he says, as with Pythagoras, who had travelled extensively in Egypt and even in Palestine, and with Plato and his disciples, a point clearly shown by Cudworth in his Intellectual System and by Bishop Warburton in the Divine Legation of Moses; yet the knowledge of this great truth was not communicated to the people but confined to the philosophers, and not improbably one design of the mysteries celebrated throughout Greece was to keep up the knowledge of the one true God. Barnes quotes Gibbon's remark that the philosophers regarded all the popular superstitions as equally false, the common people as equally true, and the politicians as equally useful, which was probably a correct account of the prevalent feelings among the ancients; and he quotes Cicero, that there is something in the nature of things which the mind of man, which reason, which human power cannot effect, and certainly that which produces this must be better than man, and what can this be called but God, and again, what can be so plain and manifest, when we look at heaven and contemplate heavenly things, as that there is some Divinity of most excellent mind by which these things are governed. They glorified him not as God means they did not honour him as God, Barnes says, which was the true source of their abominations; to glorify him as God is to regard with proper reverence all his perfections and laws, and a willingness to honour him so would effectually restrain men from sin. The obligation to be thankful is plain and obvious, and the apostle regards this unwillingness to render gratitude as one of the causes of their subsequent corruption and idolatry, for the effect of ingratitude is to render the heart hard and insensible, men seek to forget the Being to whom they are unwilling to be grateful, and to do this they fix their affections on other things; hence the heathen expressed their gratitude not to God but to the sun and moon and stars, the mediums by which God bestows his favours. Became vain means they became foolish and frivolous in their thoughts and reasonings, employing themselves in useless and frivolous questions, and imaginations means properly thoughts, then reasonings, and also disputations, so that our word speculations would perhaps convey its meaning. The word heart is not infrequently used to denote the mind or the understanding, Barnes says: we apply it to the affections, and we speak of the head when we refer to the understanding, but this was not the case with the Hebrews, who spoke of the heart in this manner. The process stated in the verse is that men had the knowledge of God, that they refused to honour him when they knew him, that they were ungrateful, and that they then began to doubt, to reason, to speculate, and wandered far into darkness; and this is substantially the process by which men wander away from God now. Ellicott says that though there were parts of God's being into which the eye could not penetrate, still they were easily to be inferred from the character of his visible creation, which bore throughout the stamp of Omnipotence and Divinity; the invisible things of him are his invisible attributes, afterwards explained as his eternal power and Godhead. There is something of a play upon words here, Ellicott says: the unseen is seen, discerned by the eye of the mind, being inferred or perceived by the help of that which is made, that is, by the phenomena of external nature. His eternal power and Godhead is a summary expression for those attributes which, apart from revelation, were embodied in the idea of God, of which power is the most obvious; St Paul does not go into the questions that have been raised in recent times as to the other qualities which are to be inferred as existing in the Author of nature, but sums them up under a name that might be used as well by a Pagan philosopher as by a Christian. Divinity would be, perhaps, a more correct translation of the expression, Ellicott says, for what is meant is divine nature rather than divine personality; and they are without excuse, for they could not plead ignorance. Of the twenty-first verse he says they knew enough of God to know that thanks and praise were due to him, but neither of these did they offer: they put aside the natural instinct of adoration and fell to speculations which only led them farther from the truth, so that the new knowledge of which they went in quest proved to be fiction, and the old knowledge that they had was obscured and lost by their folly. Starting with two things, a portion of enlightenment on the one hand and the natural tendency of the human mind to error on the other, the latter prevailed and the former became eclipsed. They became vain in their imaginations means they were frustrated, reaching no good and sound result with their speculations; and their foolish heart is not the same word as fools in the next verse, but means their unintelligent heart, their heart which by itself was endowed with no special faculty of discernment such as to enable them to dispense with the enlightenment from above. Robertson says the invisible things of him is another verbal adjective, the attributes of God's nature being defined here as his everlasting power and divinity; the word for everlasting is used in the New Testament only here and in Jude, and the word for divinity corresponds to the Latin for divine, whereas at Colossians Paul uses the word answering to deity, the one being Divine Personality and the other Divine Nature and properties, as Sanday and Headlam put it. Since the creation of the world, Robertson says, means by God and unto God as antecedent to and superior to the world; are clearly seen is a compound with a perfective force, used only here in the New Testament, with direct reference to the word for invisible; being perceived is the participle of the verb meaning to use the intellect; and the phrase rendered that they may be without excuse more likely means so that they are without excuse, the word being another verbal adjective and meaning inexcusable here. Of the twenty-first verse Robertson says that knowing God is the participle of the verb meaning to know by personal experience, a definite statement that originally men had some knowledge of God, and that no people, however degraded, have yet been found without some yearning after a god; they knew more than they did, and this is the reason for the condemnation of the heathen, the failure to do what they know. Heart is the most comprehensive term for all our faculties, whether feeling, will or intellect, and may be the home of the Holy Spirit or of evil desires; the adjective rendered senseless is a verbal from the verb meaning to put together, so that it means unintelligent, not able to put together the manifest evidence about God; and so darkness settled down on their hearts.

Clarke says the invisible perfections of God are manifested by his visible works and may be apprehended by what he has made: their immensity showing his omnipotence, their vast variety and contrivance his omniscience, and their adaptation to the most beneficent purposes his infinite goodness and philanthropy. His eternal power is that all-powerful energy that ever was and ever will exist, Clarke says, so that ever since there was a creation to be surveyed there have been intelligent beings to make that survey; and Godhead is his acting as God in the government and support of the universe. His works prove his being, and the government and support of these works prove it equally, so that creation and providence form a twofold demonstration of God, first in the perfections of his nature and secondly in the exercise of those perfections. Of the twenty-first verse Clarke says that when they had thus acquired a general knowledge of the unity and perfections of the Divine nature, they glorified him not as God: they did not proclaim him to the people, but shut up his glory, as Bishop Warburton expresses it, in their mysteries, and gave the people, in exchange for an incorruptible God, an image made like to corruptible man. Wherefore God, in punishment for their sins, thus turning his truth into a lie, suffered even their mysteries, which they had erected for a school of virtue, to degenerate into an odious sink of vice and immorality, giving them up unto all uncleanness and vile affections. They did not give him that worship which his perfections required, Clarke says, and manifested no gratitude for the blessings they received from his providence, but became vain in their reasonings; this certainly refers to the foolish manner in which even the wisest of their philosophers discoursed about the Divine nature, and who can read their works without being struck with the vanity of their reasonings as well as with the stupidity of their nonsense when speaking about God. In short, their foolish, darkened minds sought God nowhere but in the place in which he is never to be found, the vile, corrupted and corrupting passions of their own hearts; and as they did not discover him there, they scarcely sought him anywhere else. Wesley says that those things of him which are invisible are seen by the eye of the mind, and that being understood means they are seen by them, and them only, who use their understanding. Of the twenty-first verse he says that the wiser heathens did know that there was one supreme God, yet from low and base considerations they conformed to the idolatry of the vulgar; they neither thanked him for his benefits nor glorified him for his divine perfection, but became vain, like the idols they worshipped, in their reasonings, which were various, uncertain and foolish. What a terrible instance have we of this, Wesley asks, in the writings of Lucretius, and what vain reasonings, and how dark a heart, amidst so pompous professions of wisdom.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that creation, and all things made in that creation, the succession of time, the change of seasons, the alternations of day and night, the labourings of the clouds, the blasts of the winds, the fruitfulness of plants and seeds, and the various other similar phenomena, plainly point out to us that God is both the Maker of all things and that he wisely holds the keys of the creation; for he who framed all things of his alone lovingkindness can never leave neglected what he hath brought into being. Wherefore the holy Apostle says not the invisible thing but invisible things, Theodoret notes, that is, his creation, his providence, his just sentence on each person, and all his various dispensations; most unpardonable then are they who, enjoying such a multitude of teachers, yet have received no improvement from so many lessons, for the works of creation themselves almost cry out against them. Of the twenty-first verse he says that they were aware of the existence of God, as they themselves testify by their continual use of his adorable name, while yet rejecting all suitable sentiments concerning him; and that they became vain in their imaginations and their foolish heart was darkened, for they followed senseless notions and welcomed the darkness of infidelity.

debates: What from the creation of the world means: Barnes takes the phrase instrumentally, by means of the universe rather than ever since the act of creating, arguing that the design is not to state an historical fact but to show the means of knowledge were within reach; Robertson keeps the temporal sense, since the creation of the world, and reads it as marking God antecedent and superior to the world

What the word rendered Godhead carries: Robertson distinguishes it from the word used at Colossians on Sanday and Headlam's terms, Divine Nature and properties as against Divine Personality, and Ellicott prefers divinity as a translation for the same reason; Calvin's editor, following Elsner and Venema, finds in it besides the idea of goodness, since the next verse charges both a failure to glorify and a failure to give thanks

How far the light of nature reaches: Calvin holds the manifestation sufficiently clear as regards the light itself but insufficient because of our blindness, so that we conclude a Deity ought to be worshipped but cannot ascertain who or what sort of being he is, this knowledge availing only to take away excuse; Barnes holds that they knew enough to show the folly of idolatry and turns the argument on Christian lands, where the discoveries of modern astronomy leave no shadow of excuse

What the philosophers did with what they knew: Barnes, citing Cudworth, Warburton, Gibbon and Cicero, holds that they knew one God but did not communicate it to the people, the mysteries perhaps serving to keep the knowledge alive; Clarke, citing Warburton too, turns this into the charge, that they shut up his glory in their mysteries, which were then suffered to degenerate into an odious sink of vice

Where the fault lay in the reasoning: Ellicott says they were frustrated and reached no sound result, the natural tendency to error prevailing over a portion of enlightenment; Calvin says they quickly choked by their own depravity the seed of right knowledge before it grew up to ripeness; Robertson says only that they failed to do what they knew
outliers: Barnes's reference to Chalmers's Astronomical Discourses and Dick's Christian Philosopher for the modern proof of eternal power
Calvin's citation of Aristotle, that God, unseen by any mortal nature, is to be seen by the works themselves
Cicero's question, quoted by Barnes, what can be so plain and manifest, when we look at heaven, as that there is some Divinity of most excellent mind by which these things are governed
Clarke's twofold demonstration, creation proving the perfections of God's nature and providence the exercise of them
Gibbon's summary, quoted by Barnes, that the philosophers held the popular superstitions equally false, the people equally true, and the politicians equally useful
Pareus's catalogue of pagan opinion, preserved by Calvin's editor, running from Epicurus and Protagoras down to the Egyptians who worshipped crocodiles and the garlic and onions of their gardens
Theodoret's list of the phenomena that point out the Maker, from the change of seasons and the labourings of the clouds to the fruitfulness of plants and seeds
Wesley's instance of vain reasoning amid pompous professions of wisdom, the writings of Lucretius

22.pericope_label: Professing themselves wise they became fools, changed the glory of God, and were given up

schools.summary: Gill says the learned men among the Gentiles first called themselves Sophi, wise men, and afterwards, to cover their wretched pride and vanity, Philosophers, lovers of wisdom, but notwithstanding all their arrogance and their large pretensions to wisdom they became fools. God is incorruptible and immortal in his nature, Gill says, and so is opposed to all corruptible creatures and things; he has a glory which is essential to him, and a manifestative one in the creatures, which is relative and of right belongs to him. His absolute essential glory cannot be changed, cannot be taken away from him, nor given to another, but his relative glory may be said to be changed when another is worshipped in his stead and called by his name. Of the twenty-fourth verse Gill says that God gave them up to uncleanness not by putting any into them, but by leaving them to the pollution of their nature, by withdrawing his providential restraints from them, and by giving them up to judicial hardness. Calvin says it is commonly inferred from this passage that Paul alludes to those philosophers who assumed to themselves in a peculiar manner the reputation of wisdom, and that the design of his discourse is to show that when the superiority of the great is brought down to nothing, the common people would have no reason to suppose they had anything worthy of being commended; but they seem to him to have been guided by too slender a reason, for it was not peculiar to the philosophers to suppose themselves wise in the knowledge of God, but it was equally common to all nations and to all ranks of men. There were indeed none who sought not to form some ideas of the majesty of God, Calvin says, and to make him such a God as they could conceive him to be according to their own reason; this presumption he holds is not learned in the schools but is innate, and comes with us, so to speak, from the womb, and it is evident that it is an evil which has prevailed in all ages, that men have allowed themselves every liberty in coining superstitions. The arrogance condemned here is this, that men sought to be of themselves wise, and to draw God down to a level with their own low condition, when they ought humbly to have given him his own glory; for Paul holds this principle, that none, except through their own fault, are unacquainted with the worship due to God. There is an obvious reason, Calvin adds, which contravenes the interpretation he rejects, namely that the error of forming an image of God did not originate with the philosophers, but they by their consent approved of it as received from others. Calvin's editor notes that Calvin is peculiar in his exposition of this verse, most critics agreeing that those referred to were the reputed learned among all nations, as Beza says, such as the Druids of the Gauls, the soothsayers of the Tuscans, the philosophers of the Greeks, the priests of the Egyptians, the magi of the Persians, the gymnosophists of the Indians and the Rabbins of the Jews; and he quotes Haldane, that this is the greatest unhappiness of man, not only not to feel his malady but to extract matter of pride from what ought to be his shame, and Hodge, that the higher the advancement of the nations in refinement and philosophy, the greater as a general rule the degradation and folly of their systems of religion, the ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans proving it as compared with the aborigines of America. Of the twenty-third verse Calvin says that, having feigned such a God as they could comprehend according to their carnal reason, they were very far from acknowledging the true God but devised a fictitious and new god, or rather a phantom; and Paul says that they changed the glory of God, for as though one substituted a strange child, so they departed from the true God. Nor are they to be excused for the pretence that they believe God dwells in heaven and count not the wood to be God but his image, Calvin says, for it is a high indignity to God to form so gross an idea of his majesty as to dare to make an image of him; and from the wickedness of such a presumption none were exempt, neither priests, nor statesmen, nor philosophers, of whom the most sound-minded, even Plato himself, sought to find out some likeness of God. The madness noticed here is that all attempted to make for themselves an image of God, which was a certain proof that their notions of God were gross and absurd; and first they befouled the majesty of God by forming him in the likeness of corruptible man, Calvin preferring this rendering to that of mortal man adopted by Erasmus, for Paul sets not the immortality of God in opposition to the mortality of man, but that glory which is subject to no defects to the most wretched condition of man. Then, being not satisfied with so great a crime, they descended even to beasts and to those of the most filthy kind, by which their stupidity appeared still more evident. Of the twenty-fourth verse Calvin says that, as impiety is a hidden evil, lest they should still find an evasion, Paul shows by a more palpable demonstration that they cannot escape but must be held fast by a just condemnation, since such fruits have followed this impiety as cannot be viewed otherwise than manifest evidences of the Lord's wrath; and as the Lord's wrath is always just, it follows that what has exposed them to condemnation must have preceded it. By comparing the vices of which they were guilty with the impiety of which he had before accused them, Calvin says, Paul shows that they suffered punishment through the just judgment of God, for since nothing is dearer to us than our own honour, it is extreme blindness when we fear not to bring disgrace on ourselves, and it is the most suitable punishment for a reproach done to the Divine Majesty. They would never have rolled themselves in lusts so filthy, after the manner of beasts, had not the majesty of God been provoked and incensed against them. As to the manner in which God gives up or delivers men to wickedness, Calvin says it is certain that he not only permits men to fall into sin by allowing them to do so and by conniving at them, but that he also, by his equitable judgment, so arranges things that they are led and carried into such madness by their own lusts as well as by the devil. He therefore adopts the word delivered according to the constant usage of Scripture, which word they forcibly wrest who think that we are led into sin only by the permission of God; for as Satan is the minister of God's wrath, and as it were the executioner, so he is armed against us, not through the connivance, but by the command of his judge. God, however, is not on this account cruel, Calvin says, nor are we innocent, inasmuch as Paul plainly shows that we are not delivered up into his power except when we deserve such a punishment; only we must make this exception, that the cause of sin is not from God, the roots of which ever abide in the sinner himself. His editor adds that Augustine uses stronger language still, that God delivered them up not only by sufferance and permission but by power, and as it were by an efficient operation, not by making evil their wills but by using them, being already evil, as he pleased, working many things both within and without them from which they take occasion to sin more grievously; and the editor calls this an awful view of God's proceedings towards those who wilfully resist the truth, but no doubt a true one. By connecting the lusts of man's heart with uncleanness, Calvin says, Paul indirectly intimates what sort of progeny our heart generates when left to itself; and the expression about their bodies is not without its force, for it significantly expresses how deep and indelible are the marks of infamy imprinted on our bodies.

Barnes says that professing themselves to be wise was the common boast of the philosophers of antiquity, the very word by which they chose to be called meaning literally lovers of wisdom. They became fools, he says, really foolish in their opinions and conduct, and there is something particularly pungent and cutting in the remark, and as true as it is pungent; sinners of all kinds are frequently spoken of as fools in the Scriptures, as void of understanding or moral sense, and the senses in which the word is applied here to the heathen are that their speculations and doctrines were senseless and that their conduct was corrupt. Of the twenty-third verse Barnes says that changed does not mean that they literally transmuted God himself, but that in their views they exchanged him, or changed him as an object of worship for idols; they produced no real change in the glory of the infinite God, but the change was in themselves. The glory means the majesty, the honour, and stands opposed to the degrading nature of their worship: instead of adoring a Being clothed with majesty and honour they bowed down to reptiles, exchanging a glorious object of worship for that which was degrading. The word uncorruptible is applied to God in opposition to man, Barnes says: God is unchanging, indestructible, immortal, and the word conveys also the idea that he is eternal; as he is incorruptible he is the proper object of worship, and in all the changes of life man may come to him assured that he is the same. An image is a representation or likeness of anything, whether made by painting or from wood or stone, and many of the images of the ancients were in the forms of men and women, many of their gods being heroes and benefactors who were deified, such as Jupiter and Hercules and Romulus, to whom temples and altars and statues were erected; it was proof of great degradation that they thus adored men with like passions as themselves. The ibis was adored with peculiar reverence among the Egyptians, Barnes says, on account of the great benefits resulting from its destruction of the serpents which would otherwise have overrun the country; the hawk was also adored in Egypt and the eagle at Rome, and as one great principle of pagan idolatry was to adore all objects from which important benefits were derived, it is probable that all birds would come in for a share of worship that rendered service in destroying noxious animals. The ox, under the name apis, was adored in Egypt, and even the dog and the monkey, and in imitation of the Egyptian ox the children of Israel made their golden calf; at this day, he adds, two of the most sacred objects of worship in Hindoostan are the cow and the monkey. Creeping things are reptiles, animals that have no feet or such short ones that they seem to creep on the ground, as Calmet defines them, so that lizards and serpents come under the description; the crocodile in Egypt was an object of adoration, and even the serpent, and so late as the second century of the Christian era there was a sect in Egypt called Ophites, from their worshipping a serpent, who even claimed to be Christians. There was scarcely an object, animal or vegetable, which the Egyptians did not adore, Barnes says: the leek and the onion were objects of worship, and men bowed down to the sun and moon, to animals, to vegetables and to reptiles; Egypt was the source of the views of religion that pervaded other nations, and hence their worship partook of the same wretched and degrading character. Of the twenty-fourth verse he says that here is traced the practical tendency of heathenism, not as an innocent and harmless system but as resulting in the most gross and shameless acts of depravity. God gave them up means he abandoned them, or ceased to restrain them, and suffered them to act out their sentiments and to manifest them in their life; this does not imply that he exerted any positive influence in inducing them to sin, any more than it would if we should seek by argument and entreaty to restrain a headstrong youth and, when neither would prevail, should leave him to act out his propensities. It is implied in this, Barnes says, that the tendency of man was to these sins, that the tendency of idolatry was to promote them, and that all that was needful in order that men should commit them was for God to leave them to follow the devices and desires of their own hearts. To uncleanness means to impurity or moral defilement, and through the lusts of their own hearts means in consequence of their own evil and depraved passions and desires. Ellicott says of they became fools that they were made fools: it is not merely that they expose their real folly, but that folly is itself judicially inflicted by God as a punishment for the first step of declension from him. Of the twenty-third verse he says the anthropomorphism applies more especially to the religions of Greece and Rome, representations of the Deity under the form of beasts being most common in Egypt; and he quotes at length the account of Egyptian worship, that it was universally paid to cattle, lions, cats, dogs, weasels and otters, among the birds to the sparrow-hawk, the hoopoe, the stork and the sheldrake, and among fish to the eel and lepidotus, besides other creatures that received local worship: the sheep was worshipped in Sais and the Thebais but sacrificed and eaten in Lycopolis, the hippopotamus in the district of Papremis and the crocodile in the greater part of the land were considered specially sacred, but the latter was chased and eaten in Tentyra and Apollinopolis, and the sacred serpent which served as head-gear for Isis had holes in all the temples where it was fed with veal fat; and among the sacred beasts, Ellicott quotes Doellinger as saying, the first place was given to the divine bulls, of which the Egyptians worshipped four. No doubt the images in Greece and the beasts in Egypt were by some of the people regarded only as symbols of the Deity, Ellicott says, but it was in all probability only a small minority who were capable of drawing this distinction. Robertson says that professing themselves to be wise follows a regular Greek idiom, that became vain is an ingressive aorist passive from a word meaning empty, empty reasonings as often today, and that became fools is likewise ingressive, an oxymoron or sharp saying, true and one that cuts to the bone. For the likeness of an image means a likeness which consists in an image or copy, and Paul shows indignant contempt for these grotesque efforts to present pictures of a deity that had been lost; why is it, Robertson asks, that heathen images of gods in the form of men and beasts are so horrible to look upon. Of the twenty-fourth verse he speaks of Paul's inexorable logic, and says that these people had already wilfully deserted God, who merely left them to their own self-determination and self-destruction, part of the price of man's moral freedom, the withdrawal of God's restraint sending men deeper down. Three times Paul uses the same verb in this passage, Robertson notes, not three stages in the giving over but a repetition of the same withdrawal; the words sound to us like clods on the coffin as God leaves men to work their own wicked will. That their bodies should be dishonoured expresses a contemplated result, and Robertson adds that Christians had a new sense of dignity for the body, whereas heathenism left its stamp on the bodies of men and women.

Clarke says that professing themselves to be wise is most strikingly true of all the ancient philosophers, whether Greeks or Romans, as their remaining works sufficiently testify, and that the Greek word signifies not merely the professing but the assumption of the philosophic character. A dispassionate examination of the doctrine and lives of the most famed philosophers of antiquity, of every nation, will show that they were darkened in their mind and irregular in their conduct, Clarke says; it was from the Christian religion alone that true philosophy and genuine philosophers sprang. Of the twenty-third verse he says the finest representation of their deities was in the human figure, and on such representative figures the sculptors spent all their skill, hence the Hercules of Farnese, the Venus of Medicis and the Apollo of Belvidere; and when they had formed their gods according to the human shape they endowed them with human passions, and as they clothed them with attributes of extraordinary strength, beauty and wisdom, not having the true principles of morality, they represented them as slaves to the most disorderly and disgraceful passions, excelling in irregularities the most profligate of men. To birds refers to the eagle of Jupiter among the Romans and the ibis and hawk among the Egyptians, Clarke says, which were all sacred animals; four-footed beasts to the apis or white ox among the Egyptians, from which the idolatrous Israelites took their golden calf, the goat, the monkey and the dog being also sacred among the same people; and creeping things to such as the crocodile and the scarabeus or beetle. Of the twenty-fourth verse Clarke says they had filled up the measure of their iniquities, and God, by permitting them to plunge into all manner of irregularities, thus by one species of sin inflicted punishment on another; and between themselves means of themselves, of their own free accord, none inciting, none impelling. Wesley says they changed the glory of God with the utmost folly, and that here are three degrees of ungodliness and of punishment, the first described in the verses that follow this one, the second in the two after those, and the third in the twenty-eighth and following verses, the punishment in each case being expressed by God gave them up. If a man will not worship God as God, Wesley says, he is so left to himself that he throws away his very manhood; and reptiles, or creeping things, means such as beetles and various kinds of serpents. One punishment of sin is from the very nature of it, he adds, another, as here, is from vindictive justice; ungodliness and uncleanness are frequently joined in Scripture, as are the knowledge of God and purity; and God gave them up by withdrawing his restraining grace.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that Paul increases their reprobation by the very name they gave themselves, in that, while calling themselves wise, they proved by their works that they were void of understanding. Of the twenty-third verse he says that, not choosing to perceive that the Maker of all things is superior to decay and far above all that is seen, they called the likenesses of their own bodies gods; for indeed it was not intelligences, which are invisible, that their statuaries, sculptors and painters endeavoured to convey representations of, but perishable mortal bodies. Nor was this impiety enough, Theodoret says, but they must needs moreover worship the images of birds, beasts and creeping things; and while they should rather have considered that some of these men eat as food, some loathe as unclean, and some avoid as noxious, in their excess of madness and folly they made the likeness of these very things, which men thus ate, loathed or killed, into gods. Of the twenty-fourth verse he says that Paul puts gave them up for permitted, and means that, seeing them willing neither by the works of creation to be led up to the Creator, nor by the judgment of reason to choose the better and avoid the worse in practice, God deprived them of his special providence and suffered them to be carried about like an unsteady vessel, no longer enduring to direct those who had fallen into the grossest impiety, productive of a lawless life.

debates: Who is meant by those professing themselves wise: Gill, Barnes and Clarke take it of the philosophers, Clarke finding the charge strikingly true of all the ancients whether Greek or Roman; Calvin denies the restriction and calls the presumption innate and common to all nations and ranks, adding that the error of image-making did not originate with the philosophers at all; Calvin's own editor marks him as peculiar here and sets Beza's roll of Druids, soothsayers, priests, magi, gymnosophists and Rabbins against him

Whether God's giving them up is permission or act: Theodoret says Paul puts gave them up for permitted, Barnes denies any positive influence, Wesley makes it the withdrawing of restraining grace and Clarke a permitting them to plunge; Calvin says they forcibly wrest the word who make it permission only, since Satan is armed against us not by God's connivance but by the command of his judge, and his editor quotes Augustine for a delivering up not only by sufferance but as it were by an efficient operation

Whether the three times God gave them up mark stages: Wesley finds three degrees of ungodliness and of punishment answering to three groups of verses; Robertson denies any progression and calls them a repetition of the same withdrawal

How far the image-worshipper is excused by taking the image for a symbol: Calvin refuses the plea outright, since to dare make an image at all is a gross idea of the divine majesty, and notes that even Plato sought some likeness of God; Ellicott allows that some regarded the images and beasts as symbols only, but thinks that a small minority

Whether the folly was self-exposed or inflicted: Barnes and Robertson take became fools as a description, pungent and cutting to the bone; Ellicott takes the passive strictly, that they were made fools, the folly being judicially inflicted as punishment for the first step of declension
outliers: Barnes's Ophites, a second-century sect in Egypt who worshipped a serpent and claimed to be Christians
Clarke's examples of the finest human representations of deity, the Hercules of Farnese, the Venus of Medicis and the Apollo of Belvidere

Doellinger's account, quoted by Ellicott, of the sheep worshipped in Sais and eaten in Lycopolis, the crocodile sacred in most of Egypt but chased and eaten in Tentyra, and the sacred serpent fed with veal fat in holes in all the temples
Gill's note that the learned first called themselves wise men and afterwards, to cover their pride, lovers of wisdom

Hodge's rule, quoted by Calvin's editor, that the higher a nation's refinement the greater the degradation of its religion, the Egyptians, Greeks and Romans proving it against the aborigines of America
Robertson's figure of the threefold gave them up sounding like clods on the coffin
Theodoret's observation that the creatures made into gods were the very ones men ate as food, loathed as unclean, or avoided as noxious

25.pericope_label: Worshipping the creature rather than the Creator, and given up to passions against nature

schools.summary: Gill says that what was changed was not the truth of the Gospel, which they were unacquainted with, but that which might be known of God as true and was known of them by the light of nature, or the true God himself, whom they changed into a lie by ascribing to false deities, which were lying vanities, those things which were known of God, and by worshipping them instead of him. Of the twenty-sixth verse Gill says that because of their idolatrous practices God left them to very dishonourable actions, both among the men and the women; and of the twenty-seventh, that the sin here designed is the one called sodomy from Sodom, the place where we first hear of it. Calvin says Paul repeats what he had said before, though in different words, in order to fix it deeper in our minds: when the truth of God is turned to a lie, his glory is obliterated, and it is then but just that they should be besprinkled with every kind of infamy who strive to take away from God his honour and to reproach his name. He points out especially the sin of idolatry, Calvin says, for religious honour cannot be given to a creature without taking it away, in a disgraceful and sacrilegious manner, from God; and vain is the excuse that images are worshipped on God's account, since God acknowledges no such worship nor regards it as acceptable, and the true God is not then worshipped at all, but a fictitious God whom the flesh has devised for itself. The words the truth of God and a lie are Hebraistic in their meaning, Calvin says, signifying the true God and an idol, the word which means a lie being often applied in Hebrew to anything made to be worshipped; and his editor notes that Stuart renders the sentence, who exchanged the true God for a false one, while Wolfius objects to this view and prefers to take the truth of God as the truth made known to the Gentiles, which they changed into those insane and absurd notions into which they were led by their reasonings. The editor also collects the renderings of the preposition: Erasmus above the creator, Luther rather than the Creator, Beza to the neglect of the Creator, and Grotius in the place of the Creator, of which the two last are more consonant with the general tenor of the context, since the persons here spoken of did not worship God at all, and the preposition is evidently used in the sense of exclusion and opposition, as in the phrases contrary to the law and contrary to nature. What is added of God's being blessed for ever, Calvin explains as said for the purpose of exposing idolaters to greater reproach, in this way, that he is one whom they ought alone to have honoured and worshipped, and from whom it was not right to take away anything, not even the least. Of the twenty-sixth verse Calvin says that, after having introduced as it were an intervening clause, Paul returns to what he had before stated respecting the judgment of God, and brings as the first example the dreadful crime of unnatural lust; it hence appears that they not only abandoned themselves to beastly lusts but became degraded beyond the beasts, since they reversed the whole order of nature. He then enumerates a long catalogue of vices which had existed in all ages and then prevailed everywhere without any restraint, Calvin says; and it is not to the purpose to say that every one was not laden with so great a mass of vices, for in arraigning the common baseness of men it is proof enough if all to a man are constrained to acknowledge some faults. We must consider that Paul here records those abominations which had been common in all ages and were at that time especially prevalent everywhere, for it is marvellous how common then was that filthiness which even brute beasts abhor, and some of these vices were even popular; and though all were not murderers, or thieves, or adulterers, yet there were none who were not found polluted by some vice or another. He calls those vile which are shameful even in the estimation of men, and which redound to the dishonouring of God. Of the twenty-seventh verse Calvin says they indeed deserved to be blinded, so as to forget themselves and not to see anything befitting them, who through their own malignity closed their eyes against the light offered them by God, that they might not behold his glory; in short, they who were not ashamed to extinguish, as much as they could, the glory of God, which alone gives us light, deserved to become blind at noonday.

Matthew Henry says that in the horrid depravity of the heathen the truth of our Lord's words was shown, that light was come into the world but men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil, for he that doeth evil hateth the light; the truth was not to their taste, and we all know how soon a man will contrive, against the strongest evidence, to reason himself out of the belief of what he dislikes. But a man cannot be brought to greater slavery, Henry says, than to be given up to his own lusts; as the Gentiles did not like to keep God in their knowledge, they committed crimes wholly against reason and their own welfare. The nature of man, whether pagan or Christian, is still the same, he says, and the charges of the apostle apply more or less to the state and character of men at all times, till they are brought to full submission to the faith of Christ and renewed by Divine power; there never yet was a man who had not reason to lament his strong corruptions and his secret dislike to the will of God. Therefore this chapter is a call to self-examination, Henry concludes, the end of which should be a deep conviction of sin, and of the necessity of deliverance from a state of condemnation.

Barnes says this is a repetition of the earlier declaration in another form, and that the phrase the truth of God is a Hebrew phrase meaning the true God; in such a case, where two nouns come together, one is employed as an adjective to qualify the other, and most commonly the latter of the two is so used, but sometimes the former, as here. God is called the true God in opposition to idols, which are called false gods, and into a lie means into idols or false gods, idols being not infrequently called falsehood and lies because they are not true representations of God. The creature means created things, as the sun, moon and animals; and of the doxology Barnes says it was not uncommon to add an ascription of praise to God when his name was mentioned, as the Jews also usually did, in this way preserving veneration for the name of God and accustoming themselves to speak of him with reverence. He quotes Stuart, that the Mohammedans borrowed this custom from the Jews and practise it to a great extent, and that Tholuck mentions an Arabic manuscript in the library at Berlin containing an account of heresies in respect to Islamism, in which, as often as the writer has occasion to mention the name of a new heretical sect, he adds that God be exalted above all which they say. Amen is a Hebrew word denoting strong affirmation, so let it be, and implies the solemn assent of the writer to what was just said; and Barnes adds that it is mentioned of the honourable Robert Boyle that he never mentioned the name of God without a solemn pause, denoting his profound reverence, a practice which would tend eminently to prevent an unholy familiarity in regard to the sacred name of the Most High. Of the twenty-sixth verse Barnes says that in the previous verses Paul had stated their speculative belief and now proceeds to show its practical influence on their conduct. The great object of the apostle here, he says, is to show the state of the heathen world and to prove that they had need of some other way of justification than the law of nature, and for this purpose it was necessary for him to enter into a detail of their sins; the sins he proceeds to specify are the most indelicate, vile and degrading which can be charged on man, but this is not the fault of the apostle, for if they existed it was necessary for him to charge them on the pagan world, his argument not being complete without it. The shame is not in specifying them, Barnes says, but in their existence, not in the apostle but in those who practised them and imposed on him the necessity of accusing them of these enormous offences; and the mere fact of his charging them with these sins is strong presumptive proof of their being practised, since if they did not exist it would be easy for them to deny it and put him to the proof, and no man would venture charges like these without evidence. But this is not all, he adds, for there is still abundant proof on record in the writings of the heathen themselves that these crimes were known and extensively practised, and he refers the reader to the Greek and Roman writers and to Tholuck on the State of the Heathen World. Of the twenty-seventh verse Barnes says the sin specified is that which was the shameful sin of Sodom, and which from that has been called sodomy; it would scarcely be credible that man had been guilty of a crime so base and degrading unless there were ample and full testimony to it, and the evidence that the apostle did not bring a railing accusation against the heathen world is too painfully clear. It has been a matter of controversy, he says, whether the love of boys among the ancients was not a pure and harmless love, but the evidence is against it, as Dr Leland has shown; and the crime with which the apostle charges the Gentiles was by no means confined to the lower classes of the people. He assembles a long roll of witnesses: Virgil speaks of such an attachment without seeming to feel the necessity of a blush for it; Maximus Tyrius says that in the time of Socrates this vice was common among the Greeks, and is at pains to vindicate Socrates from it as almost a solitary exception; Cicero says that Dicearchus had accused Plato of it, and probably not unjustly, that the practice was common among the Greeks, and that their poets and great men and even their learned men and philosophers not only practised but gloried in it, and that it was the custom not of particular cities only but of Greece in general; Xenophon says that it is so common that in many places it is established by the public laws, alluding particularly to Sparta; Plato says the Cretians practised it and justified themselves by the example of Jupiter and Ganymede; Aristotle says that among the Cretians there was a law encouraging it; Plutarch says it was practised at Thebes and at Ellis, and that Solon, the great lawgiver of Athens, was not proof against beautiful boys; Diogenes Laertius says it was practised by the stoic Zeno; among the Romans, Cicero introduces without any mark of disapprobation a man of the first rank freely owning it and quoting ancient philosophers in vindication of it; and Seneca speaks of flocks and troops of boys, distinguished by their colours and nations, great care being taken to train them up for this employment. There is not the least evidence that this was confined to Greece and Rome, Barnes says, and he cites a traveller's account of the empire of China to the same effect; if such was the state of the pagan world, then surely the argument of the apostle is well sustained, that there was need of some other plan of salvation than was taught by the light of nature. Receiving in themselves means, Barnes says, that the effect of such passions was to enfeeble the body, to produce premature old age, disease, decay and an early death, as the history of man amply proves; but the effect on the body was not all, for it tended to debase the mind, to sink man below the level of the brute, to destroy the sensibility, and to sear the conscience as with a hot iron. Ellicott says that they ceased to worship God as he is, in his own true essential nature, and worshipped false gods instead; the phrase into a lie is literally with a lie, the lie being regarded as the instrument by which the substitution is made, and by a lie is meant here false gods, who are the supreme embodiment of falsehood. The introduction of the doxology in this verse, Ellicott says, is due to an impulse of reverential feeling: shocked at the language which he finds himself using, and at the connection in which the most Holy Name has been mentioned, the Apostle turns aside for a moment to testify to his own humble adoration. Of the twenty-seventh verse he says that in themselves means upon themselves, upon their own persons thus shamefully dishonoured; that the error is the turning from God to idols; and that the recompense of the error is seen in these unnatural excesses to which the heathen have been delivered up. Robertson says the verb rendered exchanged is an old word for exchanging in trade, and asks what a bargain they made, the truth of God for the lie, quoting Bengel's phrase, the price of mythology; the verb rendered worshipped is an old one used in late Greek for worship, and rather than the Creator means that, placed side by side, the Creator and the creature, they preferred the creature. The doxology, he adds, is one of Paul's, which may come at any moment when he is greatly stirred. Of the twenty-sixth verse Robertson says the word rendered passions originally meant any feeling whether good or bad, but in the New Testament always in a bad sense, and that the degradation of sex is what Paul here notes as one of the results of heathenism, the loss of God in the life of man: they passed by the Creator. Of the twenty-seventh he says the verb rendered turned is a causative aorist of an old verb meaning to burn out or to inflame; that the word rendered recompense is a late Pauline word, used elsewhere in a good sense and here in a bad one; and that the imperfect rendered which was due expresses an obligation still on them coming down from the past, so that this debt will be paid in full, nature attending to that in their own bodies and souls.

Clarke says that in the place of the true worship of God they established idolatry, and that in various places of Scripture idols are termed lies; the true God was known among the primitive inhabitants of the earth, and those who first became idolaters literally changed the truth of God into a lie, for they did know the true God but they put idols in his place. Of the twenty-sixth verse Clarke says their system of idolatry necessarily produced all kinds of impurity, and asks how it could be otherwise when the highest objects of their worship were themselves represented as adulterers, fornicators and prostitutes of the most infamous kind, such as Jupiter, Apollo, Mars and Venus. Of the abominable evils with which the apostle charges the Gentiles in this and the following verse, Clarke says, he could produce a multitude of proofs from their own writings, but it is needless to make the subject plainer than the apostle has left it. Of the twenty-seventh verse he says that both the women and the men, by their unnatural prostitutions, enervated their bodies, so that barrenness prevailed, together with those disorders which are necessarily attendant on such practices. Wesley says that they changed the truth, that is, the true worship of God, into a lie, that is, false and abominable idolatries, and that they worshipped inwardly and served outwardly. Of the twenty-sixth verse he says that God gave them up to vile affections, to which the heathen Romans were then abandoned to the last degree, and none more than the emperors themselves; and of the twenty-seventh, that they received the just recompense of their error, their idolatry being punished with that unnatural lust which was as horrible a dishonour to the body as their idolatry was to God.

John Chrysostom says that all these affections were vile, but chiefly the mad lust after males, for the soul is more the sufferer in sins, and more dishonoured, than the body in diseases. But behold how here too, as in the case of the doctrines, Paul deprives them of excuse, Chrysostom says, by saying of the women that they changed the natural use; for no one can say that it was by being hindered of legitimate intercourse that they came to this pass, or that it was from having no means to fulfil their desire that they were driven into this monstrous insaneness, since the changing implies possession, as he had said when discoursing upon the doctrines that they changed the truth of God for a lie. With regard to the men he shows the same thing by saying, leaving the natural use of the woman, Chrysostom says, and in a like way puts these also out of all means of defending themselves, charging them not only that they had the means of gratification and left that which they had and went after another, but that having dishonoured that which was natural they ran after that which was contrary to nature. But that which is contrary to nature hath in it an irksomeness and displeasingness, Chrysostom says, so that they could not fairly allege even pleasure, for genuine pleasure is that which is according to nature; and when God hath left one, then all things are turned upside down, so that not only was their doctrine Satanical but their life too was diabolical. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that impiety was the foundation of their iniquities, and by both they became stripped of the Divine grace; the name God is what Paul here means by the truth of God, and an idol made with hands by a lie, because that when they ought to have worshipped the true God they offered the adoration belonging to him to the creature instead. And to the same reproach do they lie open, Theodoret adds, who call the only-begotten Son of God a creature and yet worship him as God; for they ought either, admitting his divinity, to rank him not with created things but with God who begat him, or else, pronouncing him a created being, not to pay adoration to him as divine. Of the twenty-seventh verse he says that iniquity walks hand in hand with impiety, so that as they had changed the truth of God into a lie, so did they in like manner exchange the proper object and exercise of the passions for that which was abominable; and that infamy is the severest penalty of such affections, so that what not even a victorious enemy had ever attempted to inflict on them, they themselves willingly ran into, bringing on themselves a punishment heavier than any judge would impose.
