debates: How to render the preposition in worshipped the creature more than the Creator: Calvin's editor sets out Erasmus's above the creator, Luther's rather than the Creator, Beza's to the neglect of the Creator and Grotius's in the place of the Creator, and prefers the last two, since those described did not worship God at all and the preposition elsewhere marks exclusion and opposition; Robertson keeps the comparison, that placed side by side they preferred the creature

What the truth of God changed into a lie means: Barnes and Calvin read both terms as Hebraisms for the true God and an idol, and Clarke and Wesley take the change to be from true worship to idolatry; Calvin's editor reports Wolfius objecting to Stuart's rendering and preferring the truth made known to the Gentiles, changed into the insane notions to which their reasonings led them; Ellicott makes the lie the instrument rather than the object, literally with a lie

How far the charge should be documented: Barnes defends the making of it, argues that the accused could have denied it had it been false, and then assembles witnesses from Virgil, Cicero, Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius and Seneca; Clarke says he could produce a multitude of proofs from their own writings but that it is needless to make the subject plainer than the apostle has left it

What the recompense received in themselves is: Ellicott makes it the unnatural excesses themselves, the error being the turn from God to idols, and Theodoret and Wesley agree, Theodoret calling infamy the severest penalty of such affections; Barnes and Clarke take it bodily, of enervated frames, barrenness and premature decay; Robertson leaves it open, saying only that the debt will be paid in full in their own bodies and souls

Whether a catalogue of vices convicts everyone: Calvin answers that it is not to the purpose to say that no one man was laden with the whole mass, since in arraigning the common baseness of men it is proof enough that all are constrained to acknowledge some fault; Henry generalises further, that the charges apply more or less to men at all times, pagan or Christian
outliers: Barnes's report, from Tholuck, of an Arabic manuscript at Berlin whose author adds after each heretical sect that God be exalted above all which they say
Barnes's anecdote that Robert Boyle never mentioned the name of God without a solemn pause
Bengel's phrase, quoted by Robertson, that the exchange was the price of mythology
Chrysostom's argument that the word changed implies possession, so that no one may plead he was hindered of what was lawful
Chrysostom's further point that what is contrary to nature carries an irksomeness with it, so that pleasure cannot fairly be alleged, genuine pleasure being according to nature
Theodoret's turn of the verse against those who call the only-begotten Son a creature and yet adore him as God
Theodoret's observation that they voluntarily ran into what not even a victorious enemy had attempted to inflict on them

28.pericope_label: Given over to a reprobate mind, and the catalogue of vices that follows

schools.summary: Gill says this accounts for the justness of the divine procedure in leaving them to commit such scandalous iniquities, since they had some knowledge of God by the light of nature and yet did not care to retain it. Of the twenty-ninth verse he says that from here to the end of the chapter follows a large and black catalogue of the sad characters of the Gentiles, and of the best men they had among them; for the apostle is all along speaking not of the common people but of their wise professors and moral instructors, than which there never was a more wicked set of men that ever lived upon the face of the earth, who under the guise of morality were guilty of the greatest pride and covetousness and of the most filthy debaucheries imaginable. The word unrighteousness, Gill says, includes in it all manner of sin and wickedness in general, fitly expresses the condition of fallen men destitute of a righteousness, designs every violation of the law respecting our neighbour, and is opposed to that vain conceit of righteousness which these men had. Calvin says there is an evident comparison to be observed in these words, by which is strikingly set forth the just relation between sin and punishment: as they chose not to continue in the knowledge of God, which alone guides our minds to true wisdom, the Lord gave them a perverted mind, which can choose nothing that is right. There is a correspondence between the two words, Calvin says, the verb meaning to test a thing, as metal by fire, then to distinguish between what is genuine and what is not, and also to approve of what is good and valuable; and the adjective derived from it is applied to adulterated money, to men not able to bear the test, and to earth that is to produce fruits. The nearest alliteration that can be presented, his editor says, is that as they did not deem it worth while to acknowledge God, God delivered them up to a worthless mind, that is, a mind unfit to discern between right and wrong; and he surveys the attempts of others, Beza's mind void of all judgment, Locke's unsearching mind, Macknight's unapproving mind and Doddridge's undiscerning mind, none of which exactly convey the right idea, though the last comes nearest, since what is meant is an unattesting mind, not capable of bringing things to the test, not able to distinguish between things of the most obvious nature. To acknowledge God is literally to have God in recognition, and Venema says this is a purely Greek idiom, adducing parallels from Herodotus and Xenophon. By saying that they chose not, Calvin says, it is the same as though Paul had said that they pursued not after the knowledge of God with the attention they ought to have done, but on the contrary turned away their thoughts resignedly from God; he then intimates that they, making a depraved choice, preferred their own vanities to the true God, and thus the error by which they were deceived was voluntary. As he had hitherto referred only to one instance of abomination, which prevailed indeed among many but was not common to all, Calvin says, Paul begins here to enumerate vices from which none could be found free; for though every vice did not appear in each individual, yet all were guilty of some vices, so that every one might separately be accused of manifest depravity. As Paul calls them things not convenient, understand him as saying that they were inconsistent with every decision of reason and alien to the duties of men, for he mentions it as an evidence of a perverted mind that men addicted themselves, without any reflection, to those vices which common sense ought to have led them to renounce. But it is labour in vain so to connect these vices as to make them dependent one on another, Calvin says, since this was not Paul's design, but he set them down as they occurred to his mind. By unrighteousness Calvin understands the violation of justice among men, by not rendering to each his due; he renders the next word, according to the opinion of Ammonius, who teaches that the wicked man is the doer of evil, as practised wickedness or licentiousness in doing mischief, whereas maliciousness is that depravity and obliquity of mind which leads us to do harm to our neighbour. For the word rendered fornication he puts lust, though he does not object if one prefers fornication, since Paul means the inward passion as well as the outward act; and his editor quotes Stuart that the word has an extended sense. Under the word improperly rendered debate, Calvin says, Paul includes quarrels, fightings and seditions; and the word rendered malignity means a notorious and uncommon wickedness, that is, when a man, covered over as it were with hardness, has become hardened in a corrupt course of life by custom and evil habit.

Barnes says this was the true source of their crimes, that they did not choose to acknowledge God: it was not because they could not, but because they were displeased with God and chose to forsake him and follow their own passions and lusts, and this was the first step in their sin. To a reprobate mind means to a mind destitute of judgment, Barnes says, and in the Greek the same word is used here which in another form occurs in the previous part of the verse and is translated like; the apostle meant doubtless to retain a reference to that, so that as they did not approve or choose to retain God, he gave them up to a mind disapproved, rejected, reprobate, the state of their minds being such that God could not approve it. It does not mean that they were reprobate by any arbitrary decree, Barnes insists, but that as a consequence of their headstrong passions and their determination to forget him, he left them to a state of mind which was evil and which he could not approve; and things not convenient means things not fit or proper, disgraceful and shameful. Of the twenty-ninth verse Barnes says that being filled is a strong phrase, denoting that these things were so often practised that it might be said they were full of them. Unrighteousness denotes injustice or iniquity in general; fornication denotes all illicit intercourse, and was a common and almost universal sin among the ancients as among the moderns; wickedness denotes a desire of injuring others, or malice, that depravity and obliquity of mind which strives to produce injury on others, for which Barnes cites Calvin; covetousness is avarice, or the desire of obtaining that which belongs to others, a vice particularly common where men were desirous of luxury, and Rome was particularly desirous of the wealth of other nations, hence its extended wars; and the next word denotes evil in general, rather the act of doing wrong than the desire, which was expressed before. Envy Barnes defines from Webster as pain or mortification excited by another's prosperity, accompanied with some degree of hatred, and often with an effort to depreciate the person; benevolence rejoices at the happiness of others, but envy exists almost everywhere, and he quotes Pope, that all human virtue finds envy never conquered but by death. Murder means all manslaughter or taking of human life except as the punishment of crime, Barnes says, and it has prevailed in all communities but was particularly prevalent in Rome; it is necessary only to refer the reader to the common events of Roman history, the assassinations, the deaths by poison and the destruction of slaves, but in a special manner the charge was properly alleged on account of the inhuman contests of the gladiators in the amphitheatres, which were common at Rome and a favourite amusement. Originally captives, slaves and criminals were trained for combat, Barnes says, but it afterwards became common for even Roman citizens to engage in these bloody combats, and Nero at one show exhibited no less than four hundred senators and six hundred knights as gladiators; the fondness for this bloody spectacle continued till the reign of Constantine the Great, the first Christian emperor, by whom they were abolished about six hundred years after the original institution, and Gibbon reckons that several hundred, perhaps several thousand, victims were annually slaughtered in the great cities of the empire. As an instance of what might occur, Barnes recounts that during the triumph of Probus near seven hundred gladiators were reserved to shed each other's blood for the amusement of the Roman people, but, disdaining to shed their blood for the amusement of the populace, they killed their keepers, broke from their place of confinement, and filled the streets of Rome with blood and confusion; with such spectacles before them, it is not wonderful that murder was regarded as a matter of little consequence. Our word debate does not commonly imply evil, Barnes says, but denotes discussion for elucidating truth or for maintaining a proposition, as the debates in Congress, whereas the word in the original meant contention and strife and altercation, connected with anger and heated zeal, which would follow of course from malice and covetousness. Deceit denotes fraud and falsehood, and that this was common is plain: the Cretians are testified by one of the Greek poets to have been always liars, Juvenal charges the same on the Romans, asking what he should do at Rome since he cannot lie, and writers on India say that the word of a Hindoo even under oath is not to be regarded. Malignity signifies here not malignity in general but that particular species of it which consists in misinterpreting the words or actions of others, or putting the worst construction on their conduct; and whisperers are those who secretly and in a sly manner, by hints and innuendoes, detract from others or excite suspicion of them, not those who openly calumniate but that more dangerous class who give hints of evil, affect great knowledge, and communicate the evil report under an injunction of secrecy, knowing that it will be divulged; this class of people abounds everywhere, Barnes says, and there is scarcely any one more dangerous to the peace or happiness of society. Ellicott says that even as is rightly translated in the Authorised version, for as is not here equivalent to because but means rather just in like proportion as, the degree of God's punishment corresponding exactly to the degree of man's deflection from God. There is a play upon words here with reprobate in the clause following which cannot be retained in English, Ellicott says: as they reprobated the knowledge of God, so he gave them up to a reprobate mind, and as they would have nothing to do with him, so he would have nothing to do with them; reprobate means properly tried and found wanting, and therefore cast away as worthless. The word for knowledge here means exact, advanced, thorough knowledge, he adds, and they refused to hold the true idea of God so as to grow and increase in the knowledge of it; and things not convenient means what is unbecoming and disgraceful. Fornication is wanting in the best manuscripts and should be omitted, Ellicott says, as also the word implacable three verses later. Wickedness and maliciousness appear to be related together, so that the latter expresses rather the vicious disposition, vicious in the special sense of the disposition to do hurt to others, and the former rather the active exercise of it; and he notes that similar catalogues of sins are given in others of St Paul's epistles. By full of murder the Apostle means full of murderous thoughts, Ellicott says, and debate is the spirit of strife and contention generally, not, as the English would seem to imply, specially verbal contention. Robertson says the verb means they rejected after trial, just as the word is used of testing coins: they tested God at first and turned aside from him, and they had a dim memory that was a caricature. Unto a reprobate mind is a play on the earlier verb, Robertson says: they rejected God and God rejected their mental attitude and gave them over, so that they were left like an old abandoned building, the home of bats and snakes, to do those things which are not fitting, without God and in the darkness of unrestrained animal impulses; the phrase for what is not fitting was a technical term with the Stoics. Of the twenty-ninth verse he says the participle is a perfect passive denoting a state of completion, filled to the brim with four vices, unrighteousness, active wickedness, covetousness and maliciousness or inward viciousness of disposition; he notes the asyndeton, no connective in the lists in these verses, for dramatic effect, that the order of the words varies in the manuscripts, and that fornication is not genuine here, being absent from the oldest witnesses. Paul then changes from participle to adjective, Robertson says, with five substantives in the genitive, envy, murder, strife, malignity, the last being a rare word meaning a tendency to put a bad construction on things, a depravity of heart and malicious disposition; and he notes the combination of like-sounding words in envy and murder.

Clarke says it would perhaps be more literal to translate the verb, they did not search to retain God in their knowledge: they did not examine the evidences before them of his being and attributes, therefore God gave them over to an unsearching or undiscerning mind, for it is the same word in both places. They did not reflect on the proofs they had of the Divine nature, Clarke says, and God abandoned them to the operations of a mind incapable of reflection; how men of such powers and learning as many of the Greek and Roman philosophers and poets really were could reason so inconsecutively concerning things moral and divine is truly astonishing, but here we see the hand of a just and avenging God, for they abused their powers and God deprived them of the right use of them. Of the twenty-ninth verse Clarke glosses the terms one by one: unrighteousness is every vice contrary to justice; fornication is all commerce between the sexes out of the bounds of lawful marriage, though he notes that some of the best manuscripts omit the reading and others have uncleanness; wickedness is malignity, that which is oppressive to its possessor and to its object; covetousness, from words meaning more and I will have, is the intense love or lust of gain, the determination to be rich, the principle of a dissatisfied and discontented soul; maliciousness is malice or ill-will, what is radically and essentially vicious; envy, from a verb meaning to wither or pine away, is pain felt and malignity conceived at the sight of excellence or happiness in another, and Clarke prints in full Ovid's personification of Envy with Addison's translation, in which she chews a poisonous morsel, groans at a cheerful sight, never smiles but when the wretched weep, pines and sickens at another's joy, and bears her own tormentor in her breast. Murder, Clarke continues, is taking away the life of another by any means, or mortal hatred, for he that hates his brother in his heart is a murderer; debate is contention and discord, of which vile passion the Greeks made a goddess; deceit is lying and prevarication, from a verb meaning to take with a bait; malignity, from words meaning evil and custom, is bad customs founded in corrupt sentiment, producing evil habits supported by general usage, and is generally interpreted a malignity of mind which leads its possessor to put the worst construction on every action, ascribing to the best deeds the worst motives; and whisperers are secret detractors, those who under pretended secrecy carry about accusations against their neighbours, whether true or false, blasting their reputation by clandestine tittle-tattle, the whispering being well expressed by the sound of the Greek word itself. Wesley says God gave them up to an undiscerning mind, to do things not expedient, even the vilest abominations; that filled with all injustice stands in the first place of the list and unmercifulness in the last; that fornication includes here every species of uncleanness; and that the Greek word rendered maliciousness properly implies a temper which delights in hurting another, even without any advantage to itself.

John Chrysostom says that, lest he should seem to be hinting at them by delaying so long over the unnatural sin, Paul next passes on to other kinds of sins also, and for this cause carries on the whole of his discourse as of other persons; and as he always does when discoursing with believers about sins, wishing to show that they are to be avoided, he brings the Gentiles in. So here too he shows that it was to them the sins belonged, and deprives them of all excuse, Chrysostom says, for he says that their daring deeds came not of ignorance but of practice; and this is why he did not say, as they knew not God, but, as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, as much as to say that the sin was one of a perverted determination of obstinacy, more than of a sudden ravishment. It shows too that it was not the flesh, as some heretics say, but the mind, to the wicked lust whereof the sins belonged, and that it was thence the fount of the evils flowed, Chrysostom says; for since the mind is become undistinguishing, all else is then dragged out of course and overturned, when he is corrupted that held the reins. See how everything here is intensitive, he adds: Paul says being filled, and with all, and having named maliciousness in general he also further pursues the particulars, and these too in excess. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that if they had been willing to know him they would have followed the Divine laws, but now, choosing to deny their Maker, they were altogether stripped of his protecting care, whereby they recklessly ventured on every kind of wickedness. By unrighteousness, Theodoret says, Paul means that disposition which is diametrically opposed to righteousness, for from this springs every kind of reprehensible conduct, and he proceeds to detail its natural fruits.

debates: How to render the second half of the wordplay: Barnes gives a mind disapproved, rejected, reprobate; Clarke an unsearching or undiscerning mind, keeping the same word in both places; Ellicott takes reprobate as properly tried and found wanting and so cast away; Calvin's editor reviews Beza, Locke, Macknight and Doddridge, allows Doddridge the nearest, and settles for an unattesting mind not capable of bringing things to the test

Which of the two words means the disposition and which the act: Calvin, citing Ammonius, makes wickedness the practised doing of mischief and maliciousness the depravity of mind that harms a neighbour, and Ellicott agrees; Barnes reverses the pair, making wickedness the desire of injuring others and the other word the act rather than the desire, and cites Calvin for his gloss

Whether fornication belongs to the text: Barnes, Clarke, Wesley, Calvin and Theodoret all expound it, Clarke noting that some of the best manuscripts omit it and others read uncleanness; Ellicott says outright that it is wanting in the best manuscripts and should be omitted, along with implacable three verses later, and Robertson calls it not genuine here

Whom the catalogue is aimed at: Gill restricts it to the wise professors and moral instructors rather than the common people; Calvin holds that Paul turns here from one abomination not common to all and enumerates vices from which none could be found free; Chrysostom says Paul carries the whole discourse as of other persons so as not to seem to hint at his readers

Whether the fault lay in the flesh or the mind: Chrysostom insists it was not the flesh, as some heretics say, but the mind, since when he is corrupted who held the reins all else is dragged out of course; Barnes locates it in a determination to forget God, and denies any arbitrary decree of reprobation
outliers: Barnes's account of the amphitheatre, with Nero exhibiting four hundred senators and six hundred knights, and the revolt under Probus in which seven hundred gladiators killed their keepers and filled the streets with blood
Barnes's caution that the English word debate now means discussion for eliciting truth, as in Congress, where the original meant heated strife
Barnes's description of whisperers as more dangerous than open calumniators, communicating an evil report under an injunction of secrecy
Clarke's printing of Ovid's personification of Envy in Addison's translation, which never smiles but when the wretched weep and bears its own tormentor in its breast
Clarke's note that the sound of the Greek word for whisperers itself expresses the whispering
Robertson's figure of the reprobate mind as an old abandoned building, the home of bats and snakes
Robertson's observation that no connective appears anywhere in the list, for dramatic effect, and that envy and murder are paired as like-sounding words

30.pericope_label: Backbiters, haters of God and inventors of evil things, who approve those who do them

schools.summary: Gill says backbiters are those who more publicly defamed the characters of their neighbours, and hurt their good name, credit and reputation, though behind their backs; and that without understanding means without understanding of God, of his nature and worship, of things divine and even moral, being given up to a reprobate mind. Of the last verse Gill says that knowing the judgment of God means either the law of God, the law and light of nature, by which they might in some measure know the difference between good and evil and what was right and wrong, or the judiciary sentence of God against sin. Calvin says the word rendered haters of God means without doubt those who hate God, for there is no reason to take it in a passive sense, as hated of God, since Paul here proves men to be guilty by manifest vices; those then are designated who hate God, whose justice they seem to resist by doing wrong. Whisperers and backbiters are to be thus distinguished, Calvin says: the former, by secret accusations, break off the friendships of good men, inflame their minds with anger, defame the innocent and sow discords; the latter, through an innate malignity, spare the reputation of no one, and, as though they were instigated by the fury of evil-speaking, they revile the deserving as well as the undeserving. Calvin renders the next word villanies, since the Latin authors are wont to call notable injuries by that name, such as plunders, thefts, burnings and sorceries; and his editor says the three words seem to designate three properties of a proud spirit, disdainful or insolent, haughty and vainglorious. The first are those who treat others petulantly, contumeliously or insultingly, insolent being the most suitable word; the second is one who sets himself to view above others, the high and elevated, who exhibits himself as superior; and the third is the boaster, who assumes more than what belongs to him, or promises more than what he can perform, these three forms of pride being often seen in the world. Calvin himself renders the second word proud, since such being raised as it were on high look down with contempt on those below them and cannot bear to look on their equals; and boasters, he says, are they who swell with the empty wind of overweeningness. Of the words in the following verse the editor notes that faithless would perhaps be the most suitable rendering for covenant-breakers, Hesychius explaining the word as those who adhere not to compacts, and that to preserve the same negative form as the Greek the verse might be rendered unintelligent, unfaithful, unnatural, unappeasable, unmerciful; covenant-breakers are those who by their iniquities unloose the bands of society, or those in whom there is no sincerity or constancy of faith, who may be called truce-breakers. Those without natural affection, Calvin says, are they who have put off the first affections of nature towards their own relations; and as Paul mentions the want of mercy as an evidence of human nature being depraved, Augustine, arguing against the Stoics, concludes that mercy is a Christian virtue. Of the last verse Calvin says that, though the passage is variously explained, the correctest interpretation appears to him to be that men left nothing undone for the purpose of giving unbridled liberty to their sinful propensities; for having taken away all distinction between good and evil, they approved in themselves and in others those things which they knew displeased God and would be condemned by his righteous judgment. For it is the summit of all evils, Calvin says, when the sinner is so void of shame that he is pleased with his own vices and will not bear them to be reproved, and also cherishes them in others by his consent and approbation; this desperate wickedness is described in Scripture where it is said that they boast when they do evil, and that she has spread out her feet and gloried in her wickedness. He who is ashamed is as yet healable, Calvin says, but when such an impudence is contracted through a sinful habit, that vices and not virtues please us and are approved, there is no more any hope of reformation; and he sees that the Apostle meant here to condemn something more grievous and more wicked than the very doing of vices, which can be nothing but the summit of all wickedness, when wretched men, having cast away all shame, undertake the patronage of vices in opposition to the righteousness of God.

Barnes says backbiters are those who calumniate or speak ill of those who are absent, and that whisperers declare secretly and with great reserve the supposed faults of others while backbiters proclaim them publicly and avowedly. There is no charge which can be brought against men more severe than haters of God, Barnes says: it is the highest possible crime, yet a charge which the conduct of men will abundantly justify, and the truth of which all those experience who are brought to see their true character; to an awakened sinner there is often nothing more plain and painful than that he is a hater of God, his heart rising up against him and his law and his plan of saving men. Surely, if this be the native character of man, then it is far gone from original righteousness, and in no creed or confession of faith is there a more painful and humiliating representation given of human wickedness than in this declaration of an inspired apostle. Despiteful denotes those who abuse or treat with unkindness or disdain those who are present, Barnes says, whereas whisperers and backbiters calumniate the absent; pride is an inordinate self-esteem, an unreasonable conceit of one's superiority, and was particularly striking among the ancients, the sect of the Stoics being distinguished for it; men will be proud where they suppose none are superior, and it is only the religion that reveals a great and infinite God that will produce true humility. Boasters are those who arrogate to themselves what they do not possess and glory in it, closely connected with pride. Inventors of evil things doubtless refers to their seeking to find out new arts or plans to practise evil, new devices to gratify their lusts, new forms of luxury and vice, Barnes says; in cities of luxury this has always been done, for vices change their form, men become satiated, and the passions cease to be gratified with old forms of indulgence, so that men resort to new devices to rekindle their dying passions, and this was eminently true of ancient Rome, whose entertainments and games and theatres and cruel sports were little else than ever-varying inventions of evil things. Disobedient to parents expresses that they did not show to parents the honour and attention which was due, a crime of paganism in every age; and though among the Romans the duty of honouring parents was enjoined by the laws, it is not improbable that it was often violated, the feelings of pride leading to disregard, and the burden of providing for the aged and infirm producing neglect and open opposition. Of the following verse Barnes says that without natural affection denotes the want of affectionate regard towards their children, the attachment of parents to children being one of the strongest in nature, and nothing can overcome it but the most confirmed and established wickedness; yet the apostle charges on the heathen generally the want of this affection, referring doubtless to the practice so common among them of exposing their children or putting them to death. He assembles the evidence: the Canaanites sacrificed their sons and daughters, and Manasseh imitated them; among the ancient Persians it was a common custom to bury children alive; in most of the Grecian states infanticide was not merely permitted but enforced by law, the Spartan lawgiver ordaining that every child born should be examined by the ancient men of the tribe and, if found weak or deformed, thrown into a deep cavern at the foot of Mount Taygetus; Aristotle in his work on government enjoins the exposure of children naturally feeble and deformed in order to prevent an excess of population. But among all the nations of antiquity, Barnes says, the Romans were the most unrelenting: Romulus obliged the citizens to bring up all their male children and the eldest of the females, proof that the others were to be destroyed, and expressly authorised the destruction of all children that were deformed, requiring only that the parents exhibit them to their five nearest neighbours; the law of the Twelve Tables sanctioned the same practice; Minucius Felix describes the Romans exposing their infants to wild beasts and birds, or strangling them after the most miserable manner; Pliny the elder defends the right of parents to destroy their children on the ground of keeping the population within proper bounds; and Tertullian in his apology charges the Roman people with infant murder, and with choosing some of the cruellest kinds of death for their own children, such as drowning, or starving with cold or hunger, or exposing to the mercy of dogs, dying by the sword being too sweet a death for children. Nor was this practice arrested in the Roman government until the time of Constantine, the first Christian prince, Barnes says; the Phoenicians and Carthaginians were in the habit of sacrificing infants to the gods, and the crime is no less common among modern pagan nations, as he shows from travellers' accounts of Peking and of the Hindoo provinces. Of the last verse Barnes says that the Gentiles had a moral sense, or were capable of knowing the will of God in this case, their means being their own reason, their conscience and an observation of the effects of depravity. The word judgment denotes the declared sentiment of God that such things deserved death; it does not mean his inflictions or his statutes, but that God judged that they which did such things ought to die, and as they were aware of this it showed their guilt in still persevering. The word death is often used to denote punishment, and does not mean here that these deserved capital punishment from the civil magistrate, but that they knew they were evil and offensive to God. To have pleasure in those who commit sin is a grievous aggravation, Barnes says, for it greatly heightens guilt when we excite others to sin and seduce them from the ways of innocence; men do not commit sin often alone, they need the countenance of others, they join hand in hand and become confederate in iniquity, and all social sins are of this class. The charges the apostle makes here were evidently well known, Barnes adds, for he does not even appeal to their writings for proof, and a writer would not advance charges in this manner unless he was confident that they could not be denied; and they are abundantly sustained by the heathen writers themselves. He quotes Livy on the age of Augustus, that Rome had increased by her virtues until now, when we can neither bear our vices nor their remedy, and Seneca, one of the purest moralists of Rome, that all is full of criminality and vice, that the lust of sin increases daily and shame is daily more extinguished, that vice no longer hides itself but stalks forth before all eyes, and that innocence is no longer seldom but has wholly ceased to exist. Ellicott says that haters of God should rather perhaps be rendered hated by God, since there seem to be no examples of the active sense; the Apostle apparently throws in one emphatic word summing up the catalogue as far as it has gone, and then resumes with a new class of sins, having hitherto spoken chiefly of sins of malice and turning now to sins of pride. The three words that follow correspond to the distinction between act, thought and word, Ellicott says: the first implies distinctly insolence in outward bearing, the second is a strong self-esteem mixed with contempt for others, and the third is used especially of boastfulness or braggadocio in language. Without understanding means without moral or spiritual understanding, incapable of discriminating between right and wrong, expedient and inexpedient; and without natural affection means the affection founded upon natural relationship, as between parent and child or husband and wife, in illustration of which we may remember that infanticide and divorce were very common at this period. Of the last verse Ellicott says the word for knowing is again the word for full or thorough knowledge, so that it is with full knowledge of the sentence of eternal death which is in store for them; and they show that it is no mere momentary yielding to the force of temptation or of passion, but a radical perversion of conscience and reason, by the fact that they not only practise such things themselves but in cold blood commend and applaud those who practise them. Robertson says Paul changes the construction again to twelve substantives and adjectives that give vivid touches to this composite photograph of the God-abandoned soul. Whisperers is an old onomatopoetic word meaning to speak into the ear; backbiters is found nowhere else except in Hermas, and means talkers back whether secretly or openly; hateful to God is an old word which all the ancient examples take in the passive sense, and so probably here, the Vulgate reading it so; insolent is an old word for the agent from a verb meaning to give insult; haughty means to appear above others, arrogant in thought and conduct; boastful, from a root meaning wandering, means empty pretenders, swaggerers, braggarts; and inventors of evil things means inventors of new forms of vice, as Nero was, Robertson citing Tacitus on Sejanus and Virgil. Of the following verse he says covenant-breakers is another paronomasia, meaning men false to their engagements, as Sanday and Headlam put it, who treat covenants as a scrap of paper; without natural affection is a late word from a term for the love of kindred; unmerciful is a late word found only here in the New Testament; and some manuscripts add implacable, carried in from the second letter to Timothy. It is a terrible picture of the effects of sin on the lives of men and women, Robertson says, and he relates that a missionary of Canton reported a Chinaman who, getting hold of this chapter, declared that Paul could not have written it but only a modern missionary who had been to China; it is drawn to the life because Paul knew Pagan Graeco-Roman civilisation. Of the last verse Robertson says the heathen knows that God condemns such evil practices, and that the verb rendered consent is a late one for hearty approval; it is a tragedy of American city government, he adds, that so many of the officials are proven to be hand in glove with the underworld of law-breakers.

Clarke says backbiters means those who speak against others, false accusers and slanderers; haters of God means atheists, contemners of sacred things, maligners of providence and scorners, and it seems to be the finishing part of a diabolic character; despiteful means those who treat others with injurious insolence, stormy and boisterous, abusing both the characters and persons of those over whom they can have any power; proud means they who are continually exalting themselves and depressing others, magnifying themselves at the expense of their neighbours, and wishing all men to receive their sayings as oracles; and boasters means self-assuming, vainglorious and arrogant men. Inventors of evil things, Clarke says, means those who have invented destructive customs, rites and fashions, such as the different religious ceremonies among the Greeks and Romans, the orgies of Bacchus, the mysteries of Ceres, the lupercalia and the feasts of the Bona Dea, multitudes of which destructive and abominable ceremonies are to be found in every part of the heathen worship; and though filial affection was certainly more recommended and cultivated than many other virtues, there are many instances on record of the grossest violation of this great branch of the law of nature. Of the following verse Clarke says without understanding means persons incapable of comprehending what was spoken, destitute of capacity for spiritual things; covenant-breakers means persons who could be bound by no oath, because properly speaking they had no God to witness or avenge their misconduct, for as every covenant is made as in the presence of God, he that opposes the being and doctrine of God is incapable of being bound by any covenant and can give no pledge for his conduct. Without natural affection means without that attachment which nature teaches the young of all animals to have to their mothers, and the mothers to have for their young, Clarke says, the heathens in general having made no scruple to expose the children they did not think proper to bring up, and to despatch their parents when they were grown old or past labour. Implacable, from a negative prefix and the word for a libation, refers to the custom among all nations of pouring out wine as a libation to their gods when making a treaty, to appease the angry gods and reconcile them to the contracting parties, so that the word shows a deadly enmity, the highest pitch of an unforgiving spirit, persons who would not make reconciliation either to God or man; and unmerciful means those who were incapable, through the deep-rooted wickedness of their own nature, of showing mercy to an enemy brought under their power. Of the last verse Clarke says the judgment of God is the grand rule of right which God has revealed to every man, the knowledge of which he has, less or more, given to every nation of the world, relative to honouring parents, taking care of their own offspring and keeping their engagements; in the worst states of heathenism this great principle has been acknowledged, but through the prevalence of corruption in the heart this law, though acknowledged, was not obeyed, and the corruption increased so that those were highest in repute who had cast off all restraints of this kind, so that they even delighted in them and highly applauded and gladly associated with those transgressors, which argues the very highest pitch of moral depravity. Clarke closes the chapter by observing that it gives one of the finest views of the Gospel of Christ to be met with anywhere, God's method of saving a lost world in a way which that world could never have imagined, a scheme as worthy of God as it is necessary for man, in which there are no excluding clauses, being for the Jew and for the Greek, for the wise and for the unwise, and for all the nations of the universe; and that the necessity of it appears in the deep-rooted and widely extended corruption of the nations of the earth, in which almost every trace of original righteousness had been obliterated, the proofs of God's eternal power were disregarded, a vain philosophy was substituted for divine truth, and the heart was contaminated with every vice. Wesley says whisperers are such as secretly defame others, backbiters such as speak against others behind their back, and haters of God such as are rebels against him, deniers of his providence, or accusers of his justice in their adversities, having an inward heart-enmity to his justice and holiness; and inventors of evil things means inventors of new pleasures, new ways of gain and new arts of hurting, particularly in war. Of covenant-breakers Wesley says it is well known that the Romans, as a nation, from the very beginning of their commonwealth, never made any scruple of vacating altogether the most solemn engagement if they did not like it, though made by their supreme magistrate in the name of the whole people, for they only gave up the general who had made it and then supposed themselves to be at full liberty. The custom of exposing their own new-born children to perish by cold, hunger or wild beasts, which so generally prevailed in the heathen world, particularly among the Greeks and Romans, Wesley says, was an amazing instance of being without natural affection, as is also that of killing their aged and helpless parents. Of the last verse he says that to have pleasure in those who practise such things is the highest degree of wickedness, for a man may be hurried by his passions to do the thing he hates, but he that has pleasure in those that do evil loves wickedness for wickedness' sake, and hereby he encourages them in sin and heaps the guilt of others upon his own head.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus glosses the list term by term: by fornication he signifies intercourse independent of marriage; by wickedness, a savage disposition; by covetousness, the desire of getting more and more, and the carrying off of what does not belong to oneself; by maliciousness, the bent of the mind to evil, and the planning of injury to a neighbour. Bitter is the passion of envy, Theodoret says, and unable to bear the prosperity of a neighbour; it is the parent of murder and conceives deceit, for wounded by envy, and calling in deceit as a helpmate, Cain led his brother forth into the field and feared not to slay him. By malignant he means such as exercise their thoughts in laying snares and designing mischief to those around them; by whisperers, such as privily murmur into the ear abuse of others standing by; by backbiters, such as recklessly indulge in the scandal of the absent; by haters of God, such as are inimically disposed towards him; by despiteful, such as are given to petulance and insolence; and by proud, such as are overmuch elevated by every superiority they possess. Of the last verse Theodoret says that we have shown how nature teaches us to choose good and avoid evil, but these nevertheless think it not enough to commit such things unless they also commend such as do so likewise, which is the last excess of wickedness, seeing that they ought not only to hate the transgressions of others, but with loathing to reprobate even their own.

debates: Whether haters of God is active or passive: Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all take the active sense, Barnes calling it the highest possible crime and the most humiliating representation of human wickedness in any creed, and Calvin says there is no reason for the passive since Paul is proving men guilty by manifest vices; Ellicott answers that there seem to be no examples of the active sense and prefers hated by God, and Robertson says all the ancient examples are passive, the Vulgate reading it so

What inventors of evil things means: Barnes takes it of new forms of luxury and vice devised when the old cease to gratify; Clarke of invented religious observances, the orgies of Bacchus, the mysteries of Ceres and the lupercalia; Robertson of new forms of vice such as Nero devised; Wesley of new pleasures, new ways of gain and new arts of hurting, particularly in war

Whether whisperers and backbiters differ by secrecy: Barnes distinguishes them sharply, the first declaring faults secretly and with great reserve, the second publicly and avowedly, and Calvin makes the same division; Robertson refuses it, glossing the second word as talkers back whether secretly or openly

What the closing clause adds to the doing of the vices: Calvin holds Paul meant to condemn something more grievous, the patronage of vice against the righteousness of God, and adds that he who is ashamed is as yet healable; Wesley says such a man loves wickedness for wickedness' sake; Ellicott finds a radical perversion of conscience rather than a momentary yielding, since the approval is given in cold blood; Theodoret calls it the last excess

Whether implacable belongs to the list: Clarke expounds it from the libation poured at the making of a treaty, as a deadly enmity that will be reconciled neither to God nor man; Robertson says some manuscripts carry it in from the second letter to Timothy, and Ellicott had already directed that it be omitted
outliers: Barnes's dossier on the exposure of infants, from the Spartan cavern at Taygetus and the rule of Romulus to Tertullian's charge that the Romans chose drowning, cold and dogs as being crueller than the sword
Barnes's quotation of Livy, that Rome had so increased by her virtues that she could bear neither her vices nor their remedy
Barnes's quotation of Seneca, that vice no longer hides itself but stalks forth before all eyes, and that innocence has wholly ceased to exist
Calvin's note that Augustine, arguing against the Stoics from Paul's listing the want of mercy among the marks of depravity, concludes that mercy is a Christian virtue
Clarke's derivation of implacable from the libation of wine poured out to the gods at the making of a treaty
Robertson's report of a Chinaman at Canton who, reading this chapter, declared that Paul could not have written it but only a modern missionary who had been to China
Theodoret's tracing of envy as the parent of murder, with Cain calling in deceit as a helpmate to lead his brother into the field
